visits.text: St Nicholas Market, or St Nicks to Bristolians, has been open since 1743 and brings together the city's largest collection of independent businesses beneath its covered halls. It is divided into three sections: the Glass Arcade, the Covered Market and the Exchange, with more than 60 stalls. If you are there on the first Friday of the month, the open-air street food market on Wine Street is not to be missed. Inside, look for Pieminister's handmade beef or vegetable pies and the stalls selling local Somerset cheeses.

The Clifton neighbourhood, just above the centre, is home to several quality delicatessens and cheese shops. Papadeli on Whiteladies Road is a reference point for cakes, salads and its cheese counter. If you're there on a Saturday morning, Whiteladies Farmers' Market is where the city's chefs stock up on local produce.

activities.text: Bristol has several working gin distilleries in the city centre. Psychopomp, housed in a former grocer's shop on St Michael's Hill, is one of the best known and offers tasting workshops and “create your own gin” masterclasses. The larger Six O'Clock Gin has a distillery in Thornbury, about 19 km from Bristol, a 25-minute drive, offering guided tours, as well as a bar and shop on The Glassboat beside the Avon. Bristol takes gin seriously: do not leave without a bottle.

Several award-winning gastropubs occupy Bristol's streets. Bristol Lido, wrapped around its heated Victorian pool, is probably the city's most original restaurant: you can swim before dining in magnificent surroundings. The menu relies on local produce from Somerset and Devon. Book your dinner—and if you're tempted, the Swim & Dine package includes pool, spa and restaurant.

visits.text: The British Library, opened in its current building near King's Cross in 1998 after 15 years of construction, is the largest public building constructed in the United Kingdom in the 20th century. It holds more than 170 million items on 625 km of shelving and receives a copy of every publication produced in the United Kingdom and Ireland - around 3 million items a year. For visitors, one room stands out: the Treasures Gallery (free), where you will find two of the four original copies of the 1215 Magna Carta, a Gutenberg Bible from 1455 (one of 49 surviving copies), the 8th-century Lindisfarne Gospels, the 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus, Shakespeare's First Folio of 1623, and Paul McCartney's lyrics for Yesterday scribbled on an envelope. The room is kept in dim light to protect these treasures - allow 1.5 to 2 hours to see everything properly.

activities.text: If you're interested in research, request a reader's pass to access the reading rooms. Otherwise, the museum shop offers high-quality reproductions of certain manuscripts.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

visits.text: The British Museum opened in 1759 - it's the world's first public national museum. Its 8 million objects span two million years of human history. The Rosetta Stone, its most visited object, is displayed in Room 4: carved in 196 BC, it bears the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. It was this parallel that enabled Champollion to decipher hieroglyphs in 1822, opening ancient Egypt to modern understanding. It arrived in London in 1802 after French capitulation in Egypt - its potential return to Egypt is an active debate. Admission is free, plan at least 2.5 hours.

The Great Court, covered by a glass dome designed by Norman Foster and opened in 2000, is Europe's largest covered public square. It surrounds the circular Reading Room from 1857, where Marx, Lenin and Darwin worked. The north wing houses the Greek rooms with the Parthenon friezes, which Greece has been claiming back since 1983.

activities.text: If the collections are too vast to digest alone, several operators offer themed guided tours of 1.5 to 2 hours concentrating on the 20 most important works. The museum app offers free self-guided audio tours in several languages. The Bloomsbury neighbourhood around the museum deserves a walk - its 18th-century Georgian squares are among London's finest.

visits.text: Brodick Castle offers an unexpected diversion among its antique furnishings: a Victorian-inspired game room is part of the tour. The current building took its present form in 1844, above the bay, while the estate rises toward Arran’s hills. Save this visit for after the hike if you return early enough; last admission is at 4 p.m., so time your descent from Goatfell accordingly.

activities.text: Set out early from Cladach to climb Goatfell, with lunch and warm clothing in your backpack. The classic route is 10.5 km round-trip, takes 4 hours 30 minutes to 6 hours, and reaches 874 m; the final stretch winds between granite boulders. A modest elevation on paper does not make this a short walk. Turn back before the summit if the wind or visibility worsens, and allow plenty of time for the descent.

If you have to choose between one more visit and your ferry, head straight to Brodick. The service to Ardrossan takes cars and passengers back to the mainland; book using the correct vehicle category. Check the service status before leaving Machrie Moor and arrive at check-in at least 30 minutes before departure.

Ayrshire and Arran in 3 Days: Castles and Goatfell

visits.text: Despite its medieval appearance, Buckfast Abbey is largely a modern reconstruction. Monks who returned to the site rebuilt the church, which is still used by a Benedictine community: this is no ruin frozen in time for visitors. Enter quietly, check service times, and postpone exploring the interior if a service is underway.

activities.text: When the lavender blooms, the gardens at Buckfast Abbey add their fragrance to your stop. The grounds include a medicinal plant garden and a sensory garden, offering another perspective on the site beyond its religious architecture. Follow the open paths and check at reception for access conditions in the different areas.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: Buckingham Palace became the official royal residence in 1837 under Queen Victoria - before her, sovereigns lodged at St James's Palace. The East facade you see from The Mall was redesigned in 1913 by Sir Aston Webb, along with the Queen Victoria Memorial in front of the gates. In summer (generally July to September), the State Rooms open to the public - book online, morning slots are less crowded.

activities.text: The Changing of the Guard takes place on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays at 11am on the Palace forecourt, for a ceremony lasting about 45 minutes. Arrive 60 to 90 minutes early for a good spot - the steps of the Victoria Memorial offer the best elevated view. The ceremony can be cancelled in heavy rain, so check the official calendar that morning on the Household Division website.

Cross St James's Park towards Trafalgar Square. This 23-hectare royal park offers an unusual view of Buckingham Palace from the central bridge - with the lawns and the lake, it is one of the best viewpoints over the palace.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: If the church is open, step inside: the medieval glass shields lined up in the chancel are among the oldest surviving stained glass in this part of historic Berkshire. Village of a few houses, church rarely closed, free entry. The 12th-century nave and Early English chancel (around 1240) form a restrained, intact whole.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop

places.name: Burford

visits.text: The High Street slopes down to the Windrush, lining up buildings from the 15th century to Georgian fronts almost without a break. This is what they call the 'gateway to the Cotswolds'. St John the Baptist Church, founded in 1175, keeps bullet holes in the wall from 1649: Cromwell had imprisoned 340 Leveller mutineers there, executing three of them in the churchyard.

activities.text: The English pronounce Burford 'burr-furd', not 'byoo-furd'. The High Street is one of the few to earn the label 'finest in England' without blushing: 800 metres of unbroken period facades. The Royal Oak does game pies worth the stop. The Tolsey Museum, in the hall above the pillars, is free and tells the town's story in 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: Welsh Marches, Cotswolds and Bath in 11 days

map_keywords: St John the Baptist Church Burford

visits.text: Norwich was England's second city after London at the time of the Norman Conquest—that's why William the Conqueror immediately built a castle here. The current castle, with its Victorian facade (19th-century cladding replaced the original Norman stone), is now an excellent museum covering regional history, the Iceni and Boudica, the Vikings, and Norfolk arts. Take time to explore the dungeons and galleries.

Elm Hill is Norwich's most complete medieval street, and one of England's finest. Nearly all the buildings you see were constructed after the 1507 fire that ravaged over 700 houses in the city—only Briton's Arms, a thatched inn dating from 1347, survived the flames. Walking up the cobbled street, glance at the blue plaque of Pettus House (1550) and the stairs of merchants' houses whose backs gave directly onto the River Wensum.

Norwich Cathedral is one of England's great medieval cathedrals, begun in 1096 by Bishop Herbert de Losinga. Its 96-metre spire is surpassed only by Salisbury. It houses the world's largest collection of carved medieval vault bosses—over 1,000 painted bosses adorn nave and cloisters. The cloisters, England's largest, are worth a good half-hour alone. During summer, Shakespeare plays are performed here.

Holkham Beach is breathtaking—at low tide, an expanse of white, smooth sand opens as far as the eye can see, framed by pine forests planted in the late 19th century by the 2nd Earl of Leicester to protect farmland from wind. It was in this golden light that Gwyneth Paltrow walked during the final scenes of Shakespeare in Love (1998). Holkham National Nature Reserve covers 3,900 hectares and welcomes large formations of pink-footed geese in winter. Arrive early in summer.

Holkham Hall is a Palladian mansion built between 1734 and 1764 by Thomas Coke, 1st Earl of Leicester, to designs by William Kent. The marble hall with its 15-metre pressed-stucco dome is one of 18th-century England's finest interiors. The state rooms house canvases by Rubens, Van Dyck, Claude Lorrain and Gainsborough. The 25,000-acre park with its lake and red deer can be visited by bike or on foot.

Wells-next-the-Sea is an active port with a colourful quay lined with fishing boats and smoked fish shops. The town added 'next-the-sea' to its name in the 19th century to distinguish itself from other Wells. Stroll along the quay, climb to the beach huts at the end of the embankment, and listen for the tide siren—a wartime relic that still sounds to warn bathers when the sea rises.

Walsingham is a pilgrimage village active since the Middle Ages—its 12th-century Augustinian priory ruins and Catholic and Anglican shrines make it one of England's most important Marian devotion sites. To reach it from Wells, take the Wells & Walsingham Light Railway, a 4-mile narrow-gauge steam train—the longest railway of this gauge in England.

Blakeney is one of Norfolk's most beautiful coastal villages, with its flint houses and quay opening onto an estuary of great beauty. At low tide, the harbour empties almost completely, leaving boats stranded on mudflats. Climb to St Nicholas church, built in 13th-century flint brick with a secondary tower that served as a lighthouse for sailors.

Cley next the Sea, just east of Blakeney, has a 17th-century windmill on the edge of the marshes that has become the photographic symbol of North Norfolk. The mouth of the River Glaven and surrounding marshes are a premier bird reserve—bring binoculars.

activities.text: Late afternoon, arrive in Burnham Market to explore the village. This 'Chelsea of Norfolk' as locals call it is organized around a long grassy green flanked by Georgian brick houses. The independent shops, galleries and pubs make it a pleasant stop for an evening. It's an excellent base for the next two days on Norfolk's north coast.
Walk along the North Norfolk coast from Burnham Market

The boat trip to Blakeney Point to observe grey and common seals is one of Norfolk's most popular nature outings. The sand spit of Blakeney Point, managed by the National Trust since 1912, hosts one of Britain's largest grey seal colonies. Trips depart from Blakeney quay and last about 1.5 hours. Book ahead in high season.

The North Norfolk coast is best walked on the Norfolk Coast Path. From Burnham Market, the section to Holkham or Wells offers magnificent views over salt marshes and dunes. Allow 2 to 3 hours for a loop.

visits.text: Burnham-on-Crouch lives up to its nickname: the 'Cowes of the east coast'. Four sailing and yacht clubs line the River Crouch, and 'Burnham Week' - one of the UK's longest annual regattas - takes place here in late August-early September.

Burnham's historic quay is lined with red-roofed houses, old pubs, and boatyards still in operation. The Burnham-on-Crouch Museum on the quay houses a modest collection on local maritime history and prehistoric dwellings on the Dengie peninsula.

activities.text: In summer, take the ferry to Wallasea Island from Burnham-on-Crouch. Wallasea is a wetland nature reserve created by the RSPB on land reclaimed from the sea - a windswept landscape that is unusual and little visited.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Kipling wrote when he first saw the house: 'That's She! The Only She! Make an honest woman of her quick!' Bateman's, a Jacobean house from 1634 in Burwash, was his residence from 1902 until his death in 1936. He wrote Puck of Pook's Hill and the poem 'If' here. The dining room with its eighteenth-century silver-leather hangings is the finest room in the house.

The garden at Bateman's, clipped box and mill wheels by the Dudwell: Kipling felt like an English country gentleman here. The thirteenth-century water mill on the property inspired his Puck stories. You can walk to the ponds through the 300-acre estate.

activities.text: Walk around Burwash village before leaving: a bronze statue of Kipling unveiled in 2018 stands in the village centre, piercing gaze. The village preserves seventeenth-century timber-framed façades and a pub, The Bear Inn, that has changed little since the writer's time.

days_plan.itin_title: Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports

places.name: Bury St Edmunds

visits.text: The ruins of Bury St Edmunds Abbey stand at the heart of the Abbey Gardens, a public park open daily. This was one of the richest and most powerful Benedictine abbeys in England—founded in 1020 by King Cnut to house the relics of the martyr-king Edmund, killed by Vikings in 869. After Canterbury and Little Walsingham, the abbey was England's third most-visited pilgrimage site. In 1214, the English barons gathered here in secret to swear opposition to King John, an episode that led directly to Magna Carta. Henry VIII dissolved it in 1539 and had it systematically dismantled—historians reckon that if the abbey had survived, Bury St Edmunds would today be larger than Durham or Lincoln. Two remarkable medieval gateways remain: the fourteenth-century Great Gate and the twelfth-century Norman Tower, which still serves as the cathedral's bell tower.

St Edmundsbury Cathedral, right next to the ruins, deserves a detailed visit. Its nave was rebuilt around 1503 by John Wastell—the same architect who completed the fan vaulting of King's College Chapel in Cambridge. The building only gained cathedral status in 1914, when the diocese was created. The Millennium Tower, finished in 2005, at last gives it the profile of a great cathedral. Don't miss Elisabeth Frink's bronze statue of St Edmund, which stands in the precinct.

The archaeological village of West Stow, eight kilometres northwest of Bury St Edmunds, is a full-scale reconstruction of a fifth- to seventh-century Anglo-Saxon village. Excavations from 1965 to 1972 uncovered the foundations of a complete settlement, and houses have since been rebuilt on their original locations using authentic materials and techniques. It's one of the few sites in Europe where you can step inside buildings from that era and understand concretely what daily life looked like 1,500 years ago. The site is surrounded by a fifty-hectare nature reserve on the River Lark.

Make the detour to Ickworth House, seven kilometres southwest of Bury St Edmunds: it's one of England's most eccentric country houses, and it truly deserves the description. The 4th Earl of Bristol began this building in 1796 with a fixed idea: a central rotunda 30 metres high, flanked by two curved wings to display the paintings and sculptures brought back from his travels in Italy. The result looks like nothing else. The property belongs to the National Trust—allow time for the Italianate gardens and the grand landscaped park, which are worth as much as the house itself.

Newmarket, about 24 kilometres west of Bury St Edmunds, a 20-minute drive away, is the world capital of horse racing. The town has hosted official races since 1622 - Charles II himself came here to race his own mount. The National Stud, the stud farms and Palace House (the former royal residence converted into a horse-racing museum) are open to the public. If you visit on a weekday, you will see the horses training early in the morning on the Heath, a rather unique experience.

activities.text: Stroll through Bury St Edmunds' historic centre in the evening, between Angel Hill and the Victorian Corn Exchange. The town has an active covered market and a collection of Georgian pubs that make you want to linger. Try the local beers from the Greene King brewery, whose warehouses have been based in the town since 1799.

visits.text: Forty thousand hexagonal columns thrust up from a volcanic eruption 60 million years ago, UNESCO-listed in 1986. Legend says Finn McCool built the causeway to go challenge a Scottish giant. The geological truth is more brutal: basalt that fractured as it cooled. Allow two hours including the National Trust visitor centre. Walk from Bushmills if you want to save the parking fee, it's 30 minutes on the red trail.

The wind lashes the bridge's planks, 30 metres above the Atlantic. The bridge is approximately 15 km from Bushmills, a 15-minute drive. Salmon fishermen have been laying rope bridges to the islet for more than 350 years, with the first documented one dating from 1755. Fishing stopped in 2002 because there were not enough fish. The current structure was tested to ten tonnes in 2000, so breathe. Online booking is compulsory, adult tickets cost £15, and it is a 20-minute walk from the car park.

activities.text: World's oldest licensed distillery, Old Bushmills has held its licence since 1608. The tour ends with a tasting of three whiskeys, including Black Bush. Allow 1h, booking advised at weekends. If you're driving, the tasting can be taken as miniatures. Shop decently stocked for gifts.

visits.text: The fells reflect in Buttermere's calm water with almost unreal sharpness in still weather. This 2 km lake is framed by Fleetwith Pike, Haystacks (favourite fell of the great walker Alfred Wainwright, whose ashes rest here) and Red Pike. Less visited than the southern lakes, it retains an untouched wild character.

activities.text: 7 km around the lake: doable in 2 hours 30 minutes for an average walker, without significant elevation. The circuit includes forest passages, a tunnel cut through rock and several viewpoints over Crummock Water. The Bridge Hotel in the village sells packed lunches - handy for a picnic en route.

Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes and Writers’ Homes

visits.text: Buxton is England's highest market town - 300 meters elevation, a cutting cold in winter, and geothermal springs flowing at 28°C for 5,000 years. The Romans already understood the deal when they settled here in AD 78 under the name Aquae Arnemetiae. The golden age came in 1780 when the 5th Duke of Devonshire built the Crescent, an imposing Georgian facade directly inspired by Bath's Royal Crescent - some believe Buxton's is actually more accomplished. Restored and reopened in 2020 as a five-star hotel-spa, the building can also be visited via an exhibition on its thermal history.

Buxton's Opera House is a gem of Edwardian architecture - designed in 1903 by Frank Matcham, the prolific architect who designed dozens of the UK's finest theaters. The renovated interior is sumptuous: ceiling paintings, gilding, semicircular balconies. It's also, according to its inscription, the highest theater in England. The Beatles performed here in 1963 in the adjacent Octagon. If there's a show during your visit, get a ticket.

The Devonshire Dome - a former ducal stable converted into a hospital in the 19th century, now a university campus - houses a 44-meter diameter dome, one of the largest unsupported in Europe, wider than Rome's Pantheon. The adjacent Pavilion Gardens, 9 hectares laid out in 1871 along the Wye, are ideal for a late afternoon stroll.

activities.text: Poole's Cavern, west of town, is a natural limestone cave formed two million years ago. It contains Derbyshire's largest stalactite and poached-egg-shaped stalagmites - a rare formation due to aragonite deposits. Guided tours last about 45 minutes. On the way out, climb through Grin Low Country Park to Solomon's Temple, a Victorian folly from 1896 erected on a Bronze Age burial mound: the view over the town below and the Peak District hills is the region's best panorama.

Before leaving, fill your water bottle at St Ann's Well fountain, opposite the Crescent - it's Buxton mineral water, the same sold in bottles throughout the UK, flowing here at 28°C with free access. Nothing stops you from joining the queue with locals filling their containers.

days_plan.itin_title: Midlands and Peak District Road Trip: Heritage and Wild Landscapes

visits.text: Marvel at Caernarfon Castle, the mightiest of Edward I's Welsh fortresses and a UNESCO World Heritage site that has dominated this strategic spot for over 700 years. The castle's unique polygonal towers and banded masonry were deliberately designed to echo the walls of Constantinople, emphasizing Edward's imperial ambitions. This is where the investiture of Princes of Wales has taken place since 1911, most recently for Prince Charles in 1969.

Climb the castle's towers for spectacular views over the Menai Strait, the town's slate rooftops, and the mountains of Snowdonia rising dramatically to the east. The Eagle Tower, the largest of the castle's distinctive towers, offers the most impressive panorama and contains exhibitions on the castle's history and the Welsh princes it was built to suppress. The castle walls, remarkably intact after seven centuries, allow visitors to walk above the medieval town.

Explore the charming town of Caernarfon, where the castle forms a striking backdrop to narrow streets lined with independent shops, cafés and traditional Welsh pubs. The town walls, largely intact, connect to the castle. From the quay, look out over the harbour, where boats depart for trips along the Menai Strait. The Welsh language thrives here, giving visitors an authentic taste of Welsh culture and heritage.

activities.text: Photograph the castle from the town streets where medieval towers frame views of shops and daily Welsh life

visits.text: Cambridge was born from a brawl. In 1209, students driven out of Oxford after a clash with the townspeople crossed England and founded a university here, on the banks of the Cam. Since then, this place has produced more than 120 Nobel laureates—more than most countries. Start by getting lost in the streets: King's Parade, Senate House, Trinity Street. Every facade teaches architectural history, every gateway conceals a courtyard. Plan to enter at least two colleges—opening hours vary, so check the day before.

The Backs is the ribbon of gardens and lawns behind the colleges, riverside—the finest view of Cambridge, visible only from a punt or on foot. King's College Chapel (begun 1446 under Henry VI) dominates everything with its vertical limestone facade. Look up at the carved fan-vaulted ceiling inside—some historians consider it the finest Gothic ceiling in the world. Clare Bridge, the oldest surviving bridge over the Cam, dates from the 1630s: examine its 14 decorative stone balls closely. One is deliberately incomplete—legend says the architect, inadequately paid, sliced off a piece as his fee.

The Fitzwilliam Museum is one of Britain's finest art and antiquities museums—and admission is free. Its foundation story alone is worth the visit: in 1816, Viscount Richard Fitzwilliam bequeathed Cambridge 144 paintings (including works by Rembrandt, Titian, and Veronese), over 10,000 printed books and 130 illuminated manuscripts, plus £100,000 to build the museum. Architect George Basevi won the 1834 competition with a neoclassical design inspired by ancient Greece—then fell to his death from scaffolding at Ely Cathedral in 1845, never seeing the 1848 opening. Today the collection exceeds 500,000 objects: Egyptian antiquities worthy of the British Museum, canvases by Monet, Picasso, Cézanne, Van Dyck, and a major collection of Turner watercolours. Allow at least 90 minutes.

Cambridge University Botanic Garden spans 16 hectares south of the city centre. Founded in 1831 by John Stevens Henslow—the professor who encouraged Darwin to board the Beagle—it shelters over 8,000 plant species. It's also an active climate change research site. Late afternoon light on the beds is magnificent. Allow 1 to 1.5 hours.

Grantchester is a small village 3km south of Cambridge, reachable on foot along the river in 45 minutes. Poet Rupert Brooke lived here just before World War I and wrote in exile the poem 'The Old Vicarage, Grantchester' that made him famous. The village and its riverside pub remain remarkably unspoiled. If you want speed, take a punt from Cambridge.

Houghton Mill is one of the last working watermills on the Great Ouse, managed by the National Trust. Built in the 17th century, it was still grinding grain into the 1930s. You can watch the millstones turn on certain weekends and buy flour milled on site. The adjoining village of Houghton is a concentration of half-timbered cottages—ideal for a morning stroll.

St Ives is a small town on the Great Ouse with a 15th-century stone medieval bridge—on which stands a chapel, extremely rare in England. Wander along the waterfront to the central market, active since the Middle Ages. The town owes its name to a 4th-century Persian bishop whose relics were supposedly discovered here in the 10th century—one of Cambridgeshire's most unlikely stories.

Wimpole Hall, about fifteen kilometres southwest of Cambridge, is Cambridgeshire's largest mansion. Its architectural history reads like a soap opera: built from 1640, remodelled by James Gibbs in the 1710s, then Henry Flitcroft around 1749, then John Soane in the 1790s. But the real story is its last owner: Elsie Bambridge, Rudyard Kipling's only daughter. She bought the ruined estate with her father's inheritance and literary royalties—so The Jungle Book and Kim paid to restore the roof. She had a notorious temperament: when a couple once picnicked too near the house, she had her own picnic prepared on their neighbours' lawn. Upon her death in 1976, she left everything to the National Trust. The 3,000-acre park was designed by Capability Brown in 1767. The recently reopened historic library and the 1794 Home Farm with rare-breed animals complete the visit.

Ely is visible from miles away—the cathedral dominates the flat Fens like a beached liner, earning its nickname 'Ship of the Fens'. Its history begins in 673 when Princess Æthelthryth founded an abbey here. The current structure dates mainly from 1081, but the highlight is the Octagon Tower at the nave's centre: in 1322, the Norman tower collapsed in the night with such a crash the monks thought it was an earthquake. Architect Alan de Walsingham had the brilliant idea of widening the space into a 23-metre octagon, crowned by a painted-wood and lead lantern weighing 400 tonnes. A medieval engineering masterpiece that took 18 years to build. The cathedral measures 164 metres long and its nave is one of England's longest. Book a tower tour: climbing inside the structure is well worth the effort.

Oliver Cromwell's House sits two minutes from the cathedral. Cromwell inherited an Ely estate in 1636 from his uncle and lived here about ten years as a tithe collector for the cathedral—a cruel irony, since he later shut it down for a decade during the Commonwealth. The 16th-century timber-framed house is now a living museum. The town's name, 'Ely', may derive from Old English Eilig, 'island of eels'—you can still find them on some local restaurant menus.

activities.text: Don't leave Cambridge without punting on the Cam—it's the experience that captures the soul of this city. A punt is a flat-bottomed boat propelled with a pole. You can hire one yourself or book a guided tour: local guides pull out improbable anecdotes about each college you glide past. Allow 45 minutes to an hour for the classic College Backs route. In summer, arrive early morning or late afternoon—between 11am and 3pm it's mobbed.

Spend the evening wandering central Cambridge outside peak hours. The Round Church (Church of the Holy Sepulchre), built around 1130, is one of only four rare round Romanesque churches still standing in England. From there, climb toward the market—it runs weekdays and offers local produce and crafts. The pubs on King's Parade or Bridge Street are perfect for ending the day.

The countryside between Houghton, St Ives and surrounding villages is best explored on foot or by bike along well-marked paths beside the Great Ouse. The banks are flat, shaded, and popular with locals on weekends—a relaxed way to see rural Cambridgeshire away from Cambridge tourists.

After the cathedral, head down to the Great Ouse banks for a walk along the quay. This is where you truly understand the Fens landscape: a plain drained by Dutch engineers in the 17th century, with barges moored side by side. Ely market runs twice weekly and sells local produce, crafts and street food.

visits.text: Camden Town takes its name from Charles Pratt, 1st Earl Camden, who developed the area from 1791 intending to make it a genteel residential suburb. The opening of Regent's Canal in 1820, then the railway, transformed the neighbourhood into an industrial hub populated by workers, gin distilleries and warehouses. The first market opened in 1974 with 16 craft stalls. Today, it attracts over 250,000 visitors per week. Weekends are packed - if you can, come on a weekday for a more humane atmosphere.

The Stables Market, housed in the old Victorian stables and horse tunnels, is the most authentic part of the market. Horses were used to tow barges along Regent's Canal - in 1939, over 800 horses still passed annually through the stables' veterinary hospital. The brick arches under the railway tracks now house alternative fashion shops, vintage furniture and craft stalls.

activities.text: Walk along Regent's Canal east or west from Camden Lock - it's one of London's most pleasant pedestrian routes, between colourful barges, street art and hidden cafes under bridges. Westward, you reach Regent's Park and London Zoo in 30 minutes on foot. Eastward, you reach King's Cross and its converted warehouses.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Canterbury Cathedral is your essential first stop upon arrival. Founded in 597 by Saint Augustine, sent by Pope Gregory the Great, it was rebuilt in Gothic style after a fire in 1174—making it one of England's oldest Christian structures and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This is where Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered on December 29, 1170, by four knights of King Henry II. Becket was canonized three years later, and his shrine became England's most visited pilgrimage destination, immortalized by Chaucer in The Canterbury Tales. In 1538, Henry VIII ordered the shrine dismantled, its treasures carted away in 26 wagons. Look for the martyrdom site in the northeast transept, marked by a contemporary sculpture of two inverted swords. Book your tickets online to skip the queue, and arrive at opening time (9am on weekdays)—tour buses arrive after 10am.

A few minutes' walk away, the ruins of St Augustine's Abbey complete Canterbury's UNESCO ensemble—along with the cathedral and St Martin's Church, they form one of the city's three listed sites. This is where the first Anglo-Saxon kings of Kent were buried. Entry is managed by English Heritage; if you have the pass, don't miss it.

Head back toward the center through the medieval lanes and stop at the Old Weavers' House, a 14th-century timber-framed building overlooking the River Stour. It once housed Flemish weavers fleeing religious persecution. From King's Bridge, you'll also spot the famous ducking stool—a medieval punishment device—below. Continue to the Westgate Towers: built in 1380 under Richard II from local sandstone, they constitute the largest surviving medieval gateway in England. Climb to the top for panoramic views over the cathedral and the city's rooftops—this was also the city's prison for centuries.

activities.text: Treat yourself to a punt ride on the River Stour—Canterbury's answer to Cambridge punting, far less crowded. Several operators offer 40- to 65-minute guided tours departing from King's Bridge or Westgate Bridge. The guide does all the work while you glide past medieval gardens, Franciscan ruins, and timber-framed facades. Check availability in advance during summer—slots fill up quickly.

At the end of the day, stroll through Westgate Gardens along the Stour to relax before dinner. Every Wednesday, a lively market sets up in the city centre - if you are there, it is the perfect opportunity to taste local Kent products, including award-winning wines from nearby vineyards.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast England & Kent Circuit: White Cliffs and Secret Gardens

visits.text: Swim in the magical Fairy Pools, a series of crystal-clear waterfalls and pools at the foot of the Black Cuillins that have become one of Scotland's most beloved wild swimming spots. The turquoise waters, filtered through ancient rocks, are cold but invigorating, while the mountain backdrop creates scenes of extraordinary natural beauty. Even if you don't brave the water, the walk along the River Brittle through this enchanted landscape is unforgettable.

Visit Dunvegan Castle and its gardens, Scotland's oldest continuously inhabited castle and the ancestral home of the chiefs of Clan MacLeod for more than 800 years. The castle houses precious clan relics, including the legendary Fairy Flag, believed to possess magical powers to save the clan in times of danger. The magnificent gardens, boat trips to see the local seal colony and fascinating family history make it a highlight of any visit to Skye. Allow for a return trip from Carbost for this visit.

Tour the Talisker Distillery in Carbost, the oldest working distillery on the Isle of Skye, producing a distinctive peaty single malt whisky since 1830. The distillery's remote location on the shores of Loch Harport, surrounded by the dramatic Cuillin mountains, contributes to the unique character of this beloved whisky. The new tasting room offers the chance to sample the full range and learn about the craft that has made Talisker famous worldwide.

activities.text: Take a seal-spotting boat trip from Dunvegan Castle to see the resident colony basking on the rocks

places.name: Cardiff

visits.text: Cardiff Castle packs 2,000 years of history within its walls. The Romans established their first fort here around AD 55, then the Normans built a stone keep around 1091—its artificial motte, rising over 10 metres, still dominates the grounds. But what will truly take your breath away is the interior: in the 19th century, the 3rd Marquess of Bute—then reputed to be the richest man in the world—commissioned architect William Burges to transform the castle. The result: neo-Gothic apartments of absolute extravagance, smothered in mosaics, gilded woodwork and stained glass. Allow at least 90 minutes to explore the apartments, the Norman keep and the WWII air-raid shelters hidden in the walls.

Cardiff's historic centre is threaded with Victorian and Edwardian covered arcades—the Royal Arcade, opened in 1858, is one of the oldest in the UK. Inside you'll find independent shops, cafés and record stores, sheltered from Welsh rain. The Morgan Arcade and Castle Arcade are also worth exploring for their cast-iron structures and suspended bow windows. Take your time wandering: this is where Cardiff still feels like Cardiff, before the standardised pedestrian precincts took over.

Llandaff Cathedral, 3 km northwest of the centre, deserves a detour if you have time. Founded in the 6th century, rebuilt after the 1941 bombing, it houses an Epstein sculpture—Christ in Majesty—suspended above the nave. The place is quiet and often deserted: a welcome counterpoint to the bustle of the city centre.

The Glamorgan Heritage Coast is one of South Wales' most spectacular stretches—14 miles of limestone cliffs between Aberthaw and Newton, often deserted on weekdays. Nash Point is the jewel: a promontory of striated cliffs with geological layers visible to the naked eye, scattered with rock pools and ammonite fossils. Descend to the rocky beach at low tide to hunt for your own specimens—it's a serious activity here, not a vague pastime. The cliffs are unstable in places; stick to marked paths.

Nash Point Lighthouse was lit in 1832, in response to the wreck of the steamer The Frolic the previous year: 78 passengers drowned on that sandbank. Designed by James Walker, chief engineer of Trinity House, it operated with a keeper until 1998—Wales' last manned lighthouse, the UK's second-last. The large square fog house with its horns on the roof still stands beside the lighthouse. Local legend claims that on stormy nights in the 19th century, smugglers would tie lanterns to their sheep at the cliff edge to fool mariners into thinking they were navigating safe waters.

Dunraven Bay, 7 km northwest of Nash Point, reveals another side of the coast: a large pebble-and-sand beach at the foot of a cliff and a vanished castle. The beach is popular with surfers and geologists: you will find Triassic oyster fossils known as "Devil's toenails" there.

activities.text: The Principality Stadium—74,500 seats, retractable roof in 20 minutes, the UK's first stadium with a moveable roof—offers guided tours on non-match days. You'll visit the changing rooms, the players' tunnel and walk right up to the pitch edge. Fun fact: the pitch is grown outdoors then rolled inside for matches. Opened in June 1999, it hosted the Rugby World Cup in its first year, the 2017 Champions League final (Real Madrid v Juventus), and concerts by Beyoncé, Ed Sheeran and Oasis. Book your tour in advance.

Cardiff Bay is worth exploring whenever the sun makes an appearance. The former coal docks—once the world's largest coal-exporting port—have been transformed into a 200-hectare freshwater lake thanks to a barrage completed in 1999. Stroll along Mermaid Quay, peek at the Senedd (the Welsh parliament, a glass building by Richard Rogers), then walk the barrage to Penarth—2 km with sea views. Doctor Who fans will recognise Roald Dahl Plass: it was the fictional entrance to the Torchwood hub.

The coastal path between Dunraven Bay and Nash Point (about 7 km return) is one of the finest walks on the Glamorgan coast. The path follows a grassy limestone plateau with constant views over the Bristol Channel and, on clear days, as far as the Devon coast. Bring waterproof shoes—the path can be muddy after rain—and a waterproof jacket, even in summer.

If the coast has whetted your appetite for culture, the St Fagans National Museum of History, 6 km west of Cardiff, is one of the finest open-air museums in the United Kingdom - and admission is free. More than 40 historic buildings have been dismantled and rebuilt on this 40-hectare site, from 15th-century Welsh thatched cottages to workers' houses from the Industrial Revolution.

visits.text: It is best to start with the thick walls of Carlisle Castle to get a sense of this border city. The fortress held Mary, Queen of Scots prisoner in 1568, far from her Scottish kingdom. Explore the courtyards and then the keep before walking to the cathedral; leave your car in the same parking spot for both visits.

Above you, stars take the place of the sky in Carlisle Cathedral. This former church of Augustinian canons retains carved choir stalls and runic inscriptions, details quite different from its great stained-glass window. Look at the small carvings in the choir as well, and keep quiet during your visit if preparations for a service are underway.

days_plan.itin_title: Hadrian’s Wall and Northumberland: 7 Days Between the Sea and the Forts

visits.text: Built in 1177 by John de Courcy, a Norman knight who came north seeking fortune, Carrickfergus Castle is one of Ireland's best-preserved fortresses. Edward Bruce, brother of Scottish king Robert Bruce, besieged it from September 1315 to September 1316—a year of famine before surrender. The original polygonal keep still stands, six cannons on the east battery survivors of the twenty-two installed in 1811. Allow 1h30, closed Mondays outside summer.

activities.text: The A2 follows Belfast Lough northwards before turning towards the Causeway Coast. The Carrickfergus-Larne stretch is of little interest, but it leads onto the Antrim Coast Road, one of Europe's most beautiful coastal roads. Stop at Glenarm, approximately 30 km from Carrickfergus, a 30-minute drive: a small grey-stone harbour, with coffee at Steensons. There is no direct tunnel, and the road is open all year round.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Ireland in 7 days: Belfast, Causeway & Derry

visits.text: Castle Combe has had no castle since the 15th century. The Norman fortress of 1135 decayed and vanished, and the village shifted to cloth production: local wool, the River Bybrook, fulling mills on site. The Cotswold stone buildings date from that prosperous period, and no new construction has been added since the 17th century. The village is literally frozen in time.

activities.text: The bridge over the Bybrook draws a constant stream of selfies in high season. The compulsory car park is at the top of the hill, a 10-minute walk from the centre. No public transport, no chains, no traffic lights—that is the local rule. The Market Cross, a medieval market cross, marks the heart of the village.

days_plan.itin_title: Welsh Marches, Cotswolds and Bath in 11 days

visits.text: Hedingham Castle was built by the de Vere family in the 12th century—the precise date varies between 1133 and 1140 according to sources—when the de Veres held the office of Lord Great Chamberlain of England. The family owned the castle for over 500 years; one of its members was among the barons who forced King John to sign Magna Carta in 1215. Henry VIII stayed here in 1509 and Elizabeth I in 1561.

One of England's best-preserved Norman keeps—the walls are up to 3.5 meters thick at the base, and the canopied great hall on the first floor is nearly intact. The site includes 160 acres of gardens and woods with plant species from the Lindsay family, the current owners.

activities.text: Explore Hedingham Castle's 160-acre park with a walk along the linden avenue and around the lake. Entry included in the castle admission ticket. Picnics permitted on the grounds.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

places.name: Castlebay

visits.text: The CalMac ferry makes the crossing from Eriskay to Ardmhor in northern Barra in about 40 minutes. At Castlebay, Kisimul Castle sits on a small rocky islet in the middle of the water, square and medieval, with the Catholic church of Our Lady Star of the Sea rising above the village behind. Barra, 14 miles in circumference, was the Clan MacNeil stronghold for more than 400 years. In 1427, Alexander, Lord of the Isles, granted the island to the clan. In 2001, the 45th Chief of Clan MacNeil leased Kisimul Castle to Historic Scotland for 1,000 years at a rent of £1 a year and a bottle of whisky.

Kisimul Castle is reached by a 5-minute boat trip from Castlebay's quay. Dating from the 15th century, the castle was abandoned and slowly deteriorated before the 45th Clan Chief bought it back in 1937 and spent decades restoring it himself. Inside are a great hall, a tower house, a chapel and a well. The views from the ramparts over the bay are excellent. It is still technically the seat of the Chief of Clan MacNeil.

Barra is predominantly Catholic – in contrast to the strict Presbyterianism of the northern Hebrides – and the church of Our Lady Star of the Sea dominates the village from above. On the slopes of Heaval, the island's highest hill at 383 metres, stands a large white marble statue of the Madonna and Child, clearly visible from the bay. The contrast with the stern Calvinism of Lewis and Harris is palpable: here there are buses on Sundays, shops open on Sundays, and a noticeably different rhythm to island life.

Cross the causeway to Vatersay, the most southerly inhabited island in the Outer Hebrides, connected to Barra only since 1990 – before that, cattle had to be made to swim across. Vatersay has two extraordinary beaches separated by a thin strip of land: Bagh Sear (East Beach) and Bagh Iar (West Beach), both entirely deserted outside peak season. West Beach faces directly onto the Atlantic with nothing between you and Canada; East Beach is calmer and better for swimming. On a clear day, the silhouettes of the uninhabited islands of Mingulay and Berneray (the southernmost Berneray, not the one near Harris) are visible to the south.

Back on Barra, the beach airport at Traigh Mhor (Cockle Strand) is unlike any other in the world. Scheduled flights from Glasgow land on the tidal sands twice a day, at low tide. At high tide, the runway disappears beneath the sea. The local community council consults the tide tables and publishes the timetable accordingly. There is no barrier between spectators and the runway; watching a Loganair turboprop land on the sand is truly extraordinary. Check arrival times on Loganair's website. Allow for a return drive from Castlebay.

activities.text: The circuit around Barra takes about 30 minutes to drive without stopping. Don't rush it. Stop at Tangasdale beach on the west coast – white sand, blue water, and a hotel with a spectacular view from the terrace. Then drive north to Eoligarry for views across to Eriskay and South Uist.

Castlebay's social life, such as it is, revolves around the bar of the Castlebay Hotel. On good evenings - which comes down to whether the right people are in - someone produces a fiddle or an accordion and a session develops entirely organically. This is not a scheduled event; it simply happens. Sit down, order something local, and wait.

The climb to the summit of Heaval (383 m) from Castlebay takes about 1.5 hours return. The path starts from the road above the village and the view from the top - over Kisimul Castle, the Sound of Barra, South Uist and, on a good day, St Kilda far to the west - is the best panorama on the island. The white marble Our Lady of the Sea statue is passed on the way up.
