North Yorkshire Moors Railway steam train

visits.text: A village containing its own miniature: Godshill Model Village takes the idea as far as reproducing the model within the model. Buildings from Godshill and Shanklin are recreated at a scale of 1:10 amid a garden. Look for this model within a model instead of rushing along the paths; check the seasonal opening schedule.

Head uphill to All Saints’ Church in Godshill for a broader view of the village cottages. Inside this medieval church, a wall painting combines the Crucifixion with a lily motif, a less expected detail than the surrounding thatched roofs. Respect church services and view only the exterior if the church is closed.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Wight in 4 days: From Osborne to the Chalk Cliffs

visits.text: Marvel at Dunrobin Castle, the largest house in the Scottish Highlands with 189 rooms connected by a maze of corridors and crowned with fairy-tale French-style turrets. This magnificent stately home, seat of the Earls and Dukes of Sutherland since the 13th century, combines Scottish baronial architecture with the elegance of a Loire château. The formal gardens, modeled on Versailles, sweep down to the sea, and falconry displays showcase eagles, hawks and owls in flight.

Explore the castle's opulent interiors, where grand reception rooms display fine furniture, paintings and hunting trophies accumulated over seven centuries of aristocratic occupation. The museum houses an eclectic collection including Pictish stones, natural history specimens and artifacts from around the world. The contrast between the fairy-tale exterior and the lived-in warmth of the interior reveals the continuing story of one of Scotland's great noble families.

Discover Golspie by walking between its long sandy beach and small harbor, facing the Moray Firth. Then follow the wooded Big Burn trail, which runs upstream to a waterfall tucked inside a green gorge. This accessible walk combines the Highland coast, footbridges beneath the trees and a clear destination close to the stage town.

activities.text: Watch the spectacular falconry display in Dunrobin's gardens, featuring golden eagles and other birds of prey

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Highlands: 15 Days of Castles, Lochs and Wild Landscapes

visits.text: Here the Thames cuts through the Chilterns—the Gap is where two Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty meet on opposite banks. The first bridge dates only to 1837 and was replaced in 1923; before that, there was a ferry. Stop on the current bridge: the view over the lock and wooded hills is the quintessential image of the rural Thames. Free, paid parking.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop

visits.text: Take time to discover Grantown-on-Spey, a textbook case of Scottish Enlightenment urban planning: founded on June 28, 1765 by Sir James Grant of Grant, the town was laid out on a plan with a wide gray sandstone main street and central square. The first building, a linen manufactory, cost £40. Queen Victoria spent a night at the Grant Arms Hotel on September 4, 1860—the first time she'd ever slept in a public inn. She noted in her journal: "the dinner was very fair and all very clean." The excerpt is still displayed in the hotel lobby.

Head into Anagach Woods, just south of town—one of the Cairngorms' finest Scots pine forests: trails wind through centuries-old Caledonian pines to the River Spey, where you can observe otters, red squirrels, and ospreys in summer. Grantown Museum & Heritage Trust traces the Georgian town's history with the opportunity to try on period costumes.

activities.text: Grantown sits at the heart of Speyside's whisky trail. Balmenach distillery, founded in 1824 at Cromdale, produced whisky for 170 years before closing in 1993. Other active distilleries—Aberlour, Glenlivet, Balvenie—are less than an hour's drive and offer guided tours and tastings. Arrange a designated driver.

Cairngorms National Park—the UK's largest national park, created in 2003 and covering 4,528 km²—is accessible from Grantown in minutes. The road to Aviemore follows the Spey valley, Scotland's fastest-flowing river. In winter, the Cairngorm Mountain ski area is 30 minutes away. Reach Aviemore in 20 minutes to access the heart of the park and the Cairngorm Mountain funicular.

days_plan.itin_title: Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye

visits.text: Between 1799 and 1808, a great poetic adventure unfolded in the small rooms of Dove Cottage in Grasmere. William Wordsworth wrote here while Dorothy kept her journal. The tour also recreates the family’s daily life. Book your visit inside the house and allow time for a brief look at the neighboring museum.

St Oswald’s Church connects Grasmere’s poetry with real lives: William, Mary, and Dorothy Wordsworth are buried in its churchyard. The church is also the focal point of a local procession featuring rushes and flowers. Walk quietly along the paths and postpone entering the church if a service is underway.

activities.text: Continue your visit to Dove Cottage in the Garden-Orchard, set on the slope behind the house. This garden has been restored to evoke the one William and Dorothy created together: the literary landscape begins here, on a small scale. Save this walk for a break in the weather and follow the open paths.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle
Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes, Villages, and Writers
Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes and Writers’ Homes

visits.text: You can walk beneath a sailing ship without getting wet: a visit to the Cutty Sark also takes you underneath its hull. In Greenwich, this historic ship then lets you head up onto the deck and see how the crew lived. The change in perspective is just as rewarding as the ship’s silhouette seen from the quay. Book your time slot and allow time for the interior spaces; you can listen to the free audio guide on your phone.

Much more than a shelter from the rain, the National Maritime Museum deserves a visit in Greenwich. Its collections tell the story of Great Britain’s relationship with the sea, while the free galleries let you choose a subject without feeling you need to get your money’s worth from a general admission ticket. The contrast with the Cutty Sark helps you move from an actual ship to maritime history. Temporary exhibitions may require a separate ticket.

If you prefer paintings to navigational instruments, the Queen’s House is a good complement to the National Maritime Museum in Greenwich. The portrait of Elizabeth I commemorating the Armada provides a clear focal point for a visit that combines architecture and art collections. General admission is free, allowing for a focused visit without buying additional tickets.

activities.text: Walk uphill in Greenwich Park to see the museums and the Thames within the same landscape. The Royal Observatory overlooks this part of Greenwich, but you can enjoy the panorama without entering its buildings. The observatory has announced a closure for renovation starting November 2, 2026, so do not automatically count on access to the historic meridian. Keep the park walk in your plans; a phased reopening is announced for summer 2027.

days_plan.itin_title: Around London in 5 Days: Royal Palaces and Gardens

visits.text: Paved with golden sandstone and sloping steeply down towards the Wey, Guildford's High Street follows the exact Saxon street layout from the year 900 – the town received its royal charter from Henry III in 1257. The famous projecting Guildhall clock dates from 1683 and has hung over the street for three centuries. The street is regularly used as a filming location for its visual consistency. Allow 45 minutes to walk down and back up.

Guildford Castle's Norman keep is modest, but it's the only royal castle ever built in Surrey. Erected after the Conquest of 1066, it was sold to the Guildford Corporation in 1885. The garden surrounding the keep is one of the town's most flower-filled. Climb to the top for a view of the Surrey Hills on the horizon. Entry ticket around £5 (check on site).

The scent of polished wood and old ceramics at Guildford Museum heralds a richer collection than expected: the medieval merchant town, Lewis Carroll who stayed here regularly in his final years, the Arts & Crafts movement in Surrey. The life-size statue of Alice in Wonderland in the Castle Grounds commemorates Carroll, who lived with his sister in Guildford and died here in 1898. Free entry.

activities.text: Walk up the High Street to the Guildhall with its clock jutting over the road, then continue to Quarry Street to see the castle ruins and the Tunsgate Arch. Guildford offers guided walking tours departing from the Museum—ideal for catching the medieval lanes running perpendicular to High Street.

If you're passing through on a Friday or Saturday morning, Guildford's market sets up on High Street and North Street with local producers from the Surrey Hills. Cheeses, artisan breads, seasonal vegetables. Perfect for assembling a picnic for Shere the next day.

days_plan.itin_title: London to Bath: Surrey, Hampshire & Wiltshire in 10 Days
Surrey to Kent: Castles and Gardens in 10 Days

visits.text: Stand in awe before Harlech Castle, a magnificent 13th-century fortress built by King Edward I that dominates the landscape from its dramatic clifftop position overlooking Tremadog Bay. This UNESCO World Heritage site, one of the finest examples of late 13th-century military architecture in Europe, inspired the famous Welsh anthem 'Men of Harlech.' The castle's massive walls and towers seem to grow from the rocky outcrop itself, creating an unforgettable silhouette against sea and mountain.

Explore the castle's impressive gatehouse, one of the strongest built during the medieval period, designed to withstand the most determined siege. The views from the battlements stretch across to the Llŷn Peninsula, along the coast to the mountains of Snowdonia, and on clear days all the way to Ireland. The atmospheric ruins evoke centuries of Welsh history, from Edward's conquest to Owain Glyndŵr's legendary siege.

Discover Harlech's beautiful beach, a vast expanse of golden sand stretching below the castle cliffs that offers a dramatic contrast to the fortress above. The beach, backed by dunes and with the castle as a constant backdrop, provides unique photographic opportunities combining medieval architecture with natural beauty. The small town of Harlech itself retains a quiet Welsh character, with traditional shops and welcoming local pubs.

activities.text: Capture the perfect photograph of the castle from the road below, framing it against the Snowdonia mountains

days_plan.itin_title: Wales Road Trip: Conwy Castle, Pembrokeshire Coast & Snowdonia
Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: Poohsticks Bridge: ridiculously charming at 40 as it is at six. This wooden bridge in the middle of Ashdown Forest is officially called Posingford Bridge—built in 1907. A. A. Milne moved to Cotchford Farm in Hartfield in 1925 and invented the Hundred Acre Wood. Pooh Corner in the village serves bear-shaped sandwiches.

The bridge dates from 1907; A. A. Milne arrived in 1925: Ashdown Forest has changed little since. The Enchanted Place is at the top of the forest, on a heather-covered heath with panoramic views—a plaque dedicated to Milne and illustrator E. H. Shepard marks the spot. This is where Christopher Robin says goodbye to Winnie the Pooh.

activities.text: Walk through Ashdown Forest to the Enchanted Place: the hike from Pooh Corner is around 4.7 km return, easy. Look along the way for Owl's House and Piglet's House—marked by discreet wooden signs. Forest car parks are now paid (around £1.50 per week or per day).

days_plan.itin_title: Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports

activities.text: Walk to the lookout at Hartland Point to see the lighthouse below the cliffs. The coastal trail provides this view without entering the lighthouse grounds, where access is prohibited because of falling rocks. Stay on authorized paths and bring a windbreaker for this exposed headland.

days_plan.itin_title: North Devon and Exmoor: 3 Days of Headlands and Villages

visits.text: Harwich's Electric Palace Cinema, built in 1911, is Britain's least-altered purpose-built cinema: the silent-era screen, original projection booth, and ornamental façade remain intact. Actor Clive Owen is its patron. Check the program on electricpalace.com before coming.

Harwich's treadwheel crane, built in 1667, is the only known example in Britain of this adapted Roman technology: men walked inside two large wheels to lift cargo. The Treadwheel Crane, a scheduled monument, can be visited freely in the old town.

Harwich's Redoubt Fort, circular and squat, is worth the detour: a fort 60 meters in diameter, built in 1808 to defend the port against a Napoleonic invasion, with ten guns in battery. Napoleon himself plays no part in the story—but the fort is the only one of its type open to the public in England. Managed by the Harwich Society.

activities.text: Follow Harwich's Maritime Heritage Trail: starting from the Low Lighthouse Museum built in 1818, passing the treadwheel crane, Electric Palace, and barge murals, ending at Ha'Penny Pier. Allow 90 minutes for the complete 2 km circuit.

If you have 30 minutes on a Saturday between May and September, board a boat from Ha'Penny Pier to see Harwich port from the water. The maritime traffic—ferries, cargo ships, sailboats—is spectacular on this estuary.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

places.name: Hastings

visits.text: Hastings Old Town nestles between two cliffs, East Hill and West Hill, in a tangle of Tudor and Georgian lanes little changed since the 15th century. Start at the Stade, the pebble beach that's home to Europe's largest beach-launched fishing fleet. If you arrive early morning, you'll see the fishing boats returning with their catches. The tall black wooden sheds (the net shops) lining Rock-a-Nore Road are still used to store nets—a sight unique in England.

Take the East Hill Lift funicular from Rock-a-Nore Road: opened in 1902, it's the UK's steepest open-air funicular, carved into the cliff with a 78% gradient. From the top, the view sweeps over the old town, fishermen's huts, and the coast to Beachy Head and Dungeness—on clear days, you can even see France. Access to Hastings Country Park (660 acres of protected nature) is directly from the top station.

The ruins of Hastings Castle crown West Hill, accessible by the West Hill Lift funicular (Hastings' first funicular, opened in 1891, which passes through a rock tunnel—extremely rare for this type of transport). The fortress was erected by William the Conqueror in 1067, a year after the battle that decided England's history. Your ticket includes access to the tower cinema where a 20-minute film traces the history of 1066.

activities.text: Smugglers' Adventure in St Clement's Caves, accessible from West Hill, takes you into a network of natural caverns used by 18th-century smugglers. The wax recreations of the Hawkhurst Gang—which terrorized the Sussex coast for fifteen years until 1749—are remarkably realistic. Allow an hour for this tour that appeals to adults and children alike.

Explore the old town's lanes: George Street for independent shops and All Saints Street for 15th-century timber-framed houses. Look for the Cheese House—England's only triangular house, wedged into a lane corner. In the evening, several old town pubs are worth a visit, notably The Stag Inn with its garden or The Crown for its local craft beers.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast England & Kent Circuit: White Cliffs and Secret Gardens
Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports

map_keywords: Smugglers Adventure St Clements Caves Hastings

visits.text: The Old Palace at Hatfield dates to 1485: it's in this Tudor brick building that Elizabeth I spent much of her childhood—and here she learned of her accession to the throne in 1558. It remains intact from its great hall to most of its original beams.

Hatfield House, built between 1607 and 1611 by Robert Cecil for King James I, deserves a full hour. The Marble Hall, the Rainbow Portrait of Elizabeth I, and the grand staircase rank among England's most complete Jacobean interiors. The house remains inhabited by the Cecil family.

activities.text: Explore the gardens of Hatfield House and look for the “Queen Elizabeth Oak”. The park covers 40 acres, with a topiary garden, a knot garden and wooded gardens. Follow the 90-minute trail marked on the map provided at the entrance.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Skipton Castle is one of England's best-preserved medieval fortresses. Founded in 1090 by Robert de Romille, a Norman baron, it belonged to the Clifford family for over 400 years. During the Civil War, it was the last Royalist stronghold in the north: besieged for three years, it surrendered to Cromwell in December 1645. Legend says the defenders hung fleeces on the walls to cushion cannonballs — hence the fleeces in the town's coat of arms. In the cobbled inner courtyard, look for the yew tree planted by Lady Anne Clifford as a symbol of restoration after the siege.

Leaving the castle, head down into central Skipton and follow the Leeds-Liverpool Canal to the market. Skipton Market is one of Yorkshire's oldest: it runs Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday on High Street. Local produce, textiles, cheese — the atmosphere feels far more authentic than the tourist markets in bigger cities. The canal dates to 1816 and connected Yorkshire's wool mills to the ports of Liverpool.

Continue toward Hawes through Wensleydale on the A684 — one of Yorkshire's loveliest valley roads, weaving between green meadows and sheep-dotted hills. Stop at the Wensleydale Creamery. The Wensleydale cheese recipe dates back to the 12th century, brought by French Cistercian monks who perfected it at Jervaulx Abbey. In 1897, Edward Chapman founded the first commercial creamery in Hawes. In 1992, it nearly closed with 59 job losses — and Wallace and Gromit saved it: when the character Wallace declared his passion for Wensleydale in 'A Close Shave' (1995), sales jumped 23%.

activities.text: At the Wensleydale Creamery, don't just visit the shop — join the Cheese Experience: a 40-minute cheesemaking demonstration followed by a tasting of different varieties (plain, smoked, cranberry, ginger). The panoramic window overlooks the production floor where you can watch cheesemakers at work. Check demonstration times before you go.

Evening in Hawes — wander this lively market town in the heart of the Yorkshire Dales National Park. The Dales Countryside Museum, free and well-designed, traces the history of the valley's people and landscape. In good weather, a short walk to Gayle Beck on the village edge offers beautiful late-day light on the hills.

days_plan.itin_title: Yorkshire and North East England: Dales and Coasts

visits.text: A small house, a major literary career: Hill Top brings Beatrix Potter’s world down to the scale of a farmhouse in Near Sawrey. Purchased in 1905 with earnings from Peter Rabbit, it preserves objects and interiors that appear in her illustrations. Book your time slot before setting out; the allotted time includes the local round trip from Hawkshead.

Beneath slate roofs, Hawkshead’s lanes twist between building fronts and small squares. This former wool market town retains a network of passageways far more interesting to explore on foot than by car. Leave your vehicle in the village parking lot and save this short visit for after Hill Top.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes, Villages, and Writers
Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes and Writers’ Homes

places.name: Haworth

visits.text: In Haworth, walk up cobbled Main Street toward the Brontë Parsonage Museum. As you climb, you can see stone façades and alleyways branching off the main street. Stop at the windows of the independent shops, then continue to the area around the parsonage and St Michael and All Angels Church. The churchyard gives a glimpse of the Brontë family's everyday surroundings. This walk takes you through the village on foot, before visiting the museum or joining the moorland trails.

From Haworth, walk to Penistone Hill to discover the moorland near the village. The paths cross open ground with grasses, heather, and rocky outcrops. Take in the views of the hills and valley, then return toward the village along the marked trails. The landscape helps you understand the setting of the Brontë sisters' novels without undertaking the hike to Top Withens. Bring shoes suitable for wet paths and a jacket to protect against the wind.

Haworth is one of Europe's most visited literary pilgrimage destinations. Main Street climbs steeply toward the Brontë parsonage—as steep as in 1820 when the family first climbed it on arrival. The Brontë Parsonage Museum is the house where Patrick Brontë settled as parish priest in 1820, where Charlotte, Emily, and Anne grew up, and where the three sisters wrote Jane Eyre, Wuthering Heights, and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall between 1840 and 1848. The museum holds the world's largest collection of Brontë manuscripts and objects: the microscopic handwriting of the “Little Books” (childhood notebooks), Charlotte's sewing box, Emily's painting easel. Allow between 1 hour 30 minutes and 2 hours.

Across the street, St Michael and All Angels Church is where Patrick Brontë ministered—and where Charlotte, Emily, Branwell, and their parents are buried. The current building dates from 1879 (the original, considered dilapidated, was demolished), but the atmosphere of the cemetery surrounding the parsonage—with its leaning gravestones visible from the windows of the dining room where the sisters wrote—remains striking.

Behind the parsonage, the moors begin literally meters away. The path to Top Withens, the ruined farm thought to have inspired Wuthering Heights, starts from the end of the garden and climbs to a windswept plateau—6 kilometers round trip; allow 2 hours 30 minutes. Even if you don't do the full hike, walk for 20 minutes onto the moor to feel the wind that shaped the sisters' imagination.

activities.text: The Keighley & Worth Valley Railway steam line connects Keighley to Oxenhope via Haworth—8 kilometers on a heritage line entirely run by volunteers since 1968. The half-hour journey is a fine way to arrive in or leave Haworth if you plan around the timetable (check the website before departing). The line served as the setting for the 1970 film “The Railway Children”.

Haworth makes it easy to spend an evening at the pub: Main Street and its side lanes have several establishments in dark 19th-century sandstone buildings. The village also hosts an annual 1940s festival (dates vary) that transforms the village into a wartime setting with uniforms, period vehicles, and swing concerts.

days_plan.itin_title: Yorkshire's Most Beautiful Places

map_keywords: St Michael and All Angels Church Haworth

visits.text: Richard Booth, the founder, proclaimed himself King of Hay and appointed his horse as Prime Minister in 1977 to attract world attention—and it worked. This town of fewer than 2,000 inhabitants on the Welsh border counts more than 20 secondhand and antiquarian bookshops, making it the world's first book town since the 1960s. Richard Booth's Bookshop on Lion Street occupies three floors. The Hay Festival of literature takes place in late May; the rest of the year the town is quieter.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: About 18 km from Helston, a 20-minute drive, lies the southernmost point, and also the one most associated with shipwrecks. Lizard Point is the first headland ships see as they sail up the English Channel - hence the hundreds of wrecks offshore. Watch marine wildlife from the National Trust Wildlife Watchpoint: seals, dolphins and rare Cornish choughs nest here. It is less than an hour's walk from the car park.

activities.text: About 17 km from Helston, a 20-minute drive, green serpentinite runs through the cliffs like marbled paint - Kynance Cove is the most photographed cove on the Lizard. Turquoise water, rocks sculpted by the waves and a National Trust café above. Accessible only at low tide: check the tide times and arrive at least 2 hours before high tide to avoid being cut off.

days_plan.itin_title: Dark Cornwall: Arthur, Mines and Wreckers 7d

visits.text: The pink hippopotamus on the sign watches the octuple sculls pass by: it is the official mascot of Leander Club, founded in 1818 and the world's leading single-sport club according to its own record - 159 Olympic and Paralympic medals since 1908.

Closed since September 2025, David Chipperfield's River & Rowing Museum (1998, the architect's first major UK project) remains visible from the promenade. The trust is seeking a new project for the green oak building—a page is turning for Henley. Check before making a special trip.

Henley Bridge has spanned the Thames since the 18th century—five stone arches, a view over the river from Hart Street, Georgian red brick on either side. Outside the Henley Royal Regatta (early July), the town is quiet and easy to find your way around. Free.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop

visits.text: En route to Hereford, stop at the Malvern Hills—a ridge of Precambrian hills 680 million years old that surge abruptly from the Worcestershire plain. Great Malvern is a Victorian spa town that's kept its elegance: an 11th-century priory, terraced gardens. The walk from the town centre to the Worcestershire Beacon (425m) takes 1.5 hours return and offers, on clear days, views from the Welsh Black Mountains to the Cotswolds.

Hereford Cathedral houses two treasures absolutely unique in the world. The first is the Mappa Mundi, the largest known medieval map still in existence: drawn around 1300 on calfskin (1.59m x 1.34m), Jerusalem sits at the centre, Paradise at the top, monsters and strange creatures at the edges. In 1988, the diocese nearly sold it to cover a deficit—a public fundraising campaign and a donation from Paul Getty kept it in Hereford. The second is the Chained Library: the world's largest library of chained books, with 1,500 volumes including 229 medieval manuscripts still attached to their shelves by chains.

The Old House, a timber-framed building from 1621 that survived 19th-century demolitions, is the finest specimen of Jacobean architecture in the region. The banks of the Wye, two minutes' walk from the cathedral, make a pleasant pause at day's end.

Hereford is the world capital of cider—the region produces more cider than anywhere else in Britain. The Cider Museum traces 400 years of production through antique presses, barrels and the reconstruction of a Herefordshire calvados distillery. In season, several cideries around town offer tours and tastings directly in the orchards.

activities.text: The walk along the Wye in Hereford is one of the Midlands' most pleasant urban strolls: 5km between medieval bridges, willow-lined banks and the cathedral in the background. If you want to go further, the Wye Valley Walk departs from Hereford toward Wales—even 2 hours heading south are enough to see the river carve into increasingly wild landscape.

days_plan.itin_title: The Midlands and Peak District Essentials

visits.text: On the banks of the Lea, Hertford Castle is a surprise: what remains standing is a 15th-century residential wing converted into a townhouse, not a castle in the usual sense. The Norman gatehouse is Grade I listed. The gardens overlook the river, with free, open access every day.
Hertford Museum, housed in a 17th-century house on Bull Plain, offers collections of archaeology and local history including Roman artifacts found in the area. Free entry.

activities.text: Follow the River Lea in Hertford to Hartham Common, a green park opposite the castle. The 30-minute round-trip walk follows the riverbanks with views of the old town's timber-framed houses.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Hever Castle dates to 1383 in its original form and was enlarged by the Boleyns after they acquired it in 1462 – this is where Anne Boleyn grew up before becoming Henry VIII's second wife, for exactly 1,000 days. The double-moated castle greets you with a drawbridge and two portcullises in succession. Inside: period Tudor portraits, two prayer books that belonged to Anne, and a collection of Tudor portraits considered among the finest after that of the National Portrait Gallery.

Hever's interior is not authentic—William Waldorf Astor, the fabulously wealthy American owner, redid the whole thing in the early 20th century with period tapestries and furniture brought from Europe. The result is meticulous and the distinction between original and restoration well documented in the included audio guide. What is authentic, however: the moats, the drawbridge, and the 14th-century gatehouse.

activities.text: Climbing roses, shimmering moats, trimmed lime trees – Hever's gardens spread over 125 acres with an Italian Garden featuring columns brought from Italy by Astor, a hedge maze, and an artificial lake dug in 1904. Allow at least two hours for the garden alone. The rhododendrons in May are particularly spectacular.

days_plan.itin_title: Surrey to Kent: Castles and Gardens in 10 Days

visits.text: Hexham Abbey’s most unexpected detour takes you underground. Its crypt reuses Roman stones, including inscriptions and carved fragments: a second life for materials from antiquity. Ask a member of the welcome team for access before going down; you will need to be comfortable with steep steps and narrow passages.

days_plan.itin_title: Hadrian’s Wall and Northumberland: 7 Days Between the Sea and the Forts

visits.text: If you pass through Hitchin on a Saturday, the market in Market Place has been held for over 900 years according to local sources—one of Hertfordshire's oldest. The cobbled streets radiating outward still bear their medieval names (Bucklersbury, Tilehouse Street). The setting is as much of a draw as the stalls.

St Mary's Church in Hitchin conceals a carved 15th-century rood screen and several medieval brass memorials in Hertfordshire's largest parish church. The tower dates to the 12th century. Free entry, open during the day.

activities.text: In July-August, drive out to Hitchin Lavender, a few kilometers from the center: over 12 hectares of lavender in bloom, pick-your-own available, café in the barn. Arrival before 11am recommended to avoid weekend crowds.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Blickling Hall, a Jacobean manor in red brick built between 1619 and 1627 by architect Robert Lyminge (who also designed Hatfield House), rises on the site of the Boleyn family's medieval estate. Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife, who was executed in 1536, was probably born here around 1501. Legend says her ghost returns each May 19, the anniversary of her death. The 37-meter Long Gallery, with its stucco ceiling by Edward Stanyon, houses one of the National Trust's most remarkable libraries: some 13,000 volumes inherited from Sir Richard Ellys in the eighteenth century.

The Blickling estate covers 4,600 acres, including 950 of woodland and parkland. During World War II, the house served as a mess for RAF Oulton aircrews—a small museum honors them. The estate already belonged to Harold Godwinson, the last Anglo-Saxon king, before the Norman Conquest. After the 11th Marquess of Lothian's death in 1940, Blickling became the first great estate bequeathed to the National Trust under the 1937 law he himself had helped pass.

Holt, a small Georgian town rebuilt after a 1708 fire, has brick and flint facades lining its quiet streets. Its independent shops—antique dealers, booksellers, artisans—make it one of Norfolk's most pleasant market towns.

activities.text: Go birdwatching at Cley Marshes Nature Reserve, one of the UK's oldest bird reserves. The marshes host marsh harriers, avocets, bitterns and, in winter, vast flocks of pink-footed geese from Iceland and Greenland.

Stroll through the gardens of Blickling Estate—the parterre, redesigned in the 1930s by landscape designer Norah Lindsay, and the Temple Walk offer a peaceful walk among century-old yews, an orangery and a lake.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia Road Trip: Norfolk, Suffolk and Cambridge

visits.text: Wind lashes the cliffs, puffins huddle in their burrows, and South Stack's white lighthouse seems to float above the Irish Sea 100 metres from shore. The RSPB reserve shelters several thousand seabirds—guillemots, razorbills, puffins, choughs—between April and July. Ellin's Tower viewing station provides access to the reserve's binoculars. Visit between April and July for puffins; off-season the site remains striking but the nests are empty.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: At an elevation of about 350 meters, Honister Pass already feels like high mountain country. The pass connects the Buttermere and Borrowdale valleys via the B5289, with steep slopes rising above the road. Stop at the parking lot at the top to take in the landscape; avoid the pass if road conditions are poor.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes, Villages, and Writers
Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes and Writers’ Homes

visits.text: Houghton's watermill turns beside the Great Ouse in the village that won the most awards in Victorian England — Houghton won the title of most beautiful village several times. The site is a National Trust property: the mill still works at weekends, the millstone grinds grain, and the flour is sold at reception.

Hemingford Grey Manor, less than two kilometres east, is one of England's oldest inhabited houses—its main nave dates from the twelfth century. Built in grey limestone by the river, it was the home of author Lucy Boston, who wrote her 'Green Knowe' series of novels there. Visits by appointment only.

activities.text: You paddle the Great Ouse by canoe between Houghton and St Ives, following water meadows and willows. This section is known as calm and safe for beginners. Canoe hire is available at Houghton; allow two hours for the one-way journey.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: A Roman fort with latrines still perfectly visible after 1,700 years - it's the detail that captures everyone at Housesteads. This 5-acre auxiliary fort, occupied for nearly 300 years, housed up to 800 soldiers. Named Vercovicium ('the place of effective fighters'), it sits on the Whin Sill escarpment with a view towards Scotland. It's the best-preserved Roman fort in Britain according to English Heritage.

Walking along Hadrian's Wall gives a tangible sense of Roman ambition: 117 km from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, built from AD 122 on Hadrian's orders. Listed by UNESCO in 1987 - and an acknowledged inspiration for George R.R. Martin's Wall in Game of Thrones. The circular route from Housesteads to Steel Rigg and back is approximately 13 km and takes 3 hours.

activities.text: Parking at Housesteads managed by Northumberland National Park. AD122 bus from Hexham or Haltwhistle - year-round service, day ticket recommended to combine fort and Sycamore Gap in one day.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle
Hadrian’s Wall and Northumberland: 7 Days Between the Sea and the Forts

activities.text: If you have an hour and a good eye for antiques, Hungerford is your town. The Hungerford Arcade brings together a hundred dealers under one roof. The Kennet & Avon Canal towpath runs along the town, with moored narrowboats and the swing bridge by St Lawrence's Church. Atmosphere far less touristy than Avebury or Stourhead. Street market every Wednesday on High Street.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days

visits.text: Hutton-le-Hole is the kind of place you start doubting exists before you arrive. A stream wanders through the village in meandering loops across a broad green lawn edged with white fences, and sheep graze freely between stone cottages. Lonely Planet cites it as one of England's most beautiful villages—hard to argue. The name itself comes from the dips and hollows of the terrain, and the 'le' is a Victorian invention to sound more French. Arrive early morning or after 5pm—during the day coaches unload.

Ryedale Folk Museum, at the entrance to Hutton-le-Hole, is a 5-acre open-air museum assembling 25 historic Yorkshire buildings dismantled and rebuilt here: medieval timber-framed cottages, an Elizabethan farmhouse, a Victorian shop, a blacksmith's workshop. The museum traces rural Yorkshire life from the Iron Age to the 1950s. Allow at least two hours.

Lastingham, 5 minutes by car, is one of the moors' most discreet and most singular villages. Its St Mary's Church possesses an 11th-century crypt built on the foundations of a monastery founded in 654 by St Cedd—one of the missionaries who Christianised northern England. Descend the old stone steps into the dim light: Norman columns from 1078 surround the saint's tomb. It's one of Yorkshire's oldest and most silent spaces.

activities.text: The circular walk from Hutton-le-Hole to Lastingham and back across the moors runs 7 kilometres—allow two hours. You cross open moorland with 360° views of the hills before descending into the Lastingham valley. On the return, stop for a drink at the Blacksmith's Arms in Lastingham—an intact village pub serving real Yorkshire ales.

days_plan.itin_title: Yorkshire: Wild Coast & Secret Moorlands

visits.text: Hyde Park covers 142 hectares in the heart of London - Henry VIII made it a royal hunting park in 1536 and it remains Crown property. The Serpentine, a 40-acre artificial lake dug in 1730, offers swimming, pedalos and kayaking in summer. Speaker's Corner, in the park's northeast corner since 1872, is one of the few places in the world where anyone can speak on any subject without prior permission - the tradition dates back to public executions on this site in the 18th century. On Sunday mornings, speakers still debate everything and nothing.

activities.text: In summer, the Serpentine Lido offers open-water swimming in the lake - a practice available since 1930. The Serpentine Galleries (two pavilions on the lake shores) exhibit contemporary art for free. Each summer, a world-renowned architect designs a temporary pavilion - Zaha Hadid, Frank Gehry, Toyo Ito have all participated.

Kensington Gardens, adjacent to Hyde Park, houses Kensington Palace - an official residence since the 17th century and Princess Diana's home until 1997. The Kensington State Rooms are open to the public during the day. The Kensington neighbourhood to the south is one of London's finest for a walk through Victorian residential streets.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Ickworth House is one of England's most singular residences: a 30-metre-diameter central rotunda flanked by two curved wings, built by the 4th Earl of Bristol in the late eighteenth century. The Hervey family's painting collection—Velázquez, Gainsborough, Titian—is displayed in the state rooms. National Trust, 4km south of Bury St Edmunds.

The 1,800-acre park designed by Capability Brown surrounds the house with century-old woods, meadows and formal gardens. A path allows a 90-minute circuit of the estate on foot. The Ickworth Hotel restaurant, housed in the east wing, serves lunch to non-residents.

activities.text: You end the day at Ickworth House, a National Trust property built by the 4th Earl of Bristol in the late 18th century. Its central rotunda, 30 metres in diameter, and its 1,800 acres of parkland designed by Capability Brown make it a remarkable stop. Open all year; the park is accessible by car.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: It is hard to remain indifferent to Verity at Ilfracombe harbor. Damien Hirst’s sculpture depicts a pregnant woman with her anatomy exposed on one side; at 20.25 meters tall, it changes the scale of the quay. View it from both sides to appreciate the contrast, keeping your distance from the edge of the pier in windy weather.

days_plan.itin_title: North Devon and Exmoor: 3 Days of Headlands and Villages

visits.text: It’s worth stepping inside Traquair House, near Innerleithen, rather than just viewing its facade. The Stuart family has lived in this house since 1491, a continuity that adds another dimension to its historic rooms. Plan your visit for a day other than Friday from April through June and in September: the house is closed that day.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Borders in 3 Days: Castles and Great Abbeys

visits.text: Photograph Kilchurn Castle from the shores of Loch Awe, one of Scotland's most romantic ruins, jutting out on a promontory with heather-covered slopes rising behind it. On calm days, the castle's reflection is perfectly mirrored in the water, creating images that have graced countless calendars and postcards. Built in the 15th century by Sir Colin Campbell, the castle now stands as a picturesque reminder of the powerful clan that once controlled these lands. Allow for a return trip from Inveraray for this visit.

Explore Inveraray, an interesting Georgian planned town on the edge of Loch Fyne whose uniform white-painted facades create a harmonious streetscape. The high street offers eclectic shops, galleries and cute cafes, including the famous Loch Fyne Whiskies with its extraordinary selection. The War Memorial provides a great spot to take in views across Loch Fyne to the hills beyond.

Visit Inveraray Castle, the fairy-tale home of the Duke and Duchess of Argyll, whose turrets and towers rise above magnificent landscaped grounds. This grand seat of Clan Campbell has welcomed visitors for generations with its impressive state rooms, extensive armory and beautiful gardens. The castle's combination of medieval romance and aristocratic elegance epitomizes the grand houses of the Scottish Highlands.

activities.text: Sample world-famous oysters and seafood at the Loch Fyne Oyster House at the head of the loch

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Highlands: 15 Days of Castles, Lochs and Wild Landscapes

visits.text: The last section of the NC500 heads south through the Black Isle—actually a peninsula, not an island. Chanonry Point, a narrow spit on the Moray Firth south of Fortrose, is Scotland's most reliable place to see bottlenose dolphins from the shore. The Moray Firth population is the world's northernmost and one of the most studied. Dolphins fish in the strong tidal current off the point, especially on the rising tide—arrive 2 hours before high tide and stand on the beach. Sightings are possible year-round, more reliably from May to September. Plan a return drive from Inverness.

Cromarty, at the tip of the Black Isle, is one of Scotland's best-preserved 18th-century towns—a planned trading town that prospered through commerce with the Baltic states and American colonies before the railway bypassed it and sealed it in amber. The birthplace of Hugh Miller, the stonemason turned geologist and writer who became one of the Victorian era's most important scientific voices—his 1841 book The Old Red Sandstone transformed popular understanding of geology and fossils—is preserved as a museum. Miller died in 1856 aged 54, having spent his life arguing that northern Scotland's rocks held stories older than anyone had imagined. The 1782 courthouse still stands. Walk along the high street and down to the harbour. Plan a return drive from Inverness.

Back in Inverness, 8 km to the east lies Culloden Battlefield - the site of the last pitched battle fought on British soil, on 16 April 1746. The Jacobite army of Bonnie Prince Charlie was destroyed in under an hour by the Duke of Cumberland's government forces; around 1,500 Jacobites were killed against 50 government troops. The defeat ended the Stuart claim to the throne and triggered the systematic dismantling of Highland clan culture: the wearing of tartan was banned, clan chiefs stripped of their powers. The National Trust for Scotland's visitor centre (opened 2007) is one of the best battlefield interpretive centres in Britain - the immersive 360° film is genuinely affecting. Allow 1.5 hours.

Cawdor Castle, east of Inverness on the B9090, is forever associated with Macbeth—although Shakespeare's play predates the castle's title of thane of Cawdor by centuries and the historical Macbeth had nothing to do with this building. The castle itself, built around a 14th-century tower, is one of Scotland's most liveable historic houses: the present family still lives there, and the interiors feel inhabited rather than preserved. The gardens are exceptional. Plan a return trip from Inverness. Open from late April to early October.

activities.text: Glenmorangie distillery in Tain, on the southern shore of the Dornoch Firth, produces one of Scotland's most distinctive single malts—distilled in Scotland's tallest stills (5.14 metres, roughly a giraffe's height, chosen to produce a lighter, more floral spirit). Founded in 1843, it is now owned by LVMH. Tours and tastings are available, and the visitor experience is excellent. Allow 1.5 hours. Plan a return drive from Inverness.

Clava Cairns, 10 km east of Inverness near Culloden, are three Neolithic passage tombs and ring cairns built around 2000 BC. They are free to visit, almost always empty of tourists, and more immediately accessible than most prehistoric monuments - you can walk into the chambers. The Bronze Age cairns are aligned with the winter solstice sunset. If you've seen Culloden and are travelling through Outlander country, these are the stones that inspired the Craig na Dun circle in Diana Gabaldon's fiction.

days_plan.itin_title: Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye
Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye
Scottish Highlands: 15 Days of Castles, Lochs and Wild Landscapes
North Coast 500 with Orkney: Scotland's Ultimate Coastal Circuit
North Coast 500 with Orkney: Scotland's Ultimate Coastal Circuit
Haunted Scotland: 7 Days in the Land of Ghosts
Scotland: Highlands & Skye in 12 days

visits.text: Dedham Vale, on the Suffolk-Essex border, is one of the most famous landscapes in English painting—John Constable was born at East Bergholt in 1776 and painted it all his life. Stop at East Bergholt: St Mary's church has a sixteenth-century wooden bell cage standing on the ground in the churchyard—it's the only example of this type still in use in England. From there, head down to Flatford, where his father owned a mill: Flatford Mill is now managed by the National Trust, and you'll immediately recognise the landscape from The Hay Wain, painted here in 1821.

Dedham is the best-preserved village in Dedham Vale, with its great Tudor church and its Georgian houses lined up. It's also an active artists' village: the painter Alfred Munnings (1878–1959) lived here and his former home is now a museum open in summer. Walk the path from Dedham to Flatford Mill along the Stour (thirty minutes)—it's the shortest route into Constable country.

Christchurch Mansion in Ipswich is a mid-sixteenth-century Tudor house converted into a museum and art gallery in a large public park. It holds the world's largest collection of paintings by Constable and Gainsborough outside London—admission is free. The interior rooms are furnished in the style of each era, from Tudor to Victorian, making it as much an interior design tour as a painting gallery.

Ipswich's Waterfront has been entirely redeveloped around the old Victorian dock. The seventeenth-century Old Custom House, the converted red-brick warehouses and the moored boats create a particular atmosphere. Ipswich claims the title of England's oldest town (founded by the Angles in the seventh century), though Colchester disputes this claim. Head down to the quayside in late afternoon for restaurant tables on the terrace overlooking the basin.

activities.text: Walk or cycle along the River Stour between Flatford and Dedham: the waymarked path follows the historic towpath for around five kilometres, between meadows and willows, with several viewpoints over scenes almost identical to Constable's paintings. Several companies offer kayaks or rowing boats for hire in Dedham to go upriver to Flatford.

days_plan.itin_title: From Cambridge to London: Eastern England in 6 days

visits.text: Head down toward the Severn and you'll see it all at once - the cast-iron bridge spanning the gorge since 1781. Abraham Darby III had it cast with 378 tons of metal in his own Coalbrookdale foundry, using a traditional timber carpentry technique transposed to iron: mortises, dovetails, traditional joinery. The whole thing cost over £6,000 and changed the history of construction. A UNESCO site since 1986, you can walk across it for free. Go early in the morning - the low light on the wooded gorge and the metal is magnificent, and you'll avoid the coaches.

The Museum of the Gorge, housed in a Victorian warehouse on the banks of the Severn, is the best entry point into the site's history. An 8-minute video summarizes how this Shropshire valley triggered the global industrial revolution - and the collections help explain why the entire world sent its engineers here in the 18th century. ⚠️ Note: the entire Gorge museum complex was transferred to the National Trust in early 2026 and is reopening progressively - check opening times online before you go.

At Coalbrookdale, 2 km from the bridge, Abraham Darby I's old blast furnace is still there. This is where in 1709 he perfected smelting iron with coke rather than charcoal - which made mass industrial production possible and triggered everything that followed. You can see the original furnace, protected under a covered structure. Understated, but dizzying when you realize what started here.

activities.text: Blists Hill Victorian Town, a few kilometers into the gorge, is an open-air museum that recreates a Shropshire mining town circa 1900. What distinguishes it from other museums of this kind: the buildings are authentic, salvaged and moved from the region, and at the entrance you exchange your pounds sterling for Victorian currency to shop in the stores. The costumed staff fully play their roles - the blacksmith forges, the printer prints, the pharmacist advises with period remedies. Allow half a day. ⚠️ Reopening scheduled from May 2026 under National Trust management.

In the late afternoon, walk along the Severn from the bridge to the Bedlam Furnaces - ruins of 18th-century blast furnaces that vegetation is beginning to reclaim. Access is free and the evening light on the red brick and ivy is striking. It's one of Ironbridge's most powerful images, and few people make this detour.

days_plan.itin_title: Midlands and Peak District Road Trip: Heritage and Wild Landscapes
Welsh Marches, Cotswolds and Bath in 11 days

visits.text: More than seventy years of construction explain Jedburgh Abbey’s mix of Romanesque and Gothic architecture. The great arcades are impressive, but the remains of the kitchens and cellars also tell the story of the religious community’s daily life. Buy your ticket online for a lower price than at the ticket office; access to the viewing gallery remains subject to conservation restrictions announced by the site operator.

The Mary Queen of Scots’ Visitor Centre puts a human face on the conflicts of the Scottish Borders. This 16th-century tower house explores Mary, Queen of Scots’ stay in Jedburgh in 1566 through paintings, objects, and textiles. Admission is free; from April through October, it closes at 4 p.m. Monday through Saturday and at 3 p.m. on Sunday.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Borders in 3 Days: Castles and Great Abbeys

activities.text: Arrange your pickup in Keith before starting the Speyside loop. The main train station is on Station Road and has a drop-off area and parking. It provides a convenient meeting point for reaching the distilleries in a vehicle arranged in advance. Book this transfer or vehicle service: this itinerary does not assume there is a car rental agency at the station.

Return to Keith to complete the loop and spend your final night in Moray. The main train station, on Station Road, provides rail access and a pickup point; it serves as your departure landmark for the following day. Agree on a vehicle drop-off location with your rental company and keep your tickets handy: this itinerary does not assume that rental services are available on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Speyside and the Moray Coast: Whisky and Villages in 3 Days
Speyside and the Moray Coast: Whisky and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: A fairy-tale castle that remains a family home, Floors Castle is still home to the Duke and Duchess of Roxburghe. The rooms open to the public display tapestries, paintings, and porcelain, among other items. Plan this visit for a time when the interiors are open; in winter, access to the walled garden does not mean the castle is open for visits.

The Walled Garden at Floors Castle combines flower beds with vegetable growing, making it much more than a decorative castle garden. Grapes, figs, and peaches are among the crops grown in the Victorian greenhouses; some of the harvest supplies the estate’s kitchens. Allow time to reach the garden from the castle.

If you would like to compare the abbeys along the route, allow twenty minutes for the remains of Kelso Abbey. The monks settled here in 1128, near the royal castle of Roxburgh; the remains shed light on its former importance. Check whether the enclosure is open and, if it is closed, limit your visit to views from public areas.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Borders in 3 Days: Castles and Great Abbeys

activities.text: Kennacraig is just a terminal: CalMac ferries to Port Askaig on Islay leave from here. There is nothing else to see on site, so simply arrive in time for boarding.
Kennacraig marks the end of the tour: this is where the Islay ferry arrives. There is nothing to see on site, so you get straight back on the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores
Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores

visits.text: Sculpture wrongly called Janus, because the Boa Island statue doesn't have two faces on one head but two complete figures back to back. Dated between the Iron Age and early Irish Christianity (400-800 AD). 73 cm tall, arms crossed, tongue stuck out. Archaeologist Dorothy Lowry-Corry publicised it in 1933. The island's name comes from Inis Badhbha, island of the war goddess. Mysterious and genuinely solitary, almost never anyone on site.

activities.text: Waterlogged field, small rusty iron cross marks the entrance. Caldragh cemetery is still in use, keep your voice down. No information panel, no shop, no bin. Wear shoes that accept mud, especially in spring. Count time to and from the road, 15 minutes. Free, accessible year-round.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Ireland in 7 days: Belfast, Causeway & Derry

places.name: Keswick

visits.text: Arrive at Castlerigg early in the morning, before the tour coaches - at 7am mist still covers the fells and you'll be alone with 38 stones raised 5,000 years ago. This circle of volcanic lava, built around 3200 BC, is probably older than Stonehenge. From inside, you see Helvellyn, Skiddaw and Blencathra in every direction - the Neolithic builders chose this plateau as a natural amphitheatre. Coleridge had visited it with Wordsworth in 1799 and described it as a place where “the mountains stand in order as if summoned by magicians”. Free access, managed by the National Trust. From Keswick centre, allow 30 minutes on foot.

The Derwent Pencil Museum in Keswick tells a story you wouldn't expect: here, in Borrowdale a few kilometres away, the world's first pure graphite deposit was discovered in 1565. The material was so strategic that miners slept on-site to prevent theft and the Crown banned its export. The first pencils were carved locally, wrapped in string. Allow 45 minutes - it's an unusual stop 10 minutes' walk from the centre, and makes a change from the fells.

Take the detour to Ullswater, 30 minutes south-east of Keswick - many consider it the Lake District's most beautiful lake, and with good reason. It was on its shores that Dorothy Wordsworth noted in 1802 that she had seen 'a crowd of golden daffodils' - the entry that inspired her brother's most famous poem. Take the boat one way and return on foot along the lakeside path: the Ullswater Steamers have been in service since the 1850s, and combining the two gives you the best perspectives on the lake.

Aira Force is worth the detour even in the rain - especially in the rain, in fact. This 20-metre waterfall tumbles into a wooded gorge at the northern end of Ullswater, owned by the National Trust since 1906. Two stone bridges span it at different heights: go up to the upper bridge first to see the waterfall from above, then descend to the lower bridge to feel the spray. Wordsworth drew inspiration from it for several poems. There is a parking charge, but access to the waterfall is free. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the return walk from the car park. Plan a return drive from Keswick to the car park in addition to the walk.

Glenridding is a tiny village at the foot of Helvellyn, beside Ullswater. The Ullswater Steamers and walks to the summits depart from here. If you did not climb Catbells yesterday and your legs still have something left, Place Fell from Glenridding is a less well-known but superb alternative - fewer people, the same lake views. Plan a return drive from Keswick to Glenridding in addition to any walk.

activities.text: A cruise on Derwentwater with the Keswick Launches lets you go around the lake in 50 minutes, with stops at several landing stages leading to paths of varying lengths. The full circuit gives access to Friars Crag, a promontory that John Ruskin described as “one of the three most beautiful scenes in Europe”.

For experienced walkers, the ascent of Helvellyn via Striding Edge is the Lake District's most spectacular hike: 950 metres of elevation gain, a rocky ridge exposed on both sides, and a summit view taking in the whole park. Allow 6 to 7 hours from Patterdale. Not recommended in bad weather or in winter without suitable equipment. Plan a return drive from Keswick to Patterdale in addition to the walk.

The Ullswater Steamers are boats that have been in service since the 1850s. The cruise between Pooley Bridge and Glenridding takes about 35 minutes each way. Combine the outward cruise with the lakeside path on the return for a perfect half-day. Plan a return trip from Keswick to the boarding point.

activities.text: The sound of your footsteps replaces the rumble of trains on Kielder Viaduct. From the village, the former trackbed of the Border Counties Railway leads to this structure, now part of a walking route. Take a leisurely out-and-back walk before your astronomy evening; save the long hike around the reservoir for another stay so you do not arrive at the observatory tired.

If the sky clears, Kielder Observatory lets you gaze far beyond the village lights. Guided sessions combine astronomy and observation, although clouds may obscure celestial objects. Book your event before the trip and follow its access instructions: the gravel track is suitable for regular cars but remains closed outside scheduled sessions.

days_plan.itin_title: Hadrian’s Wall and Northumberland: 7 Days Between the Sea and the Forts

visits.text: The wind blows through the openings of Kilchoman Church, above the dunes of Machir Bay. The ruined church and its neighboring cemetery also preserve a medieval cross: this stop builds on the visit to Kildalton in a more exposed setting. Stay in accessible areas, observe the carvings without touching them, and avoid fragile areas if restrictions are posted.

In 1918, the wreck of the Otranto left a lasting mark on this coast. Kilchoman Military Cemetery preserves victims’ graves near the village and its old church. This understated stop gives another meaning to the ocean glimpsed from the dunes; keep a low profile and close gates behind you.

activities.text: Kilchoman Distillery connects whisky with the fields around it. At Rockside Farm, the tour links agricultural work with the stages of production; this farm setting offers a change from harborfront facilities. Book the tour available on your dates, as the winter route may differ, and leave time for Machir Bay.

You’ll head down to Machir Bay after the distillery to walk between the dunes and the Atlantic. This nearby beach gave its name to a Kilchoman whisky: here, the label becomes a landscape again. Walk along the sand with the tide in mind, without turning this exposed stop into an impromptu swim.

days_plan.itin_title: Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores

visits.text: Kildalton Cross sets its delicate interlace patterns against the open sky above the cemetery. Carved in the 8th century, this cross still stands in its original location: the landscape is as much a part of the visit as the stone itself. Walk around it without touching the relief carvings; Historic Environment Scotland lists free access year-round.

Younger than its carved neighbor, Kildalton Church tells the story of another period at the site. The church was built after 1200 and had fallen out of religious use by around 1700; its roofless walls now frame the sky. View the gravestones from the accessible paths as well, without stepping on the slabs or climbing on the masonry.

days_plan.itin_title: Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores

places.name: King S Lynn

visits.text: The Sandringham Estate is open to the public for much of the year—it's a rare opportunity to visit a private residence of the Royal Family still inhabited. The house was built in Jacobean Revival style for the Prince of Wales (later Edward VII) between 1870 and 1900. George V died here in 1936, George VI in 1952. Allow at least two hours: the museum of royal cars and the estate's nature reserve justify the trip on their own. Avoid the Christmas and early January period, when the family is in residence and the house is closed.

Houghton Hall, about 23 kilometres east of King's Lynn, a 25-minute drive away, is the Palladian home of Sir Robert Walpole, prime minister from 1721 to 1742 - the man who invented the office. The domed hall and state apartments decorated by William Kent are impressive. What makes the visit particularly interesting today is that the estate is still inhabited by Walpole's descendants and hosts major contemporary sculpture exhibitions in the gardens each summer - James Turrell, Richard Long and Zaha Hadid have exhibited there. If you visit in summer, check which exhibition is scheduled that year.

Set aside an hour to wander King's Lynn's historic centre—it's one of England's best-preserved medieval ports and it's largely ignored by tourists. Head down to the quayside on the Great Ouse to see the seventeenth-century Old Custom House, the town's emblematic image. The Guildhall of the Holy Trinity (1421) is one of the rare civic buildings from Henry V's era still in use. For an anecdote worth the detour: look for the Hanseatic Warehouse, built in 1475, one of the very few surviving Hanseatic League trading posts in England—proof that King's Lynn traded directly with Baltic towns in the Middle Ages.

Castle Rising, eight kilometres northeast of King's Lynn, is one of England's best-preserved Norman keeps. Built around 1140, it served as the residence of Isabella of France after her exile from court in 1330—the Queen Mother, nicknamed the “She-Wolf of France”, lived here for nearly 30 years until her death in 1358. The twelfth-century outer ramparts and the keep are open to the public.

activities.text: Watching migratory birds at The Wash reserve, the shallow estuary between Norfolk and Lincolnshire. It's one of Europe's most important wader sites: up to 350,000 birds winter or stop here during migration. The best observations take place at rising tide, when the birds gather on the few remaining exposed areas. Several access points from the coastal roads between Hunstanton and Snettisham.

East Anglia Circuit: Cambridge, Suffolk Coast and Royal Norfolk

map_keywords: True's Yard Fisherfolk Museum King's Lynn

visits.text: The Deep, at the tip of Sammy's Point where the River Hull flows into the Humber Estuary, is one of the UK's largest aquariums — 5,000 marine species across 50 spaces in an iceberg-shaped building designed by Terry Farrell. It opened in March 2002 with funding from the Millennium Commission, at a total cost of £52 million. The highlight: a tunnel 9 metres below the surface in the heart of a 2.5-million-litre tank containing 87 tonnes of salt — several species of sharks pass overhead. Divers feed the sharks in front of visitors every afternoon. Allow at least 2 hours.

The Ferens Art Gallery, on Queen Victoria Square, has been open since 1927 — local MP Thomas Robinson Ferens paid for the building out of his own pocket after spending 22 years giving the city money to buy paintings. The permanent collection is one of the finest regional collections: 17th-century Flemish masters, maritime paintings of Hull, and a portrait of a young woman by Frans Hals. In 2017, the gallery hosted the Turner Prize as part of Hull's year as City of Culture. Free admission.

Wilberforce House, on High Street in the Old Town, is the birthplace of William Wilberforce (1759–1833), the MP who devoted his life to abolishing slavery across the British Empire. The museum, opened as early as 1906, traces the reality of the transatlantic slave trade and Wilberforce's decades-long battle leading to the Abolition Act of 1807. Personal journals and belongings are on display. Don't miss the garden out front, named after Nelson Mandela. Free entry.

Hull Minster—formerly Holy Trinity Church—is one of England's largest parish churches by floor area. Its brick tower dates from the 14th century: Hull built in brick because the city imported materials from the Netherlands via the estuary, lacking local stone. It was in this church that the city gathered in 1642 to decide to close its gates to King Charles I—an act that directly helped trigger the English Civil War. Allow 30 to 45 minutes.

The Streetlife Museum of Transport, free to enter, traces 200 years of transport history with a genuine collection of carriages, trams and period bicycles. The place is less touristy than The Deep and often quieter — ideal in the middle of the day when children start flagging. Allow an hour.

Humber Street Gallery occupies a converted warehouse in the Fruit Market, Hull's creative quarter along the estuary. Since Hull City of Culture 2017, this contemporary art space has become the heart of the local arts scene — rotating exhibitions, regional artists' work and international shows. Check the online programme before visiting.

The Paragon Arcade, in the city centre, is a Victorian glass-roofed shopping arcade dating from 1887. You'll find second-hand bookshops, independent record shops and small cafés — the kind of place that no longer exists in modern shopping centres. Half an hour is enough for a wander.

activities.text: Hull's Old Town has its historic lanes clustered between High Street and the River Hull. Look for Ye Olde White Harte, a Grade II* listed pub built in 1550 — tradition has it that the governor of Hull refused to hand over the keys to the city to Charles I here in 1642, precipitating the start of the English Civil War. The carved oak interior is worth a detour.

Come evening, head to the Fruit Market for dinner: the area around Humber Street has transformed since 2017 into a hub of independent restaurants. Fresh fish from the Humber, local craft beers, terraces facing the estuary. A way to end the day by the water rather than in the city centre.

days_plan.itin_title: Yorkshire: Wild Coast & Secret Moorlands
North York Moors Road Trip: Coast and Villages

visits.text: To get a sense of Agatha Christie, Greenway offers more than a mystery setting. Her vacation home retains a 1950s atmosphere and family collections; a frieze painted in 1944 also recalls its military occupation. You must reserve parking if you’re arriving by car, then continue to Kingswear after your visit.

activities.text: You’ll walk down through Greenway’s gardens to the Boathouse on the banks of the Dart. This boathouse provides a crime scene in Dead Man’s Folly, while the wooded gardens offer views of the river. Allow for the climb back up and wear shoes with good traction; access to the Boathouse interior depends on volunteer availability.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

places.name: Kirkwall

visits.text: The east coast of Caithness is flat, agricultural and windswept - a dramatic change from the mountain scenery of Sutherland. Before catching the ferry at Scrabster, make time for Duncansby Head, 3 km east of John O'Groats along a track from the car park. The headland is the true north-east corner of the mainland, and the Duncansby Stacks - three tall sea stacks separated from the cliffs by narrow geos - are among the most striking rock formations on the north coast. Fulmars nest on every ledge. The 20-minute walk from the lighthouse takes you to the cliff edge above the largest stack.

The Castle of Mey, 12 km west of John O'Groats on the A836, was a derelict 16th-century castle when Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother bought it in 1952 as a personal retreat after the death of George VI. She renovated it herself and used it as a private holiday home until her death in 2002. It is now a charitable trust and open to the public from May to September. The walled garden is particularly well maintained. If you have time before the ferry, allow 90 minutes.

Skara Brae, on the Bay of Skaill, lay buried under sand for almost 4,000 years until a severe storm in 1850 swept away the dunes and revealed the roofs of a Neolithic village. What emerged was northern Europe's best-preserved prehistoric village: eight stone houses connected by covered passages, with stone furniture—beds, dressers and hearths—still in place as left around 2500 BC. The residents raised cattle and sheep, grew grain, fished and made pottery. Who they were, why they abandoned the village and where they went remain unknown. A replica house beside the visitor centre shows the interiors at full scale. Book ahead in summer—visitor numbers are managed. Plan a return drive from Kirkwall.

The Ring of Brodgar and the Stones of Stenness lie between two lochs and form part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site “Heart of Neolithic Orkney”, designated in 1999; plan a return trip from Kirkwall. The Ring of Brodgar is a true circle 130 metres in diameter, originally with 60 stones, of which 27 survive, surrounded by a ditch cut into the rock up to 3 metres deep. It is estimated to have taken 80,000 person-hours to build. The Stones of Stenness, erected around 3100 BC, are older, and the four remaining megaliths stand up to 6 metres high. Both stone circles are free to visit. Maeshowe, the passage tomb whose entrance aligns with the winter solstice sunset, is nearby—book a guided visit ahead; the runic inscriptions left by Norse raiders in the 12th century are extraordinary.

The Churchill Barriers, four causeways connecting the southern islands of Orkney, were built between 1940 and 1945 to block the eastern approaches to Scapa Flow after a German U-boat torpedoed HMS Royal Oak in the anchorage in October 1939, killing 833 men. The 1,700 Italian prisoners of war who built the barriers also constructed the Italian Chapel on Lamb Holm - two Nissen huts converted into a remarkably ornate Roman Catholic chapel with trompe l'oeil, a concrete screen and an altar fronted with painted iron. The main craftsman, Domenico Chiocchetti, returned in 1960 and 1964 to restore the work he had done as a prisoner. It is one of the most affecting places in Scotland.

Scapa Flow, the natural harbour enclosed by the southern Orkney islands, was the main base of the British Grand Fleet in both World Wars. After the German fleet surrendered in 1918, 74 ships were interned here. In June 1919, the German admiral ordered all ships run aground rather than allow them to be taken as prizes - 52 sank, some in shallow water. Seven warships still lie on the seabed, offering some of the best wreck diving in the world. The Orkney Museum in Kirkwall tells the Scapa Flow story well, with artefacts from both German and British ships.

activities.text: The NorthLink Ferries service from Scrabster to Stromness (Orkney) takes 90 minutes and runs twice daily. As the ferry crosses the Pentland Firth - a stretch of water with some of Europe's strongest tides - look back towards the Old Man of Hoy, a 137-metre sea stack visible from the upper deck. Then look forward: the low green coastline of Orkney Mainland emerging from the water with no mountains, no drama, just a flat ancient landscape - which makes the concentration of Neolithic monuments waiting there all the more astonishing. Book well in advance in summer, particularly with a car.

St Magnus Cathedral in Kirkwall, begun in 1137 by Jarl Rögnvald in memory of his uncle Magnus who was martyred in 1117, is the most northerly medieval cathedral in Britain and has been in continuous use for nearly 900 years. It is built entirely from red and yellow Orkney sandstone with no imported stone - one of the purest expressions of local materials in Scottish ecclesiastical architecture. Entry is free. In the choir, human remains later identified as those of Magnus himself were found concealed in a pillar in 1919.

The ferry from Houton to Hoy must be followed by a road journey to Rackwick Bay, then the walk to the Old Man of Hoy—a 137-metre sandstone sea stack first climbed in July 1966 by Tom Patey, Hamish MacInnes and Pete Crew. The following year, a BBC broadcast of a second ascent involving Chris Bonington, Patey and MacInnes was watched by about 15 million people—one of history's most-watched climbing broadcasts. The cliff walk above the stack from Rackwick Bay takes about 3 hours return across moorland. A longer 8 km circuit via the summit plateau is one of Orkney's best day hikes. Note that Houton is a 30-minute drive west of Kirkwall—allow for this when planning the day. Book the ferry ahead.

visits.text: With its thoroughly Gothic façade—turrets, gargoyles, domes—Knebworth House hides a Tudor brick house dating to 1490 behind its Victorian stucco. This is where Edward Bulwer-Lytton, the novelist who coined the phrase “it was a dark and stormy night,” worked in a study adorned with a crystal ball. The Lytton family still lives here. Guided tours available in season.

Knebworth House's park opens onto 250 acres of Hertfordshire countryside, with a dinosaur trail for children, a golden garden, and a rose garden. The view of the façade from the main lawn is the one that appears in all the castle photographs.

activities.text: Get lost in the maze in Knebworth's garden—entry is included in the park ticket. Visit the house in the morning when there are few groups, and save the maze for the afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: At Lacock Abbey, the atmosphere changes as you move from one space to the next: monastic spaces sit alongside a family home. After the abbey closed in the 16th century, the building was converted into a residence. Start with the indoor spaces you want to see and check their last admission times: opening hours for the cloister and rooms may differ.

In 1835, a window at Lacock Abbey became the subject of a photographic experiment by William Henry Fox Talbot. The Fox Talbot Museum places this image within the early history of photography: a domestic detail offers a window onto an invention that changed the way we see. Check its opening hours separately before continuing your visit to the village.

If you enjoy examining the details of facades, leave time for the village of Lacock. Its stone houses, medieval barn, and St Cyriac’s Church offer a brief introduction to the village on foot, beyond the abbey. Stay in publicly accessible areas: the doors and windows you photograph also belong to people’s homes.
