The Impressionist room is always packed—arrive at 10am or during lunch. Allow 2 to 3 hours minimum.

activities.text: Free audio guides are available via the National Gallery app—an excellent way to delve deeper into the most important paintings without following a group.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

places.name: National Maritime Museum

visits.text: The National Maritime Museum in Greenwich is the world's largest maritime museum, with nearly 2.5 million objects in its collections. Established by Act of Parliament in 1934 and opened in 1937, it occupies the buildings of the former Royal Hospital School, including the 17th-century Queen's House designed by Inigo Jones. The museum's most moving object—and one of the most poignant in all of England—is the admiral's coat Nelson wore at the Battle of Trafalgar on 21 October 1805. You can still see the bullet hole in the left shoulder of the uniform, at the precise spot where the French marksman from the Redoutable shot him at 1:15pm. The right sleeve is pinned—a reminder that Nelson had lost that arm at the Battle of Santa Cruz de Tenerife in 1795. He died a few hours later knowing that the Franco-Spanish fleet had been defeated. Don't miss the gilded 19-metre state barge built in 1732 for the Prince of Wales, and Turner's largest painting, The Battle of Trafalgar (1824). Make the trip to Greenwich: the area deserves a full half-day, between the museum, the Royal Observatory and the Greenwich meridian.

activities.text: Take advantage of your Greenwich visit to climb to the Royal Observatory—15 minutes on foot uphill from the museum. You can photograph yourself straddling the prime meridian and see John Harrison's H4 marine chronometer, which solved the longitude problem in the 18th century.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

map_keywords: Nelson Trafalgar coat National Maritime Museum

visits.text: The National Portrait Gallery, a stone's throw from the National Gallery, reopened in 2023 after a major renovation and presents historical and contemporary portraits of people who shaped British history - from Queen Elizabeth I to today's celebrities. The collection is arranged chronologically: start from the top floor and work your way down through the centuries. If you are short of time, focus on the Tudor and Stuart galleries, where you will find the most striking portraits, including a portrait of Shakespeare.

activities.text: The top-floor restaurant, opened since the 2023 renovation, offers sweeping views over Trafalgar Square and London's rooftops—a good option for lunch after visiting the neighbouring National Gallery.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

visits.text: The Natural History Museum opened in 1881 in its neo-Romanesque South Kensington building designed by Alfred Waterhouse. Hintze Hall has housed Hope since 2017 - a female blue whale 25.2 metres long (221 bones, 4.5 tonnes) stranded in Wexford harbour, Ireland in March 1891 and purchased by the Museum for £250. She's suspended from the ceiling in a spiralling diving posture - the only blue whale in the world presented in this position. In the 1960s, an estimated 400 blue whales remained worldwide; it was in London in 1966 that their commercial hunting was banned. Admission is free.

The Dinosaur galleries (Blue Zone) house some of the most complete fossils ever found in the UK. The Minerals gallery (Red Zone) includes fragments of Martian and lunar meteorites. Two hours minimum to see it properly.

activities.text: South Kensington concentrates three free national museums within a 300-metre radius: the Natural History Museum, Science Museum and Victoria & Albert Museum. If time permits, push on to the V&A - its fashion, design and decorative arts collections are among the world's finest.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries
What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: In clear weather, the Outer Hebrides – Benbecula, South Uist – stand out on the horizon as seen from the lighthouse. This is Skye's westernmost point. The 2.2 km return path descends steeply to the lighthouse, lit since 1 November 1909 and now automated from Edinburgh.

Neist Point lighthouse has been lit since 1 November 1909 and automated since 1990. In season, the surrounding cliffs shelter gannets, guillemots and razorbills. At sea: basking sharks, dolphins, porpoises and occasionally orcas.

activities.text: The car park fills quickly, but the headland stays peaceful: visitors cluster mainly at sunset, one of Skye's most spectacular. From the gate at the top, the path forks—right towards the cliffs for the classic view, left towards the moorland for solitude. No toilets on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Scotland: Highlands & Skye in 12 days

visits.text: The Welsh call it the island of the lovers' saint: Llanddwyn is dedicated to Saint Dwynwen, Welsh patron saint of lovers since the 5th century, whose feast day on 25th January corresponds to the 'Welsh Valentine's Day'. The peninsula only becomes an island at the highest tides. You reach it on foot from Newborough car park, through the dunes and forest of the national reserve—about 30 to 45 minutes. The ruins of the medieval chapel, the lighthouse, and the views across to Snowdonia reward the effort.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: The museum is free, small, and far better than its address in a Jacobean clothworkers' building might suggest. The West Berkshire Museum documents the two Battles of Newbury from the English Civil War: in September 1643, the Earl of Essex's Parliamentary army halted the Royalist advance in the fields of Wash Common; in October 1644, the second battle around Donnington Castle deepened the Royalist quagmire. Historians consider the First Battle of Newbury a turning point in the Civil War. Open Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday, 11am-4pm. Free.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days

visits.text: Exposed to the wind, Newcastle's promenade offers views of Dundrum Bay and the Mourne Mountains. Slieve Donard rises above the seaside resort: the mountain begins almost immediately behind the streets. Stop along the waterfront to get a sense of the terrain before your walks, keeping a windproof layer handy.

activities.text: Take the Red Trail through Tollymore Forest Park along the Shimna River. This three-mile loop, approximately 4.8 km, passes the Hermitage and crosses the river at Parnell's Bridge before returning via the Old Bridge. Look for the red arrows as you leave the parking lot; roots and stones become slippery after rain.

The right compromise for this short stay is the Glen River at the foot of Slieve Donard. From Donard Park, the trail climbs through Donard Wood and crosses several bridges before reaching open mountain terrain. Plan to turn back in the woods after about 40 minutes; climbing to the summit requires an extra day on this itinerary.

days_plan.itin_title: Mourne and Strangford in 3 Days: Gardens, Sea, and Woods
Mourne and Strangford in 3 Days: Gardens, Sea, and Woods

places.name: Newcastle Upon Tyne

visits.text: Go down to the Quayside and look at the bridges. The Tyne Bridge - the great green arch inaugurated in 1928 by King George V - is Newcastle's icon, and it hides a story almost nobody knows. The same engineering firm, Dorman Long of Middlesbrough, later built Australia's Sydney Harbour Bridge. At the opening, their representative said clearly that Newcastle had served as a 'full-scale trial for the Sydney bridge'. Compare the two photos: the arches are virtually identical. Another detail: at its construction, the Tyne Bridge was Britain's longest steel arch bridge.

Cross the Gateshead Millennium Bridge on foot - it is the only tilting bridge of this type in the world, and it is as simple as that. Its two steel arcs tilt together like a blinking eye, allowing boats through with 25 metres of clearance. The manoeuvre takes 4 and a half minutes: 36,000 people gathered on the banks to watch the first tilt in June 2001. Across the river on the Gateshead bank, the BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art occupies a former flour mill converted in 2002 - admission is free, and the exhibitions change regularly.

Newcastle Castle Keep deserves 45 minutes - and not because it's grand, but because it's strange. The castle that gave the city its name is today wedged between two Victorian railway viaducts that literally pass through its former bailey. Henry II had it built in 1167 on an earlier Norman fortification. Climb to the top of the keep for views over the Tyne and bridges - and to see just how little the Victorians hesitated to run their trains straight through the middle of a medieval castle.

activities.text: If you want to see Newcastle off the beaten track, head to the Ouseburn Valley - 15 minutes' walk east of the centre. This is the creative quarter: artists' studios, microbreweries, concerts in converted Victorian warehouses. The Victoria Tunnel, a former 19th-century coal transport tunnel dug beneath the city, offers tours by head torch. Book ahead, slots go quickly.

The Quayside in the evening is a Newcastle institution. Bars and restaurants line both banks between the Tyne Bridge and Swing Bridge, and the Geordie atmosphere - that's the nickname for Newcastle residents - is direct and warm. If you want to try local food: the stottie is a thick round bread typical of the region, and pease pudding (split pea purée) is eaten in sandwiches. You won't find this anywhere else in England.

days_plan.itin_title: England Grand Tour: From Cornwall to the Northern Lakes
Lake District and North-East Loop: Lakes, Dales and Cathedrals
Yorkshire and North East England: Dales and Coasts

map_keywords: BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art Gateshead

visits.text: Charles I stayed at Carisbrooke Castle as a prisoner rather than a sovereign before his trial. Viewed from the keep, the ramparts create a very different scene from Osborne’s drawing rooms; at the well, donkeys still turn the wheel during demonstrations. Ask for demonstration times when you arrive: the bucket is raised from a depth of 49 meters.

If you pass through central Newport, stop at St Thomas’ Square. Newport Minster stands on this square in the island’s county town, while the quays meet the navigable stretch of the Medina. Save this brief exterior visit for after Carisbrooke; you can then have dinner and spend the night in Newport without driving again.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Wight in 4 days: From Osborne to the Chalk Cliffs

visits.text: Ride the waves at Newquay, England's undisputed surf capital, where Atlantic swells create some of the best surfing conditions in Britain. Whether you're an experienced surfer or complete beginner, numerous surf schools and board rental shops cater to all abilities on the town's many beaches. The surf culture has shaped Newquay's laid-back character and vibrant nightlife, making it a favorite destination for active visitors.

Explore the dramatic coastline around Newquay, where low-slung cliffs and hidden coves create perfect conditions for coasteering adventures combining climbing, jumping and swimming. Fistral Beach, consistently ranked among the best surf beaches in Europe, hosts international competitions that draw the world's top surfers. The surrounding headlands offer spectacular walking with views along the coast in both directions.

Discover the family-friendly attractions around Newquay, including the excellent zoo and several National Trust manor houses set in the rolling countryside slightly inland. As one of the larger towns in Cornwall, Newquay offers a wider range of accommodation, restaurants and entertainment than smaller coastal villages. The permanent population of 20,000 can multiply five times during peak summer season, a testament to the town's enduring popularity.

activities.text: Book a surf lesson on Fistral Beach to experience the thrill of riding Cornish waves

days_plan.itin_title: Cornwall Coastal Road Trip: Castles, Secret Coves & Celtic Heritage Guide

visits.text: Behind its imposing facade, Mount Stewart also tells a family story. The Londonderry family's home preserves rooms and collections connected to their role in British political and social life. Allow 1 hour inside, then continue on foot to the gardens and lake.

Cypress hedges frame Mount Stewart's Spanish Garden. Edith, Lady Londonderry, drew inspiration from a description of the Generalife in Granada; the ornamental well was purchased at the Chelsea Flower Show in 1926. Then compare these enclosed layouts with the estate's other gardens, keeping the map provided at reception handy.

activities.text: Follow Mount Stewart's Lake Walk for a change of scale after the precisely laid-out gardens. This 0.96 km loop offers views of the lake before returning toward the house, passing beneath a cork oak along the way. The National Trust lists a walking time of 45 minutes: allow that much time for stops, even over this short distance.

days_plan.itin_title: Mourne and Strangford in 3 Days: Gardens, Sea, and Woods

visits.text: Northallerton is a North Yorkshire market town you might pass through without stopping - but its lively High Street offers a welcome contrast with the wild landscapes before and after. The town is mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086; the Battle of the Standard, in 1138, was fought two miles north.

activities.text: A strategic lunch stop on the High Street before the approximately 113 km and 1 hour 35 minute drive to Windermere. The Golden Lion, a former coaching inn on the main street, serves Yorkshire dishes at reasonable prices. Northallerton is also known for its independent shops - a café and a short stop are welcome.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle

places.name: Norwich

visits.text: Norwich Castle dominates the city from arrival: its Norman keep sits on an artificial mound above the centre, visible from everywhere. William the Conqueror ordered its construction as early as 1067—98 Saxon houses were razed to clear the site. The stone keep, built between 1094 and 1121 in limestone imported from Caen, is one of the most decorated of the Norman era: its blind arcading is exceptional. After a five-year restoration, it reopened in 2025 with the interior recreated in its twelfth-century state—it's a good time to visit. The museum inside deserves time: it houses notably the paintings of the Norwich School and, an anecdote not to be missed, Britain's largest collection of ceramic teapots.

Norwich Cathedral is a Norman cathedral begun in 1096 at the same time as the castle. Its 96-metre spire is the second highest in England after Salisbury's. The two-storey cloisters contain more than 400 medieval carved bosses in their vaults - look up and take the time to decipher them: they depict scenes from the Apocalypse, fantastic animals and biblical episodes of remarkable quality. The cathedral was built using limestone imported from Caen, carried by barge from the River Wensum to the foot of the building site through the watergate at Pull's Ferry, whose remains are still visible today.

Norwich Market is one of the largest and oldest open-air markets in England, with nearly 200 stalls. It was established here by the Normans in the eleventh century and has never moved since. Right next door, Elm Hill is Norwich's best-preserved medieval street: its fifteenth- and sixteenth-century timber-framed houses now house antique dealers, galleries and cafés. In late afternoon, the oblique light on the cobbles and leaning façades is particularly beautiful.

Take twenty minutes to visit the Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts on the University of East Anglia campus—admission is free and the building alone is worth the trip. Norman Foster designed it in 1978: a great hangar of aluminium and glass that was a revolutionary piece of architecture at the time. Inside, you'll find African sculptures, Etruscan bronzes and works by Giacometti, Francis Bacon and Henry Moore presented in the same space, without partitions—a deliberately unusual arrangement. If you like art or architecture, you won't regret the stop.

activities.text: Evening in the Norwich Lanes, the quarter of independent lanes between the market and the cathedral. This is where the historic pubs, restaurants and the town's most original shops are concentrated. If you like craft beers, several pubs serve the local productions of Norfolk's breweries.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia Road Trip: Norfolk, Suffolk and Cambridge
From Cambridge to London: Eastern England in 6 days

map_keywords: Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts Norwich

visits.text: Notting Hill draws its character from its complex social history: a poor neighbourhood in the 1950s, it welcomed a large Caribbean community who launched the Notting Hill Carnival in 1966 - today Europe's largest street carnival with over a million participants each late August. The pastel facades you see resulted from 1980s-90s gentrification. Portobello Road is the market's main street: on Saturdays, antiques and bric-a-brac stalls extend nearly a kilometre from Notting Hill Gate to Golborne Road. Avoid Saturdays if you hate crowds.

activities.text: The Electric Cinema on Portobello Road is one of Britain's oldest working cinemas - opened in 1910. Its interior preserves its leather armchairs and two-seater sofas. Westbourne Grove, the street parallel to Portobello, concentrates the neighbourhood's best independent fashion and design shops - more local atmosphere, less touristy.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

places.name: Nottingham

visits.text: The real medieval castle of Nottingham was demolished by Cromwell after the Civil War - what stands today is a 17th-century ducal palace converted into a museum. Don't come for a castle: come for the caves. Beneath the building, a network of medieval tunnels carved into the red sandstone burrows into the rock - dungeons, wine cellars, secret passages, some occupied since Anglo-Saxon times. The underground guided tour is the best thing to do here.

The Lace Market is the former heart of the global lace industry - in the 19th century, Nottingham manufactured the machine lace worn throughout Europe. The red brick Victorian warehouses are now bars, galleries, and restaurants. St Mary's Church, in Perpendicular style, is the church where Robin Hood supposedly married Maid Marian according to legend. The National Justice Museum, in a former Lace Market courthouse, displays 14th-century courtrooms and dungeons from 1449.

Sherwood Forest, approximately 35 km from Nottingham, a 35-minute drive, is home to the Major Oak, a monumental oak estimated to be between 800 and 1,000 years old. Experts have considered it dead since June 2026, but it remains standing, preserved as a natural monument and wildlife habitat. The forest that once covered a quarter of Nottinghamshire is now reduced to a 420-hectare nature reserve, but the trail from the visitor centre to the tree takes 15 minutes and the atmosphere of the ancient oak woodland is genuine.

activities.text: Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem is carved directly into the sandstone rock beneath the castle - rooms hewn by hand, low ceilings, with raw rock ceiling above the tables. The sign claims 1189 as its founding date, when crusaders stopped here before joining Richard the Lionheart. The exact date is debated, but the pub has existed at least since the 17th century and the underground atmosphere is perfectly authentic. Stop here for a drink before hitting the road.

To return: direct train from Nottingham Station to London St Pancras in 1h40, frequency every hour. The M1 motorway links Nottingham to London in about 2h depending on traffic. East Midlands airport is 20 km southwest of the city - connections to major European cities.

days_plan.itin_title: The Midlands and Peak District Essentials
Midlands and Peak District Road Trip: Heritage and Wild Landscapes

map_keywords: Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem Nottingham

visits.text: A castle without a keep, a collection of royal horseshoes, and a centuries-old tradition: Oakham Castle is one of England's curiosities. The Norman Great Hall, built around 1180–1190, houses over 200 horseshoes given by visiting nobles and monarchs—tradition dictates that every peer of the realm passing through Oakham must give a horseshoe to the lord. Free entry.

Rutland Water glistens east of town—a 1,255-hectare reservoir that's one of Western Europe's largest artificial lakes. Created in the 1970s, it now attracts yachts, birdwatchers, and cyclists who complete the circuit (38km). The bird observation centre at Egleton is particularly active in winter.

activities.text: You cycle around the reservoir — or part of it — on the marked cycle path along the shores. Bikes are available at Whitwell on the north shore. In autumn, migratory geese and ducks arrive by the thousands. The panorama from the north shore, with Normanton church in the water, is Rutland's postcard view.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: The CalMac ferry from Castlebay to Oban takes about 5 hours – long enough to feel like a proper sea passage, with the small islands of Eigg, Rum and Muck visible to the north and the coast of Mull emerging to the east as you approach. This is one of the most scenic ferry routes in Scotland. Book as early as possible – this route is popular and cabins sell out quickly. Arrive in Oban in the late afternoon. The town is the main ferry hub on the west coast and earns its nickname “gateway to the islands” with something between efficiency and charm.

McCaig's Tower, the circular stone colosseum that crowns the hill above Oban, was built between 1895 and 1902 by local banker John Stuart McCaig as a memorial to his family and as a way of providing winter employment for local stone masons. He died before the interior was completed. It's never been anything but a shell, but the walk up from the harbour takes 10 minutes and the view over the bay and the island of Kerrera is worth it, particularly in the evening light.

Dunstaffnage Castle, north of Oban, is a 13th-century royal fortress that once housed the Stone of Destiny before it was moved to Scone. Robert the Bruce captured it in 1308. Flora MacDonald, who helped Bonnie Prince Charlie escape after Culloden by disguising him as a maid, was briefly imprisoned here in 1746. The ruin stands on a rock above Loch Etive and takes about 45 minutes to visit properly.

The road south from Oban via the A816, or inland via the A85 towards Glasgow, passes through some of Argyll's most beautiful scenery. If you have time before leaving, the Bridge over the Atlantic at Seil Island, a tiny hump-backed stone arch over the narrow Clachan Sound built in 1792, takes about 20 minutes to reach from Oban. Easdale Island just beyond is the smallest permanently inhabited island in the Inner Hebrides; it is reached by passenger ferry.

activities.text: Oban Distillery, at the bottom of Stafford Street in the town centre, has been producing single malt since 1794, making it one of the oldest distilleries in Scotland. The visitor experience is good - the distillery is surprisingly compact given how central it is - and the 14-year-old expression is one of the defining West Highland malts. Book a tour in advance.

The Oban seafood hut on the pier - a converted CalMac waiting room - is one of the best places in Scotland to eat langoustines, dressed crab and cold-smoked salmon, and it is completely unpretentious about it. It has no tables inside and the seating faces the ferry terminal. Queue, order, find a bollard to sit on. This is the right way to end the ferry journey.

A short passenger ferry (10 minutes, bicycles accepted) crosses to Kerrera from Gallanach, south of Oban. The island has a ruined MacDougall castle at its southern tip and a tea garden halfway round a 6 km walking loop around the island. It is a complete contrast to the mainland's busy ferry harbour and a pleasant way to spend a final half-day before heading south.

days_plan.itin_title: Outer Hebrides Road Trip: Lewis, Harris and the Island Chain
Outer Hebrides Road Trip: Lewis, Harris and the Island Chain

visits.text: Local legend claims Old Harry takes its name from Harry Paye, Poole pirate who died in 1419—or perhaps from the Devil's English nickname. Three chalk stacks detached from Handfast Point by erosion, marking the eastern end of the Jurassic Coast. The first 'wife' of Old Harry collapsed in 1896.

Walk from Studland village, about a mile (20 minutes) on flat path along the South West Coast Path. On clear days you spot the Needles on the Isle of Wight in the distance—remnants of the same chalk ridge that once connected Purbeck to the island. Cliffs are unstable; keep children close.

activities.text: The Bankes Arms in Studland serves local ales in a sprawling garden with sea views, perfect lunch stop before reclaiming the car. South Beach car park is free for National Trust members, otherwise paid.

days_plan.itin_title: England's South Coast 6d: Bristol to Brighton

visits.text: Storr comes from Old Norse, likely meaning 'great': the Vikings named this 49 m pinnacle long before the postcards. Legend says a buried giant left his thumb protruding from the ground. The site was born from a massive landslip on the Trotternish ridge. Car park £6, 7 miles north of Portree.

The pinnacles surge from the mist like teeth: in overcast weather, the Old Man takes on a gothic dimension that sunshine never gives it. The ascent takes 45 minutes on a 2.3 km return trail. At the top, views over the Sound of Raasay and the mainland.

activities.text: 2.3 km return, 45 minutes at normal pace—reasonable, but the final slope is steep. Crowds peak between 10 AM and 3 PM. Arrive at opening for morning light and fewer people. Waterproof footwear mandatory.

days_plan.itin_title: Scotland: Highlands & Skye in 12 days

visits.text: Twelve sides, none round: Orford Castle is the only surviving polygonal castle of this type in England. Built by Henry II from 1165, it dominates the village and sea from its 30-metre keep. From the roof, the view over Orford Ness — a spit of shingle and low-growing vegetation protected by the National Trust — is striking. The “Wild Man of Orford”, a merman captured here in the twelfth century, is part of local folklore.

You take the ferry to Orford Ness, an isolated coastal spit that was a classified military testing ground throughout the twentieth century. Abandoned experimental buildings survive among the vegetation, creating a unique atmosphere. The National Trust manages the site and runs regular crossings from Orford quay.

activities.text: Butley Creek oysters, smoked shrimps, and North Sea crab: Orford quay is where you eat these specialities direct from the fishermen. The Butley Orford Oysterage, founded in the 1950s, still smokes its herrings and eels on site. Avoid summer weekends—tables fill up fast.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: Oundle is one of Northamptonshire's best-preserved small towns — its streets are lined with honey-coloured limestone houses that give the centre the air of a provincial Cambridge. The town has been home for centuries to Oundle School, founded in 1556, whose buildings blend into the urban fabric. The Thursday morning market is one of the region's oldest.

St Peter's Church dominates the town with its bell tower — Northamptonshire's tallest at 64 metres. There has been a church on this site since the eighth century, but the current building dates mainly from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries. The Venerable Bede mentions a monastery at Oundle as early as 709. The interior is accessible outside services.

activities.text: You head down to the River Nene through the meadows of Barnwell Country Park, two kilometres south of Oundle. This nature park around former lakes offers flat paths and opportunities to observe waterbirds. Lyveden New Bield — an unfinished sixteenth-century manor, 8 km away — is worth a detour for Elizabethan history enthusiasts.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: It is best to book Christ Church before filling up your day: this visit deserves its own time slot. The route takes in courtyards, the cloister, the Great Hall, and the cathedral, bringing university life and a place of worship together within the same grounds. Access to these spaces also depends on how they are being used. Choose your ticket in advance, then head to the visitor reception by Meadow Gate; Tom Gate is not the usual entrance for sightseeing visits.

Lower your voice beneath the vaults of the Bodleian Library: visitors share the space with a working library. A guided tour provides access to the historic rooms, while the Weston Library and its exhibitions are open to the public free of charge. These access options are therefore not interchangeable. Book the 60-minute tour and follow the meeting-point instructions on your ticket; university ceremonies may alter the route.

The Radcliffe Camera catches your eye before you even see the books: its dome anchors the entire view of Radcliffe Square. The building belongs to the Bodleian and remains a reading room, rather than a museum you can enter freely. Walk around it from the square to enjoy different angles without disturbing readers. This itinerary includes the exterior; entering the building requires a tour that explicitly includes the Camera.

A Bridge of Sighs, but no lagoon: Oxford’s Bridge of Sighs spans New College Lane. This walkway connects Hertford College buildings separated by the street, a practical solution that has become a photography subject. Its appeal lies as much in its function as in its silhouette between the facades. View it from street level and keep the passage clear; the detour is easy to combine with Radcliffe Square.

It is best to choose a few collections at the Ashmolean Museum rather than try to see everything in one morning. This university museum of art and archaeology opened in 1683 in a different building from the one it occupies today. Its collections take you from ancient Egypt to more recent art without leaving Oxford. Start with the galleries that interest you on the map, then leave time for what comes next: general admission is free.

Skulls, vertebrae, animal silhouettes: at Oxford’s Museum of Natural History, shapes take precedence over words. The permanent displays bring together dinosaurs, other animals, and mineral collections, with objects that can be compared directly by size or shape. This makes a tangible transition between the art at the Ashmolean and the neighboring collections of human cultures. Admission is free; keep this stop brief so you can continue to the Pitt Rivers Museum.

The Pitt Rivers Museum feels like a collection of questions arranged in display cases. Instruments, weapons, and tools are grouped by object type rather than simply divided by country, making comparison the thread that guides your visit. Choose a few cases and read their labels instead of trying to take inventory of everything. Access is through the Museum of Natural History on Parks Road; enter that building to reach the museum.

activities.text: You will stop for lunch at the Covered Market, among its counters and sheltered aisles. Opened in 1774, the market remains a place for everyday shopping, with stores and places to eat, rather than a market hall reduced to a backdrop. Browse the aisles before deciding what to order. Come during the day: the market’s general opening hours do not guarantee that every vendor will still be serving at the same time.

You will finish at Christ Church Meadow with a walk by the water, away from the display cases. This meadow retains its pastoral use: Longhorn cattle graze in the floodplain fields in the heart of the university city. Follow the paths to enjoy views of the buildings and the river. Access is free during daylight hours; plan this walk before nightfall.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop
Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop
Oxford and Blenheim in 4 days: Colleges and Churchill
Oxford and Blenheim in 4 days: Colleges and Churchill

visits.text: Oxford Street is Europe's busiest shopping street - around 500,000 visitors daily at peak times. The street follows the route of an old Roman road and took on its commercial vocation in the 18th century. Selfridges (opened in 1909 by American Harry Gordon Selfridge, who introduced the concept of decorative window displays to London) is the most emblematic - its Christmas windows are an annual event. Avoid Saturday afternoons if you're allergic to crowds.

activities.text: Bond Street is the address of the fashion houses and jewellers - Cartier, Tiffany, Burberry and Chanel have their flagship stores here. Mayfair, the residential district around Bond Street, is one of the most expensive in the world in property terms and one of the most beautiful for an aimless stroll. If you play Monopoly, you are standing on the most expensive square on the board.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Padstow is nicknamed 'Padstein' by Cornish locals, a nod to Rick Stein, who opened his first restaurant on the quay in 1975 and has steadily expanded his empire ever since: The Seafood Restaurant, St Petroc's Bistro, Rick Stein's Café, the fishmonger on the harbour, the cookery school, and even a pub in the neighbouring village of St Merryn. The Seafood Restaurant remains the heart of the operation—it received the AA Food Service Award 2024 for hospitality standards. The menu changes with the catch, but expect lobster thermidor, turbot hollandaise and seafood platters. Book well ahead in summer.

Padstow harbour is steps from the restaurant: you'll see fishing boats unloading their catch directly on the quay, and Stein's fishmonger stocks the same species served in the restaurants—turbot from Trevose Head, lobsters and crabs from the Boscastle Belle. If you want ultra-fresh without fine dining, stop by the fishmonger one morning.

About 79 km from Padstow, a 1-hour drive, Newlyn Fish Market is one of Great Britain's busiest fishing ports. The daily auction takes place early in the morning: early risers can watch mackerel, sardines, sea bass and scallops being auctioned. It is the true starting point of Cornwall's fish supply chain.

activities.text: Stein's cookery school in Padstow offers one- or two-day courses focused on Cornish seafood: how to choose a whole fish, fillet it, prepare a court-bouillon or cook a lobster. The level is open to all. It's one of the best ways to understand why Rick Stein has been repeating for 50 years that 'nothing is more exhilarating than fresh fish simply cooked'.

North Cornwall coast oysters are among the country's finest—order them fresh, plain or with a squeeze of lemon, at The Seafood Restaurant's oyster bar or from harbour stalls. It's the most direct way to taste the Cornish sea.

days_plan.itin_title: England's Gastronomic Trail: Markets, Pubs & Culinary Heritage

visits.text: Peebles High Street offers a welcome break between monuments, with shops and cafés setting the pace. The town stretches along the River Tweed, which you’ll walk to afterward. Keep this stop brief so you can have lunch without jeopardizing your afternoon visit to Traquair House.

activities.text: You’ll walk along the River Tweed in Peebles to stretch your legs before getting back on the road. Riverside paths take you quickly from the shops to the riverbanks without embarking on a hike in the hills. Choose a short out-and-back walk that fits the time available, and turn back if the riverbanks are flooded.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Borders in 3 Days: Castles and Great Abbeys

visits.text: A ruin across from the train station makes a good final stop: Penrith Castle rounds off the route without a detour into the hills. Richard, Duke of Gloucester and the future Richard III, transformed this fortress into a residence. Explore the park before your final night in Penrith; check its closing time, which is earlier in winter.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes, Villages, and Writers
Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes and Writers’ Homes

visits.text: Penshurst Place was granted in 1552 by Edward VI to Sir William Sidney, his tutor and steward – the castle had previously served as a hunting lodge for Henry VIII during his courtship of Anne Boleyn (Hever Castle is six kilometres away). The Sidney family still owns it, making it one of England's oldest family homes. The 14th-century Baron's Hall is one of the rare examples of a medieval domestic great hall still intact.

The Sidney male line died out in the 18th century, but their heirs took up the name – today the De L'Isles – and continue to manage Penshurst. Queen Elizabeth I stayed here on several occasions and the Queen Elizabeth Room bears her name. There's also a Toy Museum with toys from successive generations of Sidneys, including a doll's house and 19th-century lead soldiers.

activities.text: Explore the 11 acres of walled gardens at Penshurst, divided into “rooms” by more than a mile of yew hedges – a structure resembling what Vita Sackville-West would create at Sissinghurst a generation later. The rose beds in June and tulips in April–May are highlights. The orchard of old apple trees is also worth a detour in autumn.

days_plan.itin_title: Surrey to Kent: Castles and Gardens in 10 Days

visits.text: Travel to Land's End, the westernmost point of mainland England, where spectacular cliffs plunge into the Atlantic Ocean and views extend to the Isles of Scilly on a clear day. This legendary place has captivated visitors since antiquity; even the Greeks knew it, calling it 'Belerion', meaning 'place of the sun'. The famous signpost showing distances to faraway destinations has become an iconic photo opportunity for visitors from around the world. Land's End is approximately 15 km from Penzance, a 15-minute drive.

Discover the Minack Theatre, one of the most unique and spectacular performance venues in the world, carved into the cliff overlooking Porthcurno Bay. Nearly 100 years ago, Rowena Cade began sculpting this remarkable amphitheatre into the cliff's granite rock, creating an open-air stage with the Atlantic Ocean as its backdrop. Even when no performance is scheduled, visiting the theatre to admire its ingenious design and magnificent setting is worthwhile. It is approximately 15 km from Penzance, a 15-minute drive.

Explore the golden sands of Porthcurno Beach, regularly ranked among the most beautiful beaches in the United Kingdom, where turquoise waters lap against spectacular cliffs. The beach's sheltered position and crystal-clear waters make it popular for swimming, while the surrounding cliffs offer excellent hiking. The nearby Telegraph Museum tells the fascinating story of the submarine cables that once connected Great Britain to the world from this isolated Cornish cove. The beach and museum are approximately 15 km from Penzance, a 15-minute drive.

activities.text: Catch an evening performance at the Minack Theatre for an unforgettable cultural experience

days_plan.itin_title: Cornwall Coastal Road Trip: Castles, Secret Coves & Celtic Heritage Guide
England Grand Tour: From Cornwall to the Northern Lakes
Dark Cornwall: Arthur, Mines and Wreckers 7d

visits.text: Piccadilly Circus was created in 1819 at the junction of Piccadilly and Regent Street, laid out by John Nash for the Prince Regent. The Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain at the centre - often mistaken for Eros - actually represents the Angel of Christian Charity. It was inaugurated in 1893 and is the first statue cast in aluminium in London. The giant illuminated advertising panels appeared in the 1910s; they were switched off during both world wars for blackout. Piccadilly Circus is far livelier in the evening than during the day.

activities.text: From Piccadilly Circus, Carnaby Street is a 5-minute walk north - symbol of Swinging London in the 1960s, when fashion boutiques and musicians like the Rolling Stones converged there. The surrounding network of alleys (Kingly Court, Newburgh Street) retains an independent character. More elegant, Regent Street deserves a walk for its Georgian architecture.

Leicester Square, a 3-minute walk east, is the heart of the West End's theatre and cinema district. The TKTS booth on the square sells discounted tickets for evening shows on the day - if you want to see a musical without paying full price, come in early afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: The heather turns purple in August across the North York Moors - 554 km² of open moorland, one of the largest heather moorlands in the UK. The road from Pickering to Whitby via Saltersgate crosses breathtaking ridges. The views are most intense between Fylingdales and Goathland.

activities.text: The North Yorkshire Moors Railway crosses 18 miles of moorland by steam locomotive between Pickering and Whitby. It's one of England's finest heritage lines, also used as backdrop in several TV productions. A single journey takes 1 hour 30 minutes - you can get off at Goathland (Aidensfield in Heartbeat) and catch a later train.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle

visits.text: Leaving Edinburgh northwards, stop at Blackness Castle on the shores of the Firth of Forth — a 15th-century fortress shaped like a stone ship, sitting right on the waterfront. It has served as a state prison, royal arsenal and filming location for the Outlander series. Admission is modest, the view across the Forth justifies the stop.

The Kelpies at Falkirk are what you see from the motorway without expecting them: two steel horse heads 30 metres tall, the height of an eight-storey building. Glaswegian sculptor Andy Scott completed them in October 2013 — each weighs 300 tonnes and is built from 30,000 hand-assembled steel pieces. The name comes from Scottish folklore: kelpies are shape-shifting water horses said to possess the strength of ten normal horses. In practice, the sculptures pay tribute to the Clydesdale horses that hauled barges along Scotland's canals for centuries. Access to The Helix park is free — nearly a million people visited in their first year.

Stirling Castle dominates Scotland's central plain from a basalt outcrop exactly as Edinburgh Castle dominates its city — the two fortresses controlled the country's two strategic gateways. This is where Mary Queen of Scots was crowned in 1543 at nine months old, and where James VI, future James I of England, spent his childhood. The Great Hall from 1503, restored in its original canary yellow, is one of Scotland's largest surviving medieval halls. From the ramparts on clear days, you can see both the Wallace Monument and Bannockburn battlefield — two of the great sites of Scottish independence.

Doune Castle, 15 km north of Stirling, merits a detour if you have an hour. This 14th-century fortress served as the filming location for Monty Python and the Holy Grail (1974) — the scenes where knights imitate horses with coconuts were shot here — and more recently for Game of Thrones and Outlander. Audio guides are available: one of them is narrated by Terry Jones himself, Monty Python member.

Blair Castle at Blair Atholl has been the Murray clan's seat for over seven centuries — the first stones date to 1269, when a Comyn clan lord began building on land that didn't belong to him. Its 30 rooms span 750 years of history. What strikes you immediately is the Ballroom: the ceiling and walls are decorated with 175 pairs of deer antlers, making it one of Scotland's most peculiar rooms. Look for the baroque entrance hall with its arsenal of muskets and broadswords used at the Battle of Culloden in 1746 — the castle was besieged by Jacobites during this final act of the rebellion, in the last siege conducted on British soil. Queen Victoria's visit in 1844 had unexpected consequences: so impressed by the castle guard, she granted the Atholl Highlanders the unique right to maintain a private army — the only private regiment still active in Europe today.

Blair Athol Distillery sits at the entrance to Pitlochry — you can't miss it with its grey granite buildings. Founded in 1798, it's one of the oldest working distilleries in the Highlands. The water feeding production descends from Ben Vrackie through peat moorland, giving the whisky its characteristic spicy and lightly smoky notes. The tour includes a tasting and takes you through the fermentation rooms and bonded warehouses.

Make the detour to Queen's View following the B8019 west of Pitlochry — it's a viewpoint above Loch Tummel with one of the Highlands' most reproduced vistas. The loch stretches between wooded hills, with Schiehallion (a conical 1,083-metre peak that looks like a child's drawing) as backdrop. The name supposedly comes either from Queen Victoria who stopped here in 1866, or from Isabella of Scotland, wife of Robert the Bruce — both accounts circulate. The car park is paid but the view is free.

The Pass of Killiecrankie, 5 km north of Pitlochry on the A9, is a wooded gorge where the River Garry rushes between rock faces covered in forest. This is where in 1689 Viscount Dundee defeated government troops in the first Jacobite uprising — but he was himself killed during the victory, which sealed the movement's failure. A fleeing English soldier allegedly jumped 5.5 metres across the river to escape the Highlanders: the spot is still called the Soldier's Leap. The path along the gorge floor from the visitor centre is flat and takes 45 minutes round trip.

activities.text: The scenic A9 route to the Highlands from Stirling is one of the journey's finest transitions: within a few dozen kilometres, farmland gives way to the wooded hills of Perthshire, then to the first Highland peaks. Take a break in Dunkeld, a small cathedral town on the River Tay — the seven-arched bridge from 1809 and the medieval cathedral ruins merit 30 minutes.

Walk along the River Tummel from Pitlochry: the wooded trail running from the town centre to Pitlochry Dam is flat, easy and gives access to the salmon ladder. From April to October, you can watch Atlantic salmon climb the 34 stepped pools built in the 1950s when the dam was erected — a compromise between hydroelectricity and wildlife conservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye
Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye
Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye
Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye
Haunted Scotland: 7 Days in the Land of Ghosts

visits.text: Plockton is arguably the most unexpected village in the Highlands: thanks to the Gulf Stream's influence, Cordyline australis—New Zealand palms—grow along the waterfront, planted in the 19th century. The village was founded in 1801 as a herring port by Sir Hugh Innes. At its 1841 peak, it had over 500 inhabitants; today around 470. The BBC drama Hamish Macbeth, starring Robert Carlyle, was filmed here in the 1990s. At low tide, you can walk to Eilean nan Gamhainn, an islet that briefly connects to the village. Stroll along Harbour Street and dine in one of the pubs that often feature traditional music in the evenings.

10 km east of Plockton, don't miss Eilean Donan Castle, one of Scotland's most photographed images. Set on an islet at the confluence of three lochs (Loch Duich, Loch Long, and Loch Alsh) and connected to shore by a stone arch bridge, it was built in the 13th century to defend the lands of Kintail against the Vikings. In 1719, 46 Spanish soldiers supporting the Jacobite cause were besieged here by three Royal Navy frigates—the 343 barrels of gunpowder stored within its walls were used to blow it up. It was purchased in 1911 and rebuilt in 1932. Highlander (1986) and the James Bond film The World Is Not Enough (1999) were filmed here. Admission charged—inside, the banquet halls with their 4-meter-thick walls are worth as much as the exterior setting.

activities.text: Boat trips from Plockton's pontoon allow observation of common seals and otters in Loch Carron. If you're there at low tide, the coral beach 25 minutes' walk north of the village is a cove of white sand and translucent water—one of the area's finest surprises. Free access.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Highlands: 15 Days of Castles, Lochs and Wild Landscapes
Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye

visits.text: The Eden Project, in a former china clay quarry near St Austell, was built between 1998 and 2001 at a cost of £141 million. Allow a day for the return trip from Plymouth. Two biomes made of ETFE bubbles – 100 times lighter than glass – house the world's largest indoor tropical biome (55 metres high, 200 metres long) and a Mediterranean biome. The hexagonal bubble design was sketched on a napkin in a pub in 1996. The biomes were used as a setting for the James Bond film “Die Another Day”. Book online.

The Lost Gardens of Heligan, near Mevagissey, are Europe's largest garden restoration. Allow a day for the return trip from Plymouth. Before the First World War, 22 gardeners maintained these 200 acres for the Tremayne family. Sixteen died at the front, and the gardens were abandoned for 70 years – until their rediscovery in 1990. Restoration began in 1991. Do not miss the Jungle with its giant tree ferns, or the pineapple pit – the only one still operating in Europe.

Plymouth Hoe is the grand esplanade overlooking Plymouth Sound. Here Francis Drake supposedly finished his game of bowls before confronting the Spanish Armada in 1588. The Mayflower Steps in the Barbican mark the embarkation point of the 102 Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower on 6 September 1620. The Pilgrims weren't meant to pass through Plymouth; a Channel storm forced them here.

activities.text: Boat trips from the Mayflower Steps explore Plymouth Sound and cruise up the River Tamar to Devonport Naval Dockyard. Companies offer guided tours lasting 1.5 to 2 hours.

days_plan.itin_title: England Grand Tour: From Cornwall to the Northern Lakes
South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth
Southeast Cornwall in 3 Days: Harbors and Manor Houses

visits.text: The Polperro Heritage Museum of Smuggling and Fishing reveals another side of this small harbor. Fishing and smuggling come to life through the collections of a museum housed beside the harbor basin in a former sardine-processing building. The museum lists daily opening hours through October, from 10:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with last admission at 4 p.m.

activities.text: Walk down to Polperro’s harbor along narrow lanes between light-colored houses. The village sits at the bottom of a narrow valley, which explains its tight passageways and the lack of visitor parking in the center. Park at the entrance and allow time for the climb back up, rather than blindly following your GPS.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast Cornwall in 3 Days: Harbors and Manor Houses

visits.text: Explore Poole, home to the largest natural harbor in Europe, where centuries of maritime history blend with modern watersports and a thriving yachting scene. The historic quay bustles with boat trips, waterfront restaurants and the departure point for ferries to Brownsea Island. This ancient port has welcomed traders and travelers since Roman times, and its sheltered waters now attract paddleboarders, kitesurfers and sailors from across Britain.

Discover Sandbanks, the exclusive peninsula at the entrance to Poole Harbour that has one of the highest land values by area in the world. This millionaires' playground features stunning beaches backed by some of Britain's most expensive properties, yet the golden sands and clear waters remain accessible to all visitors. The views across to Brownsea Island and the dramatic cliffs of the Jurassic Coast make this one of Dorset's most scenic spots.

Take a boat tour from Poole to see Old Harry Rocks, the dramatic chalk stacks that mark the eastern end of the UNESCO World Heritage Jurassic Coast. These gleaming white pillars rising from the turquoise sea have been sculpted by millennia of wind and waves, creating one of England's most iconic coastal landmarks. The boat trip offers unique perspectives on the cliffs and coastline impossible to appreciate from land.

activities.text: Try paddleboarding or kitesurfing in the sheltered waters of Europe's largest natural harbor

days_plan.itin_title: Dorset's Jurassic Coast: Prehistoric Cliffs, Castle Ruins and Dream Beaches

activities.text: You do not need a long outing for a change of scenery in Porlock. A short walk toward Porlock Marsh takes you from the village to coastal meadows, with a shingle ridge in the background. Follow public access routes and turn back according to the time available; the allotted 45 minutes do not cover the full loop through Bossington.

days_plan.itin_title: North Devon and Exmoor: 3 Days of Headlands and Villages

visits.text: The detour to Finlaggan deserves more than a quick photo of the ruins. The islets of Loch Finlaggan were a political and symbolic center for the Lords of the Isles, heirs to the Gaelic and Norse worlds. The Trust currently states that its visitor center is closed but Eilean Mòr remains accessible; check the situation and bring footwear suited to wet terrain.

activities.text: Port Askaig is the arrival harbour on Islay, on the sound that separates it from Jura. There is little to see beyond the harbour; take a moment on the quay, then follow the A846 to Port Ellen and its distilleries.

Jura’s outlines stand out opposite Port Askaig, across the Sound of Islay. A short walk through the village lets you locate access to the two ferry routes: Kennacraig and Feolin. Stay clear of boarding lanes and check the next day’s departure before heading to your accommodations.
Back in Port Askaig, off the Jura ferry: CalMac ferries to Kennacraig leave from here. There is little to see beyond the harbour; just allow a margin between the two crossings.

days_plan.itin_title: Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores
Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores
Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores

places.name: Port Charlotte

visits.text: To understand Islay beyond whisky, the Museum of Islay Life deserves a place in your day. Housed in a former church in Port Charlotte, it brings together evidence of island life rather than telling a story limited to distilleries. Check opening days before visiting: its schedule is seasonal, and it is not open every weekend.

The Islay Nature Centre offers a fresh perspective on the seaweed, birds, and small creatures along the shore. Located in Port Charlotte and run by the Islay Natural History Trust, the center adds context to the landscapes with explanations of their wildlife and plants. Call before making the trip: published hours are seasonal and may be from the previous year.

activities.text: You’ll head to Bruichladdich Distillery from Port Charlotte to follow the production process through its Victorian facilities. Here, the buildings and equipment offer a different sense of the scale of whisky production from the large coastal facades of the south. Book the guided tour advertised as lasting 90 minutes; take this short excursion before spending the night in Port Charlotte.

days_plan.itin_title: Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores

map_keywords: Museum of Islay Life Port Charlotte

visits.text: Lagavulin Bay deserves a stop even without a tasting. The buildings of Lagavulin Distillery, founded in 1816, face the water; the ruins of Dunyvaig Castle recall the presence of the Lords of the Isles. Stick to exterior views here: a production tour is planned at Laphroaig to leave time for the coast.

Ardbeg’s white walls contrast with the dark rocks along the shore. Ardbeg Distillery combines production facilities, visitor services, and a café on the coast beyond Lagavulin. Stop here for the seaside setting and buildings; if you prefer its guided tour, replace the Laphroaig tour rather than booking both.

activities.text: You’ll start at Laphroaig with the guided tour booked in advance. Laphroaig Distillery retains floor malting and kilns where peat is used in drying, giving the smoke a very tangible history. Check which production areas will actually be accessible when you book; the driver should save the tasting until all driving is done.

If you want to travel between the distilleries without immediately getting back in the car, take the Three Distilleries Path from Port Ellen. This walking and cycling path serves Laphroaig, Lagavulin, and Ardbeg. Limit this outing to a partial out-and-back walk to fit your reserved time slot; if you want to walk the entire route, arrange your return before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Islay and Jura in 4 Days: Whisky, Crosses, and Shores

places.name: Port Isaac

visits.text: Fall in love with Port Isaac, a quintessential Cornish fishing village snuggled around a tiny harbor in North Cornwall. A cluster of whitewashed and slate-fronted cottages tumble down steep lanes to the pocket-sized beach where colorful fishing boats bob at their moorings. The village's protected harbor has preserved its historic character, even as the fishing industry that built it has declined, creating one of the most photogenic destinations in Cornwall.

Explore Port Isaac's narrow lanes and atmospheric corners that have featured in numerous film and television productions, including the popular Doc Martin series. The village's history is intimately tied to fishing, an industry that peaked here in the early 19th century when pilchards were exported across Europe. Today, traditional fishing continues alongside a thriving tourism industry, with crab and lobster pots stacked on the quay.

Walk the spectacular stretch of the South West Coast Path connecting Port Isaac to Tintagel, a 10-mile route that takes in dramatic rock formations and lesser-visited beaches. This section of Cornwall's coastline is particularly spectacular in spring when wildflowers carpet the clifftops, adding splashes of color to the green headlands. The walking offers constantly changing perspectives on the rugged North Cornwall coast.

activities.text: Watch for the Fisherman's Friends, the local sea shanty group who sometimes perform on the harbor's Platt

days_plan.itin_title: Cornwall Coastal Road Trip: Castles, Secret Coves & Celtic Heritage Guide

map_keywords: South West Coast Path Port Isaac

visits.text: Two villages face each other across the water: Portaferry's quay gives you a sense of the width of the Narrows, at the entrance to Strangford Lough. Here, the ferry connects the Ards and Lecale peninsulas, carrying cars as well as passengers. Join the line before quarter past or quarter to the hour: these are the usual departure times from Portaferry.

days_plan.itin_title: Mourne and Strangford in 3 Days: Gardens, Sea, and Woods

visits.text: Discover the Lizard Peninsula, one of the most spectacular stretches of coastline in all of England and a personal favorite for many visitors to Cornwall. Thanks to limited road access and minimal development, this southernmost point of mainland Britain retains an unspoiled character and get-away-from-it-all atmosphere that feels increasingly rare. The peninsula's serpentine rock creates distinctive green and red coloring in the cliffs and has been worked by local craftspeople for centuries.

Visit the Cornish Seal Sanctuary, where injured and orphaned seals receive treatment and rehabilitation before being released back into the wild. Unlike typical zoo attractions, this facility focuses primarily on rescue and recovery, giving visitors the opportunity to see these charismatic marine mammals while supporting important conservation work. The sanctuary offers insight into the challenges facing Cornwall's seal population and the dedicated efforts to protect them.

Explore the idyllic fishing villages of Coverack and Cadgwith, where thatched cottages nestle around tiny harbours that have changed little over the generations. These authentic communities offer perfect places to enjoy fish and chips while watching the fishing boats come and go. The spectacular coastal scenery surrounding these villages, with its imposing cliffs and hidden coves, rewards those who venture off the beaten tourist track. They are approximately 15 to 20 km from Porthleven, a 15- to 20-minute drive.

Marvel at Kynance Cove, often considered one of Cornwall's most beautiful beaches, with its turquoise waters, white sand and spectacular serpentine rock formations. This superb cove, owned by the National Trust, offers excellent swimming opportunities when conditions allow and spectacular photographic opportunities throughout the year. The unique geology creates islands and caves that are revealed at low tide, adding an element of exploration to every visit. It is approximately 15 km from Porthleven, a 15-minute drive.

activities.text: Hike the South West Coast Path along Lizard's spectacular cliffs, with views towards Lizard Point. It is approximately 20 km from Porthleven, a 20-minute drive.

days_plan.itin_title: Cornwall Coastal Road Trip: Castles, Secret Coves & Celtic Heritage Guide

visits.text: Explore the Isle of Portland, the southernmost point of Dorset, a limestone peninsula linked to the mainland by Chesil Beach and steeped in military history. The artificial harbour, critically important during both World Wars, testifies to Portland's strategic importance, while today the island offers tranquillity, abundant wildlife and spectacular coastal landscapes. The distinctive Portland stone quarried here was used to build some of Britain's finest buildings, including St Paul's Cathedral.

Visit Portland Bill Lighthouse, the striking red and white tower that has guided ships around this dangerous headland since 1906. The lighthouse offers tours revealing the workings of this vital navigational aid, while the surrounding cliffs provide excellent opportunities for birdwatching and coastal photography. The views from Portland Bill extend across Lyme Bay, with the outline of Devon visible on clear days.

Discover Portland Castle, one of England's best-preserved coastal fortresses from the reign of Henry VIII, built in the 1540s to defend against French and Spanish invasion. This artillery castle, with its distinctive rounded walls designed to deflect cannonballs, tells the story of Tudor England's precarious position in European politics. The castle later served as a private residence and now offers fascinating insights into 500 years of English history.

activities.text: Visit Pulpit Rock, the dramatic coastal feature near the lighthouse, and watch the waves crash against the stone platform

days_plan.itin_title: Dorset's Jurassic Coast: Prehistoric Cliffs, Castle Ruins and Dream Beaches

visits.text: Enter the whimsical world of Portmeirion, an enchanting Italianate village on the North Wales coast that feels like a slice of the Amalfi Coast transported to the shores of Snowdonia. Designed by visionary architect Sir Clough Williams-Ellis between 1925 and 1975, this unique village features colorful buildings, campaniles, and piazzas nestled in subtropical gardens cascading to the Dwyryd Estuary. The pastel-painted facades and Mediterranean architecture create an otherworldly atmosphere unlike anywhere else in Britain.

Wander through Portmeirion's labyrinthine paths discovering hidden courtyards, ornate fountains and architectural salvage from across Europe incorporated into Williams-Ellis's grand design. The village gained worldwide fame as the setting for the cult 1960s television series 'The Prisoner,' and fans still visit to explore the iconic locations. Every corner reveals unexpected details, from classical statues to whimsical follies, creating endless opportunities for exploration.

Explore the extensive woodland gardens surrounding the village, where exotic plants thrive in the mild coastal climate created by the Gulf Stream. The wild gardens, planted with rhododendrons, hydrangeas and rare specimens from around the world, offer miles of scenic coastal walks along the estuary. The views across to Snowdonia's peaks provide a stunning backdrop to this unique architectural fantasy.

activities.text: Take a scenic coastal walk through the woodland gardens with views across the estuary to Snowdonia

days_plan.itin_title: Wales Road Trip: Conwy Castle, Pembrokeshire Coast & Snowdonia
Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

places.name: Portree

visits.text: Stop at Urquhart Castle on the shores of Loch Ness — its spectacular ruins occupy a rocky promontory directly on the water and one of the Grant Tower's five storeys is accessible for a view over the loch. This castle was one of medieval Scotland's largest, and its history reads like a summary of the Wars of Independence: seized and re-seized between Scots and English in the 13th and 14th centuries, then attacked almost continuously by the Macdonald Lords of the Isles until 1545. Finally abandoned, its government troops blew up the gate in 1692 to prevent Jacobites using it. Those collapsed blocks you still see on the ground are from that explosion. Book your slot online: 547,000 people visited in 2019, Scotland's third most-visited site after Edinburgh and Stirling.

Eilean Donan Castle, halfway to Skye on the A87, is Scotland's most photographed castle — and it entirely justifies its reputation. Sitting on an islet at the confluence of three lochs, it was destroyed during the Jacobite wars of 1719 then entirely reconstructed between 1919 and 1932. Stop at least for photos from the bridge: the late-afternoon light on the golden walls with the lochs as backdrop is the image of Scotland.

Before crossing to Skye via the Kyle of Lochalsh bridge, stop at the Five Sisters of Kintail to look back towards the Highlands: five peaks exceeding 900 metres rise like a curtain behind Glen Shiel. It's one of the most striking mountain ranges on the Scottish mainland. You'll find a car park and viewpoint on the A87 — allow 20 minutes for photos.

Arrive in Portree in late afternoon — Skye's only real town, with its harbour ringed by colourful houses. Stroll along the quay to see the fishing boats and eat local seafood. Skye's lobster and crab rank among Scotland's finest.

The Old Man of Storr is Skye's most iconic image: a 55-metre rock column standing alone on a ridge above the Trotternish peninsula, north of Portree. The climb from the car park takes about 45 minutes — the trail is well-marked but heavily trafficked. Leave early morning to avoid tour buses. If mist shrouds the basalt columns, it's even more dramatic. From the top, the view across the Sound of Raasay and the islands below is vertiginous.

The Quiraing, further north on the same Trotternish peninsula, is landscape of another nature. Successive geological landslips have created a labyrinth of cliffs, pinnacles and high grassy ledges. The road skirting this slope from Uig is itself a spectacle — one of Skye's finest scenic drives. The hike into the Quiraing itself demands 2.5 to 3 hours for the full circuit.

The Fairy Glen near Uig is a small valley with spiralling grassy mounds that geology has sculpted into a limestone hollow — it's easy to see why locals associated these rounded forms with fairy rings. It's small, quiet and otherworldly. Allow 30 to 45 minutes for a circular walk around the mounds.

Kilt Rock on Trotternish's east coast merits a 20-minute stop: a basalt cliff of hexagonal columns plunging straight into the sea, with a waterfall leaping off the edge from the plateau. The resemblance to pleated kilt fabric is striking. There's a secure clifftop viewpoint — the views across the sea and jagged coastline are impressive.

The Fairy Pools of Glenbrittle are Skye's most popular hike — and they deserve their reputation. A series of translucent turquoise pools fed by waterfalls descends at the foot of the black Cuillin range. The water colour is real: reflections from sky and rocks create this blue-green even under clouds. The trail from the car park is easy, 2.4 km to the first pools. In 1601, these pools were the scene of a bloody battle between the Macdonalds of Sleat and the Macleods of Dunvegan — the waters supposedly ran red for days. Arrive as early as possible: tour buses arrive from 10am. Car park is paid but access to the pools is free.

Stop at the old Sligachan Bridge returning to Portree — this 19th-century stone bridge over the River Sligachan is one of the classic viewpoints of the Cuillin. Local legend says dipping your face in the river water for 7 seconds grants eternal beauty. The Sligachan Inn, open since 1830, faces the bridge and serves local whiskies.

activities.text: A cruise on Loch Ness from Clansman Harbour to Urquhart Castle is a different way to discover the site — you'll approach the ruins from the water, with the view of the Highlands unfolding behind. The cruise ticket includes castle entry. Operators run these cruises from Drumnadrochit. Book ahead in high season.

Horse riding across Skye's moorland from the Skye Riding Centre — a different experience to see the island from the saddle rather than on foot. The centre offers rides for all levels across open landscapes of the peninsula. Book in advance.

If you have the energy and good hiking shoes, the walk to Talisker Bay on Skye's west coast rewards the effort: a black pebble beach at the foot of spectacular cliffs, with volcanic rocks sculpted by the sea and, in clear weather, views as far as the Outer Hebrides. Allow 3 hours for the round trip from the Carbost car park. In the evening, stop at Talisker Distillery to taste a peated whisky.
