visits.text: Five hundred years of Royal Navy concentrated in one place—that's Portsmouth Historic Dockyard. HMS Victory, Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar in 1805, is undergoing its biggest conservation project since construction, started in 2022. Still viewable: you board and watch shipwrights at work, an experience that'll vanish once the job finishes around 2032.

Sunk in 1545 in the Solent, the Mary Rose, Henry VIII's favourite ship, was raised in 1982 with 19,000 objects. Fragile timbers sprayed for 30 years to stabilize, displayed behind glass in a climate-controlled hall. World's largest Tudor artefact collection.

The Royal Navy's first iron-hulled warship, HMS Warrior 1860, never fired a shot in anger. Her mere existence rendered every wooden fleet obsolete. Visit the lower decks with costumed interpreters sometimes.

activities.text: Grab the Ultimate Explorer ticket (around £45) covering everything plus a harbour tour of about 45 minutes, valid one year. Allow a full day, don't rush it. Mary Rose Café or Camber Lights for breaks, with views of Royal Navy frigates on exercise.

days_plan.itin_title: England's South Coast 6d: Bristol to Brighton

visits.text: Completed in 1693, Portsoy’s old harbor is compact enough to take in almost at a glance. Two piers and a quay that turns inward frame its basin, lined with old houses and warehouses. Observe the upright stones in the masonry from the inner quays; in rough seas, these viewpoints let you avoid venturing onto the exposed ends of the piers.

Portsoy also has a new harbor, built between 1825 and 1828 to support the growth of herring fishing. The contrast with the old basin is apparent in the openness of the harbor structures and the protection they provide from the sea. Reach this second basin via the quays on the town side to compare the two harbors; keep routes used by boats and their crews clear.

days_plan.itin_title: Speyside and the Moray Coast: Whisky and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: The Clapper Bridge at Postbridge impresses without arches or decoration: large stone slabs span the East Dart. This old crossing stands beside the road bridge, letting you compare two ways of crossing the same river. Walk over from the parking area and avoid wet slabs; the view from the bank is enough when the stone is slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: If you arrive at dawn in winter, thousands of wigeon cover the flooded meadows at Pulborough Brooks: a sound of continuous whistles impossible to describe otherwise. The RSPB reserve of 256 hectares in the Arun valley is designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest and Ramsar site. In summer, nightingales sing until June.

Pulborough Brooks, 256 hectares of wetland in the Arun Valley of the South Downs National Park: flood meadows, reedbeds, heaths and woods. The reserve hosts wintering duck and wader species, spring lapwings and nightingales in display, summer dragonflies. Views over the South Downs from the hides.

activities.text: Settle into one of the hides before 8 a.m. for the best observations. RSPB volunteers are on hand during the day to identify species. The Wetland Trail is closed to dogs—the woodland trail is open to them on leads.

days_plan.itin_title: Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports

visits.text: The Quiraing is Iceland in miniature without the flight or the expense. Landslips have sculpted a succession of rock tables, ridges and gullies that clouds pass through before your eyes. The single-track road over Bealach Mòr pass is already a spectacle before you've put on your boots.

In foul weather, the Quiraing's rocks turn treacherous: the full circuit isn't recommended in driving rain. But even 200 m on the main path opens onto a striking panorama. The section to the first pinnacles is accessible in 20 minutes from the car park.

activities.text: Full 7 km circuit, 2 hours in good weather: you climb the ridges, descend into gullies and emerge on the cliff side. The Table – a grassy plateau hidden behind a rock wall – is the reward for taking the long circuit. Discreet wild camping spots exist along the ridge.

days_plan.itin_title: Scotland: Highlands & Skye in 12 days

activities.text: Facing the sea, Rame Head’s chapel seems perched at the very tip of the headland. This medieval building overlooks the entrance to Plymouth Sound; in clear conditions, Eddystone Lighthouse is visible offshore. Walk up from the parking lot, keeping to the trails, and avoid the tip if the wind makes your footing unsteady.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast Cornwall in 3 Days: Harbors and Manor Houses

visits.text: London - Reform Club: Phileas Fogg bets he can travel around the world in eighty days, triggering a timed journey from the heart of London.
Port of London: embarkation for Suez, first maritime stage marking the passage from a regulated life to a race against time.
Return to London: Fogg believes he has lost his bet before realizing he has gained a day by crossing the globe eastward.
Reform Club: final scene where he presents himself at the last moment to prove he has accomplished the trip around the world within the deadline.

activities.text: Stroll between Westminster, the City and the clubs of Pall Mall to feel the Victorian atmosphere of Fogg's London.
Follow the Suez Canal and observe the ballet of ships, symbol of the shortening of distances in Fogg's era.
Retracing Fogg's steps through London by measuring the contrast between the fixity of the city and the movement of the journey accomplished.

days_plan.itin_title: Driving Phileas Fogg's Route: A Modern "Around the World in 80 Days" Itinerary
Driving Phileas Fogg's Route: A Modern "Around the World in 80 Days" Itinerary

visits.text: Regent's Park was laid out by John Nash from 1811 on the orders of the Prince Regent (the future George IV), who wanted a royal residence surrounded by gardens. The residence was never built, but the 166 hectares of parkland remained. Queen Mary's Gardens hold one of the largest rose gardens in England, with more than 12,000 rose bushes of 85 varieties - at their peak in June. The Open Air Theatre, active since 1932, stages Shakespeare plays and musicals from May to September.

activities.text: Climb Primrose Hill, the hill north of the park that peaks at 78 metres - it's one of the best free panoramas over London's skyline, with the Shard, London Eye and City clearly identifiable. The spot is particularly popular with Londoners in the evening and on weekends.
London Zoo has stood on the northern edge of the park since 1828 - it is the oldest scientific zoo in the world still in operation. Allow half a day if you want to see all of it.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Three Cliffs Bay is often cited as the most beautiful beach in Wales. Three limestone arches plunge straight into the sea at the end of a long sandy beach crossed by an estuary you must ford at low tide—which adds to the end-of-the-world feel. No car access to the beach: allow 25 minutes on foot from the Southgate or Pennard car park. The effort is amply rewarded.

On the ridge overlooking Three Cliffs Bay, the ruins of Pennard Castle emerge from the dunes. Built by the Normans in the 12th century to control the coastline, it has been gradually invaded by sand since the 14th century—local legend says it was buried as divine punishment. Access from the coastal path is immediate and the view from the ruined walls over the bay is striking.

On the way to Rhossili, Oxwich Bay deserves a stop: a wide 3 km beach facing south, sheltered by a pine forest and classified as a National Nature Reserve. The Oxwich Burrows dunes behind the beach are one of Gower's largest dune systems, home to rare plant species.

activities.text: The coastal loop from Southgate around Three Cliffs Bay and Pennard Burrows is one of the best walks in Gower: 8 km, little elevation, scenery that changes every ten minutes between cliffs, dunes, estuaries and beaches. Pass behind Pennard Castle for the plunging view over Three Cliffs from the rear.

days_plan.itin_title: South Wales Circuit: Mountains and Coast
Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: 24 arches, 400 metres, over 100 deaths according to the parish registers of Chapel-le-Dale: the human cost of Ribblehead Viaduct. Built between 1870 and 1875 for the Midland Railway, it stands 32 metres high and cost £343,000 at the time. The 2,300 navvies lived in camps christened Sebastopol and Belgravia. The Settle-Carlisle train still crosses.

activities.text: The wind whistles between the arches like inside an open-air cathedral. A 20-minute walk from the B6255 car park leads beneath the viaduct to appreciate the scale of the pillars. The Station Inn, right next door, offers pints with direct views - one of the finest outposts of its kind.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle

visits.text: Did you know that Richmond in Virginia, Richmond in Australia and Richmond-upon-Thames in London all owe their names to this small Yorkshire town? Henry Tudor had inherited the title of Earl of Richmond; after becoming Henry VII, he named his palace at Sheen after his Yorkshire estate - and the London district has borne that name ever since. Climb to Richmond Castle to understand why: perched on a cliff above the Swale, built by Alan the Red after the Norman Conquest around 1071, it possesses more 11th-century Norman architecture than any other castle in England. Local legend claims King Arthur and his knights sleep beneath the foundations - the English love their legends.

Don't miss the Georgian Theatre Royal just below the castle - it's Britain's most intact Georgian theatre, founded in 1788, closed in 1848 and used as a warehouse for a century before being restored and reopened in 1963. Its 200-seat auditorium with original painted decor is tiny and fascinating. If there's a performance during your visit, it's a rare experience not to be missed.

Take the road west from Richmond and you enter Swaledale - the wildest of the Yorkshire Dales. Dry-stone walls divide the pastures endlessly, 18th-century hay barns dot the hills, and villages such as Reeth and Muker seem unchanged for two centuries. Drive to Keld at the far end of the valley for the Kisdon Force waterfalls. Plan a return drive from Richmond to Keld, followed by the walk to the waterfalls.

activities.text: Walk in Swaledale to the hidden waterfalls around Keld: several short paths (2-4 km) lead to Kisdon Force and Catrake Force from the village. The landscape of moorland and dry-stone walls is different from anything you have seen in the Lake District. Plan a return drive from Richmond to Keld in addition to the walk.

The Wensleydale Creamery at Hawes, heading up the valley of the same name from Richmond, offers creamery tours with tasting. Wensleydale is a crumbly, slightly honeyed cheese, produced in this valley since Cistercian monks from Roquefort settled here in 1156 and brought their maturing techniques. Hawes is about 45km from Richmond.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake District and North-East Loop: Lakes, Dales and Cathedrals
Yorkshire and North East England: Dales and Coasts

Around London in 5 Days: Royal Palaces and Gardens

visits.text: The Rye valley absorbs sound, moss covers everything, and Rievaulx's ruins emerge without warning. Northern England's first Cistercian abbey, founded in 1132, housed up to 140 monks and 500 lay brothers under Abbot Aelred. Dissolved in 1538, 22 monks still remained. From Rievaulx Terrace above, the view of ruins in their wooded bowl ranks among England's most arresting. Less crowded than Fountains; lunch in Helmsley afterwards.

days_plan.itin_title: Gothic Yorkshire: Dracula, Abbeys & Witches – 8 days

visits.text: Smugglers' village: too beautiful to be honest. Robin Hood's Bay, clinging to the cliff, served as the Yorkshire coast's principal smuggling port in the 18th century. Local legend claims a bale of French silk could traverse the entire village from beach to summit without ever seeing daylight, passing cellar to cellar. Lanes still bear names like Brandy Alley. Look for wall hooks and concealed passages.

activities.text: Legend says a bale of French silk crossed the entire village without seeing daylight – beach to summit – via a network of tunnels connecting cellars. Local historians have uncovered bricked-up passages and unusual cellars, without confirming the network's full extent. The Robin Hood's Bay and Fylingdales Museum, volunteer-run, preserves smuggling archives. Walk down to the beach, exposed only at low tide.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle
Gothic Yorkshire: Dracula, Abbeys & Witches – 8 days

visits.text: Beneath the vaults of Rosslyn Chapel, your gaze wanders among the stone carvings. Founded in 1446, this chapel in Roslin also owes its fame to The Da Vinci Code, but its carved details alone make it worth visiting. Reserve your 90-minute time slot; photography is prohibited inside.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Borders in 3 Days: Castles and Great Abbeys

visits.text: The Royal Academy of Arts has occupied Burlington House on Piccadilly since 1868. Founded in 1768 with Joshua Reynolds as its first president, it is the oldest institution devoted to the fine arts in the United Kingdom. Its temporary exhibitions are among the most popular in London - the annual Summer Exhibition, held without interruption since 1769, is the longest-running series of exhibitions in the world. Check the programme before you go: the permanent collections are less spectacular than the major temporary exhibitions.

activities.text: Check the current exhibition programme on the Royal Academy website before planning your visit—some blockbuster exhibitions sell out weeks in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

visits.text: On the way from Brighton, detour to Hever Castle: Anne Boleyn's childhood castle, Henry VIII's second wife, lies about twenty minutes north of Tunbridge Wells. Built in the late 13th century and surrounded by a double moat, it houses original Tudor portraits and the two prayer books annotated in Anne's hand. The gardens created in the early 20th century by American millionaire William Waldorf Astor span 60 hectares and offer one of Kent's most beautiful settings.

Tunbridge Wells developed around a chalybeate spring discovered in 1606, which attracted all of English aristocracy for two centuries. The historic heart is the Pantiles—a 17th-century tree-lined colonnade bordered by shops. Its name comes from the pan tiles that originally paved the ground. Princess Anne donated £100 in 1698 to repair the paving after her son slipped. Today, the Pantiles house restaurants, markets, and open-air concerts. Look for the chalybeate spring still in operation—you can drink the iron-rich water according to a 400-year tradition.

activities.text: About twenty minutes southeast of Tunbridge Wells, Scotney Castle offers one of Kent's most romantic tableaux: the ruins of a 14th-century medieval castle in the middle of a lake, surrounded by English-style gardens planted with rhododendrons. In May-June, the blooming is spectacular. Managed by the National Trust.

Kent is England's garden—literally. Several vineyards in the region offer tastings: the Medway Valley and hills around Tunbridge Wells produce sparkling wines comparable to champagne. Plan to contact an estate in advance to arrange a visit and tasting.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast England & Kent Circuit: White Cliffs and Secret Gardens
Surrey to Kent: Castles and Gardens in 10 Days

visits.text: Rye is arguably the best-preserved medieval town in southeast England. Perched on a hill that was once an island surrounded by marshes, it was part of the Cinque Ports—the confederation of ports that supplied ships to the Crown in exchange for trading privileges. Start with Mermaid Street: this isn't a reconstruction, it's one of England's oldest streets, with timber-framed houses dating back to the 12th century. The Mermaid Inn was rebuilt in 1420 after a French raid; in the 18th century, the Hawkhurst Gang, a terrifying band of smugglers, made it their headquarters. Legend has it that one evening, twenty gang members fired shots in the neighbouring street for fun, and a too-curious passerby, James Marshall, disappeared without a trace.

Ypres Tower, built in 1249 to defend the town from French attacks, is Rye's oldest monument. It served successively as a fortress, private residence, courthouse, prison, and morgue before becoming a museum. Climb to the top for views over the Rother estuary and Romney Marsh in the distance. Don't miss the prison cells and the medieval herb garden below. The Women's Tower in the same complex was, in 1857, the country's first women-only prison.

Lamb House, on Church Square, is one of Kent's most intimate literary addresses. Henry James lived here from 1898 to 1916 and wrote several of his major novels here, including The Wings of the Dove. E.F. Benson succeeded him and transformed Rye into Tilling, the setting for his comic series Mapp and Lucia. The Georgian house and its walled garden now belong to the National Trust. Allow 45 minutes for the visit.

Finish your tour at St Mary's Church, whose history goes back 900 years. The chiming clock installed in 1561 is the oldest church clock with original mechanism still operating in the UK. Climb the bell tower—entry is paid but modest—for panoramic views over Rye's rooftops, the marshes, and, on clear days, out to sea.

activities.text: Get lost in Rye's twittens—those narrow Sussex alleyways that connect streets. They were much favored by smugglers in the 18th century for slipping between houses unseen. Rye is also known for its antique dealers; if you enjoy browsing, the Strand and its surroundings have several shops worth checking out. If you'd like to pick up a good bottle for the next leg, Gusbourne and Oxney Organic Estate vineyards are about 20 minutes' drive away.

In the evening, settle in at the Ypres Castle Inn, a 17th-century pub nestled in the tower gardens, with a lovely walled garden in summer and a stone fireplace in winter. The place is frequented by locals—you won't find the touristy pub atmosphere of the town center.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast England & Kent Circuit: White Cliffs and Secret Gardens
Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports

visits.text: The dark timbers of Saffron Walden's Tudor houses frame streets that nobody ever had to rebuild — the decline of the wool trade in the sixteenth century preserved the town better than any conservation scheme. Church Street and Bridge Street are the most striking examples. The Saturday morning market has brought the square to life for centuries.

'Never rebuilt, never sacked': Audley End House is one of England's finest Jacobean examples. Henry VIII gave the estate to Sir Thomas Audley after the dissolution of the monasteries, and successive owners preserved its state rooms, Victorian kitchens, and gardens designed by Capability Brown. Walking distance from the station, 2km.

activities.text: You wander through the Bridge End Gardens, a Victorian plant maze hidden behind an unassuming gate. These garden rooms—formal lawns, rose garden, kitchen garden—were created by local banker Gibson in the nineteenth century. Free entry; the hedge maze is the only element requiring a key available from the tourist office.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: Between the boat hulls and the houses, the Salcombe estuary fills the landscape. The town rises along its western shore, facing the beaches of East Portlemouth: looking across helps explain why a few hundred meters of water change the access routes. Park before walking to the harbor, rather than searching for a space on the quays.

activities.text: Walk to North Sands from Salcombe along Cliff Road. This beach near the center offers a break beside the estuary without arranging a boat trip, and its size depends on the tide. Check the tide before setting out; the space available for a stop by the water differs from that available for a walk on the sand.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: Beneath the soaring vaults of Salisbury Cathedral, the light first draws your eye to the stonework. The chapter house then shifts the scale of the visit: it holds one of the four surviving copies of the Magna Carta of 1215, a document far less conspicuous than the spire. Allow time for this display and check the day’s opening hours, as services can affect access to visitor areas.

A vanished town, but earthworks you can still read: at Old Sarum, the banks tell as much of the story as the ruins. The site combines an Iron Age enclosure with a Norman motte and castle; the town later moved to Salisbury, in the valley. Walk around the remains to understand this sequence, then look toward the present-day cathedral. Bring a windbreaker for this largely exposed site.

Central Salisbury deserves more than a quick walk between the station and the cathedral. Around Poultry Cross, the shopping streets reveal another side of the city, while the gates of Cathedral Close mark the entrance to the cathedral precinct. Some of the stones in its walls came from Old Sarum: the town’s relocation also involved reusing materials. Explore this area on foot and save driving for sites outside the city.

activities.text: You’ll follow the Town Path along the Harnham meadows for a different view of Salisbury. This path connects the neighborhood to the rest of the city, alongside meadows irrigated by branches of the River Nadder. The cathedral remains in view during the walk without counting as a separate visit. After heavy rain, check the condition of the path: this low-lying area can flood, making the route impassable.

days_plan.itin_title: England's South Coast 6d: Bristol to Brighton
Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days
Stonehenge and Salisbury: 3 Days in the Heart of Wiltshire

places.name: Saltburn By The Sea

visits.text: Sandsend, around 26 km from Saltburn-by-the-Sea, a 25-minute drive, and 5 kilometres north of Whitby, is a sand and pebble beach on the Jurassic coast - one of the richest stretches of the English coast for marine fossils. Ammonites, belemnites and marine reptile teeth from the Upper Jurassic regularly emerge from the cliff after storms. No special equipment is needed: the shore at low tide is enough. The beach is quiet outside the main season.

Staithes, wedged between two cliffs (Cowbar Nab and Penny Nab) at the mouth of a small valley, is one of the most authentic fishing villages on the north coast. Its lanes are so narrow — the narrowest, Dog Loup, is 45 cm wide — that the sun only enters at midday. Leave your car at the clifftop car park and walk down. In 1745, the young James Cook, aged 16, came here to work as a grocer's apprentice under William Sanderson. He didn't last 18 months: fascinated by the boats in the harbour, he left for Whitby to join the merchant navy. Sanderson's shop was destroyed by a storm but its materials were reused to build a cottage you'll still find on Church Street.

The Captain Cook and Staithes Heritage Centre, in the former 1880 Methodist chapel at the top of the village, holds over 200 books, 61 original engravings from Cook's voyages and dozens of objects related to his life. The upper floor recreates William Sanderson's shop as it was in 1745—the only such recreation in the world. Free entry, donations welcome.

The Saltburn Cliff Tramway is the oldest water-balanced funicular still operating in the UK. Opened in June 1884, it connects the Victorian town atop the cliff to the pier and beach 37 metres below, on 63 metres of track at a 71% gradient. Its operating principle has barely changed in 140 years: a 1,100-litre water tank is filled in the upper car until its weight exceeds that of the lower car — the journey from one level to the other takes 55 seconds, with a brakesman controlling the brakes himself. Allow 15 minutes for the round trip.

Saltburn's Victorian pier, inaugurated in May 1869 and listed Grade II*, is the only large pleasure pier remaining along the entire north-east coast of England. It extends 200 metres over the North Sea. Walk to the end to see the coastline receding in both directions - on a clear day, the cliffs at Boulby (203 metres) are visible.

Saltburn-by-the-Sea beach, a long strip of sand and shingle at the foot of the cliffs, is a recognised surf spot on the north coast. Beyond the water, the Victorian seafront—colourful bathing huts, esplanades, valley gardens in the background—is intact and particularly photogenic at sunset when the light takes on an orange tint.

activities.text: Sandsend is around 26 km from Saltburn-by-the-Sea, a 25-minute drive. Hunt for fossils on the beach and cliffs at Sandsend: with a keen eye and patience, you'll find ammonites on the surface of the pebbles after storms. Providers such as Yorkshire Coast Rock organise guided outings along this stretch of coast if you want to improve your chances. Book ahead — groups are small.

Walk down into Staithes to the harbour: allow 15 minutes downhill (very steep for the last 200 metres) and 20 minutes back up. At the bottom, the quay is tiny, the cobles (small flat-bottomed boats) are often hauled onto the bank. Take time to follow Staithes Beck to the sea. Don't attempt to drive down—the lanes are too narrow for any non-resident vehicle.

Surfing or stand-up paddleboarding lesson on Saltburn beach: equipment hire providers operate on the main beach in season. Saltburn's surf spot is one of the most highly regarded in northern England — consistent swell, sandy bottom, cold water but manageable in a wetsuit. If you'd rather watch, stay atop the cliff and watch the surfers battle the tide.

Ride the Saltburn Cliff Tramway: take the car both ways if you want to see the mechanism at work, and watch the brakesman operate the brakes at the top. The view over the beach and pier from the tracks, halfway down the slope, is one of the finest on this stage of the trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Yorkshire: Wild Coast & Secret Moorlands
Yorkshire: Wild Coast & Secret Moorlands
North York Moors Road Trip: Coast and Villages

map_keywords: Captain Cook and Staithes Heritage Centre

visits.text: Sandringham Estate has been the British royal family's private residence since 1862, when Queen Victoria purchased it for her eldest son, the future Edward VII, for £220,000. The current red-brick Jacobean-style house was built in 1870 by architect A.J. Humbert. George V wrote of Sandringham: 'the place I love better than anywhere in the world'. George VI died here in 1952. Eight ground-floor rooms, virtually unchanged since Edwardian times, open to the public from late March to early October. The 24-hectare Country Park is open year-round for free.

St Mary Magdalene church, on the Sandringham estate, is the royal family's parish church—where the Christmas service watched by Britons on television each year is held. Built in the 14th century and extensively remodelled by Edward VII, it houses several royal memorials. Don't miss the Silver Jubilee Gate in solid silver, a gift from the royal family in 1977.

activities.text: After the house and church, wander freely in Sandringham Country Park—24 hectares of woods and heathland open year-round. In season, the estate's organic farm sells its own produce at the shop. It's a good moment to catch your breath before the final day.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia Circuit: Cambridge, Suffolk Coast and Royal Norfolk

visits.text: The RSPB reserve at Bempton Cliffs, around thirty kilometres south of Scarborough, is one of England's great wildlife experiences. The white chalk cliffs rise to 120 metres above the North Sea, and between April and July they host more than 200,000 nesting birds - a colony of northern gannets (more than 11,000 pairs), puffins, guillemots, razorbills and kittiwakes. The gannets have a wingspan of 2 metres and sometimes glide at eye level past the viewing platforms. Bring binoculars - the puffins blend in among the guillemots. The best time: May to July.

Flamborough Head, around 32 km from Scarborough, a 25-minute drive, is the chalk headland jutting into the North Sea and has two lighthouses: the old one (1674, in white chalk, England's oldest intact lighthouse) and the new one (1806, still in operation). From the coastal paths around the headland, you look down over sheer cliffs and sea caves below - keep an eye out for seals that sometimes rest on the rocks.

Scarborough Castle dominates a 91-metre-high rocky headland with cliffs on three sides, between the town's two bays. The site has been occupied for 3,000 years: a Roman signal station in the 4th century, an Anglo-Saxon chapel, then a royal fortress from 1159 when Henry II took possession of it and had the great stone tower built. It was here that Edward II's favourite, Piers Gaveston, took refuge in 1312 before being captured. In December 1914, German naval bombardment (SMS Derfflinger and SMS Von der Tann) damaged the keep — the shell impacts are still visible. Managed by English Heritage, it's a vast 16-acre site with panoramic views over both bays. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

South Bay, the great sandy beach sheltered below the castle, is Scarborough's historic beach—the town claims to be England's first seaside resort, having attracted spa visitors to its mineral springs as early as the 1620s. In season, the colourful bathing huts and the Victorian Spa are an almost intact period backdrop. For you, the essentials: a seaside walk and an ice cream.

The Scarborough Maritime Heritage Centre, near the old harbour, traces the town's history of deep-sea fishing and maritime trade. Collections of model boats, fishing gear and accounts from seafarers' families. Small but well documented, the place is often quiet — an hour is enough.

activities.text: The coastal path around the castle headland links South Bay to North Bay via the ramparts — a 45-minute walk with views down over both bays and the fishing harbour below. Start from the castle entrance and descend to the old harbour on the far side to see the fishing boats.

North Bay, quieter and less touristy than South Bay, is Scarborough's surf spot. If you don't have a board, local operators offer lessons and rentals on the beach in season. The water's cold even in summer—wetsuit essential.

days_plan.itin_title: North York Moors Road Trip: Coast and Villages

visits.text: The Science Museum in South Kensington holds more than 300,000 objects in its collections and is home to one of the most striking pieces in all of London: the Apollo 10 capsule nicknamed Charlie Brown, the only Apollo spacecraft on display outside the United States. In May 1969, Thomas Stafford, John Young and Eugene Cernan carried out in this capsule a dress rehearsal for the first Moon landing, coming within 14.5 km of the lunar surface without touching down. The capsule arrived at the Science Museum in 1976 and is now housed in the new Space gallery opened in 2025, alongside the Soyuz TMA-19M capsule that brought British astronaut Tim Peake back to Earth. You can still see on the inside walls the calculations scribbled by hand by the astronauts.

activities.text: If you're visiting with children under 14, the Wonderlab is an interactive space dedicated to scientific experiments—plan for a separate ticket and book ahead.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

visits.text: The Seven Sisters draw seven white chalk humps plunging sheer into the Channel. The loop from Cuckmere Haven to the first cliffs covers about 8 km, ideal for a half-day. No barriers, unstable cliffs—stay back from the edge.

Backdrop for numerous films (including Atonement), Cuckmere Haven sees its river meander in oxbows to the sea. The coastguard cottages perched above the beach face erosion threats, several collapses in recent years.

activities.text: Park at Seven Sisters Country Park (Exceat) or South Hill Barn in Seaford. The easy-access trail departs from South Hill Barn and stays accessible to pushchairs and wheelchairs, with identical views of the cliffs. The Cuckmere Inn for an end-of-walk pint.

days_plan.itin_title: England's South Coast 6d: Bristol to Brighton

activities.text: If sea conditions allow, board a boat at Seahouses Harbour for the Farne Islands. Bird colonies are most concentrated during the breeding season, from May to July; seals and cliffs round out the trip. Explicitly choose an excursion with or without a landing, as boat tickets and admission to Inner Farne are separate.

days_plan.itin_title: Hadrian’s Wall and Northumberland: 7 Days Between the Sea and the Forts

visits.text: The sound of water drowns out the noise of the seaside resort in Shanklin Chine. The wooded gorge descends from the old village toward the beach; its interpretive center also tells the story of PLUTO, the undersea pipeline used to supply Allied forces in Normandy. Wear shoes with good traction for the wet steps and check the site’s opening dates.

activities.text: You will extend your stop in Shanklin Old Village, then head to the Esplanade for a walk along the beach. Here, the old village center sits on higher ground, while the waterfront stretches along the foot of the cliffs. Plan for the climb back to your parking spot; check your chosen access route rather than always relying on the elevator.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Wight in 4 days: From Osborne to the Chalk Cliffs

visits.text: Film set and real village: Shere plays both roles effortlessly. The Holiday was shot here in 2006 with artificial snow – the village is already so photogenic that producers dared not alter it. The Tillingbourne crosses the main street beneath a low stone bridge, ducks linger there, and the 16th–17th-century half-timbered houses lean slightly. Fewer than 1,000 residents, no traffic lights, a handful of shops.

Mentioned in the Domesday Book, Shere's St James's Church dates in its current form from the 12th century. Inside is a tiny walled-up cell in which Christine Carpenter, a religious anchoress, voluntarily enclosed herself in the 14th century. The window through which food was passed to her is still visible. Free entry, generally open during the day.

activities.text: Walk from the village toward Newlands Corner, a viewpoint about 3 km into the Surrey Hills where on clear days the vista extends to the South Downs. It's near here that Agatha Christie's car was found in 1926 when the novelist staged her own disappearance. Well-marked path, roughly 90 minutes return.

days_plan.itin_title: Surrey to Kent: Castles and Gardens in 10 Days

places.name: Shiplake

visits.text: Tennyson married here on 13 June 1850—he gave the vicar a poem instead of a fee. St Peter & St Paul dates from the 13th century and perches on a wooded cliff above the Thames. The view from the churchyard over the river makes the stop worthwhile. Free entry, parking on Church Lane.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop

map_keywords: St Peter St Paul Church Shiplake

visits.text: Ironbridge Gorge has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986—and the title 'birthplace of the Industrial Revolution' is no exaggeration. This is where Abraham Darby I, in 1709, developed the technique of smelting iron with coke, making metal production infinitely cheaper and faster. His grandson, Abraham Darby III, erected the world's first iron bridge across the Severn in 1779: 30 metres span, 378 tonnes of cast iron from the Coalbrookdale foundries. The first tolls on this bridge weren't collected until 1 January 1781. You can still cross the bridge on foot—it's been closed to traffic since 1934.

The ten museums of the Ironbridge Gorge site cover the entire industrial history of the valley—you needn't do them all, but three deserve your time. Start with the Coalbrookdale Museum of Iron, housed in the old blast furnaces: this is where it all began in 1709. Then push on to Blists Hill Victorian Town, a full-scale recreation of an 1900 industrial town with working shops and costumed actors—allow at least 2 hours. If you have a soft spot for decorative arts, the Jackfield Tile Museum is worth the detour: the faience tiles produced here once adorned London Underground stations and palaces worldwide. A combined Passport ticket covers all ten sites with no time limit.

Shrewsbury, 30km northwest of Ironbridge, is a near-intact medieval town nestled in a meander of the Severn—the river encircles the old town on three sides. The historic centre contains more than 660 timber-framed buildings dating from the 15th and 16th centuries. The Old Market Hall from 1596 still presides over the main square. Wander the 'shuts'—covered passageways between houses dating from the Middle Ages—to lose yourself in the lower town.

Shrewsbury Castle, in red sandstone, has overlooked the river since the 11th century. It now houses a military museum, but the view across the medieval rooftops of the old town from the castle gardens is worth the visit. The Quarry park, on the banks of the Severn, contains 'the Dingle'—a sunken garden maintained since the 19th century, one of England's most floral.

activities.text: The Severn at Ironbridge is a working and accessible river. Local operators offer kayak or canoe trips from the banks below the Iron Bridge—an original way to see the gorge from the water, where barges once carried cast iron downriver to Bristol. Allow at least 2 hours.
Local companies run boat trips on the Severn from Shrewsbury, passing under the old stone bridges and along the wooded banks of the meander. Some evening cruises include a meal on board.

days_plan.itin_title: The Midlands and Peak District Essentials
Midlands and Peak District Road Trip: Heritage and Wild Landscapes

visits.text: You will visit the Silent Valley Visitor Centre to understand the landscape as a work of hydraulic engineering. The reservoir was built from 1923 to 1933: behind the scenery of the Mournes lies infrastructure still in operation. Check the center’s opening hours and permitted access routes before heading to the dam.

activities.text: If access routes are open, walk to Silent Valley Dam from the visitor parking lot. The reservoir supplies Belfast and part of County Down; its shores offer a different perspective on the mountains from the valley floor. Stay on authorized paths and check NI Water notices, particularly for the lower loop.

days_plan.itin_title: Mourne and Strangford in 3 Days: Gardens, Sea, and Woods

visits.text: Wrest Park's Long Water reflects a mansion in the style of a French château — incongruous in the middle of Bedfordshire, and that's exactly the intended effect. This 300-metre-long reflecting pool is surrounded by three centuries of layered gardens, from seventeenth-century formal parterres to landscaped woodland designed by Lancelot Brown around 1758. The Baroque Archer Pavilion at the Long Water's end is one of England's most elegant garden pavilions.

Thomas de Grey designed Wrest Park house himself between 1834 and 1839, inspired by Loire châteaux — this first president of the Royal Institute of British Architects had clear ideas. The interior is partially furnished, with exhibitions on the de Grey family's history. Closed Mondays and Tuesdays.

activities.text: Wrest Park offers one of Bedfordshire's most comprehensive garden walks — a real jigsaw of styles to explore at your own pace. The Bath House hidden in the woods, William Chambers's Chinese Temple and the restored rose garden each merit a detour. Allow at least two hours to explore the gardens, not counting the house.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

places.name: Sir John Soane S Museum

visits.text: Sir John Soane's Museum at Lincoln's Inn Fields is one of London's strangest and most fascinating places—and it's free. John Soane (1753–1837), architect of the Bank of England, transformed three adjoining townhouses into a labyrinth of rooms where he crammed his collections according to personal logic: Egyptian sarcophagi, Roman columns, Hogarth paintings, architectural models, Greco-Roman antiquities. The house is preserved exactly as it was at his death in 1837, by an Act of Parliament he had passed during his lifetime. The Picture Room is a marvel of ingenuity: Soane installed hinged panels that unfold to reveal 118 paintings hidden behind each other—including Hogarth's eight-painting series A Rake's Progress (1733). In the Sepulchral Chamber rests the alabaster sarcophagus of Pharaoh Seti I, discovered in Egypt in 1812 and considered one of the most important objects ever found in Egypt. Arrive early—the museum is very popular and space is limited.

activities.text: The Picture Room panels are opened at fixed times (11am, 2pm, 3pm, 4pm)—plan your visit to witness the opening of the panels, it's a special moment.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

map_keywords: Sir John Soane Museum Lincoln's Inn Fields London

visits.text: In 1930, Vita Sackville-West paid £12,375 for these ruins – no running water, no electricity, no heating. She saw them as a substitute for Knole, the ancestral house she had been barred from inheriting. What she created in thirty years remains one of England's most influential gardens: seven walled garden “rooms”, each with its own theme. The geometric structure came from her husband Harold Nicolson; the romantic chaos of the planting, from her.

White, silver-grey, pale green – the White Garden explodes in June with its white roses, silvery foliage, and clematis climbing the central framework. The mulliganii rose cascading over the central arbour in mid-June has been photographed for decades. Arrive before 10am on a Friday or Monday to visit without crowds.

The Elizabethan tower is small, the 78 wooden stairs steep and worn—but the view from the top over the seven gardens and the 450-acre estate is worth the effort. Vita's study on the first floor is preserved as she left it. This is where she wrote her garden columns for the Observer until her death in 1962. Queue in high season.

activities.text: Explore the 450 acres of farmland beyond the formal gardens – a working farm with marked paths through Weald woods and meadows. The main loop takes 90 minutes and passes the old barns and original oast houses. Maps at reception. The estate is accessible even without a ticket for the formal garden.

In June, come early: the Rose Garden reaches its peak in the third week of the month, when Vita's old roses are in simultaneous bloom. She preferred heritage roses to modern hybrids—an almost militant stance for the time. Sissinghurst closes Wednesdays and Thursdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports
Surrey to Kent: Castles and Gardens in 10 Days

visits.text: Aysgarth Falls in Wensleydale is the Thames, Yorkshire-style: the River Ure tumbles over three tiers of limestone ledges in an oak woodland. Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves (1991) was filmed here. Take the detour to the lower falls - less busy than the upper ones and much more impressive after rain, which is hardly unusual in England. Plan a return drive from Skipton to the car park, followed by the walk to the falls.

Skipton Castle deserves more than a glance from the street. Built from 1090, remodelled in the 14th century, it withstood a three-year siege during the Civil War (1642–1645) before being partially dismantled on Cromwell's orders. Lady Anne Clifford restored it in the 1650s - the yew tree she planted in the inner courtyard is still there, three and a half centuries later. Climb onto the ramparts for views over the town and canal. It's one of England's best-preserved medieval castles and ticket prices remain reasonable.

Make the detour to Bolton Abbey, 8km east of Skipton on the banks of the Wharfe - one of England's most beautiful monastic ruins, and entry is free for pedestrians. The 12th-century Augustinian ruins sit alongside a priory still used for Sunday worship, creating a strange and endearing mix. The estate belongs to the Duke of Devonshire. The 5km walk around the river's meander is easy and magnificent - allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

activities.text: Skipton market is one of Yorkshire's oldest and liveliest, held since 1204. It runs Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday on the High Street. If you visit on one of those days, you'll find local cheeses, charcuterie, artisan breads and produce from surrounding farms in the Dales.

The walk along Skipton's ramparts follows the Leeds-Liverpool Canal - the longest canal built in Britain with a uniform navigable depth (204km, completed in 1816). A 3km round trip from the castle gives you a sense of the peaceful atmosphere of Yorkshire's canals.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake District and North-East Loop: Lakes, Dales and Cathedrals

visits.text: Snape Maltings rises from the Alde's reed beds: these nineteenth-century red-brick maltings were transformed into a concert hall in 1967 on Benjamin Britten's initiative. The main hall — remarkable acoustics in a raw industrial setting — is recognised as one of Europe's finest chamber music venues. Galleries, shops and a café with a riverside terrace complete the site.

The salt marshes around Snape Maltings are part of the Suffolk Coast Path, the coastal trail linking Snape to Aldeburgh along the Alde's banks. The view over reed beds at dusk, with sheep in the meadows and yachts at anchor, explains why Britten composed here.

activities.text: You drive to Snape Maltings for a walk along the Alde's banks, facing reed beds and mudflats. This nineteenth-century maltings building, converted into a concert hall in 1967, also houses galleries, shops and a good café with a terrace. Concerts for the Snape Proms and Aldeburgh Festival are staged here every summer.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: Immerse yourself in the breathtaking landscapes of Snowdonia National Park, home to Wales' highest peaks and most dramatic mountain scenery. The park encompasses 823 square miles of rugged mountains, glacial lakes, ancient forests and wild moorland that has inspired artists, poets and adventurers for centuries. On clear days, the views across the peaks create some of the most spectacular panoramas in Britain.

Challenge yourself on Mount Snowdon, the highest mountain in Wales at 1,085 meters, whose summit can be reached by several hiking trails of varying difficulty or by the famous Snowdon Mountain Railway. The Pyg Track and Miners' Track are popular routes offering stunning views over Glaslyn and Llyn Llydaw, glacial lakes that shimmer like jewels in their mountain bowls. On the summit, on clear days, views extend to Ireland, Scotland and England.

Discover the park's hidden valleys, cascading waterfalls and ancient oak woodlands that create a landscape of endless variety and beauty. Historic slate quarries, their terraces carved into mountainsides, tell the story of the industry that shaped North Wales and exported Welsh slate across the world. The mountain villages, with their stone cottages and Welsh-speaking communities, maintain traditions stretching back centuries.

activities.text: Take the Snowdon Mountain Railway from Llanberis for a scenic ascent to the summit without the hiking effort

days_plan.itin_title: Wales Road Trip: Conwy Castle, Pembrokeshire Coast & Snowdonia

visits.text: Soho developed from the 17th century as the neighbourhood of Huguenot refugees fleeing France after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685. This tradition of welcoming marginalized communities persists: Soho successively became the Victorian artistic bohemia neighbourhood, of jazz in the 1950s, of rock in the 1960s, then the heart of Britain's LGBTQ+ community. Old Compton Street has been its living centre since the 1970s. In the evening, Wardour Street and its surroundings concentrate an exceptional density of bars, restaurants and concert venues for such a small area.

activities.text: The West End begins east of Soho - Shaftesbury Avenue alone concentrates six theatres. The TKTS booth on Leicester Square sells discounted tickets for evening performances on the day - turn up in early afternoon to have choice. London theatres often offer 'standing tickets' sold an hour before the show for a fraction of the price.

For dinner, Soho offers one of London's most diverse restaurant offerings in such a compact area - Vietnamese cuisine on Wardour Street, Japanese izakayas on Brewer Street, trattorias on Dean Street. Frith Street houses one of London's oldest jazz clubs still active, open since the 1950s - check the programme before you go.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

activities.text: Southampton is the starting point: Red Funnel ferries to East Cowes on the Isle of Wight leave from here. If you have time, take the chance to visit the city before the crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Wight in 4 days: From Osborne to the Chalk Cliffs

visits.text: Don't miss Sutton Hoo en route to Southwold—one of Europe's most important archaeological sites. In June 1939, self-taught archaeologist Basil Brown uncovered beneath a burial mound a 27-metre-long ship and a burial chamber filled with early 7th-century Anglo-Saxon treasures: 37 solid gold coins (Frankish tremisses), 5th-century Byzantine silverware, garnets from Sri Lanka and a human-faced helmet that became the symbol of the Anglo-Saxon period. The deceased is probably King Rædwald of East Anglia, who died around 625. The originals are in the British Museum, but the National Trust-managed site offers an excellent exhibition and visits to the mounds. Allow 1.5 hours.

Framlingham Castle is one of England's best-preserved medieval castles, with a wall-walk on the battlements offering clear views across the Suffolk countryside. Built between 1190 and 1210 by Roger Bigod, it's famous as the place where Mary Tudor awaited the battle result that would carry her to the English throne in 1553. The town of Framlingham invites a stroll: its market, pubs and quiet atmosphere are typically Suffolk.

Southwold Pier, built in 1900 to welcome steamships from London, has been rebuilt several times after storms. Its current 623-foot version dates from 2001. Enter the Under the Pier Show: a collection of deliberately absurd slot machines, the work of artist Tim Hunkin, where you can notably 'sell modern art with a machine gun'. The pier is free to access, games cost extra.

Southwold's multicoloured beach huts are the town's postcard image—there are 266, all privately owned. Originally they were Victorian 'bathing machines' on wheels allowing ladies to change unseen. The golden sand beach is one of Suffolk's finest. Heading back to the centre, explore the lanes around Market Place—independent shops, pubs, and the local brewery producing beers since 1872.

Walberswick, on the other bank of the Blyth, is a peaceful fishing village with a long sandy beach and RSPB-managed bird marshes. Much quieter than Southwold, it's a good counterpoint for anyone seeking solitude.

Orford Castle is one of England's most fascinating castles, with its 21-sided polygonal keep—unique in the country. Henry II had it built between 1165 and 1173 to counter the power of Suffolk barons, notably Hugh Bigod of Framlingham. Construction cost £1,413 sterling, a colossal sum at the time, and detailed accounts are preserved in the royal Pipe Rolls. Climb to the roof for views over Orford Ness. Inside, read the legend of the Wildman of Orford: in 1167, fishermen supposedly caught in their nets a wild man covered in hair, held six months in the castle without ever speaking a word, before escaping to the sea.

Aldeburgh is a former Tudor port town turned discreet and elegant seaside resort, intimately linked to composer Benjamin Britten who founded the Aldeburgh Festival here in 1948—still one of Britain's major classical music festivals. On the shingle beach, the 16th-century Moot Hall now sits at the water's edge, after coastal erosion swallowed everything around it. Fishermen's huts sell smoked fish and crabs directly on the beach.

Thorpeness, 2km north of Aldeburgh, is an entirely artificial village designed from 1910 by eccentric Stuart Ogilvie: a neo-Tudor holiday community with a 65-acre artificial lake (the Meare). The 'House in the Clouds' perched at 21 metres actually concealed a 50,000-gallon water tower—decorated on the facade to look like an ordinary house so as not to spoil the village aesthetic. Impossible not to smile seeing this.

activities.text: Arriving in Southwold late afternoon, take an initial tour of the seafront. The white 31-metre lighthouse, built in 1887 right in the town centre, is open for visits—113 steps for a panoramic coastal view. On Gun Hill, six 18th-century cannons face the sea: they commemorate the 1672 Battle of Sole Bay where the Anglo-French and Dutch fleets clashed right here. An excellent appetizer for the rest of your stay.

The small rowing ferry crossing between Southwold and Walberswick is one of the little joys of this coast. The service is seasonal (generally April to October)—otherwise take the bridge on foot, 20 minutes. On the other side, walk along the beach to the RSPB marshes for birdwatching, then return via the dunes. Allow 2 hours round trip.
Small pedestrian ferry crossing between Southwold and Walberswick

Walk on Southwold Pier, built in 1900 as a landing stage for steamers bringing tourists from London. Dynamited during World War II to prevent a German landing, struck by a drifting mine in 1941, hit by storms in 1955, it was completely rebuilt and now extends 190 metres. It houses a collection of eccentric coin-operated machines created by inventor Tim Hunkin.
Visit the local brewery, established since 1872 on East Green, on a site where beer has been brewed for at least 670 years. Tasting of craft beers and spirits distilled on site.

East Anglia Circuit: Cambridge, Suffolk Coast and Royal Norfolk

visits.text: Verulamium was Roman Britain's third-largest city, founded after the conquest of AD 43. The Verulamium Museum displays mosaics and everyday objects from its former inhabitants, with reconstructions of period shops and rooms. What makes St Albans unusual is that the modern city developed slightly away from ancient Verulamium, so most remains are still beneath the park's lawns, available for future excavation.

St Albans Cathedral's nave blends Roman bricks salvaged from Verulamium with eleventh-century Norman pillars — a mixture of eras that exists nowhere else. Erected on the site of the martyrdom of Alban, Britain's first Christian martyr, who was executed around AD 209, the cathedral is one of the country's oldest. Free entry.

activities.text: You finish with the Roman Theatre of Verulamium, one of the few Roman theatres still visible in Britain. Its semi-circular stage, excavated in 1934, could accommodate thousands of spectators. It's adjacent to Verulamium Museum—a combined ticket is available. St Albans is 20 minutes by train from London St Pancras: easy access to finish the circuit.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: The sky replaces the vaulted ceiling at St Andrews Cathedral, whose ruins spread out near the shore. Its consecration took place in 1318 in the presence of Robert the Bruce, after construction was interrupted by a storm and war, among other setbacks. St Rule’s Tower belongs to the earlier religious complex. Walk through the site of the nave to appreciate the space between the surviving structures; this ground-level visit does not require climbing the tower.

A siege can also unfold underground: St Andrews Castle preserves a mine and countermine associated with the fighting of 1546–1547. This bishops’ residence also served as a fortress and prison; the dungeon cut into the rock adds another dimension to the sea views. Start with the dungeon and sea views, then leave the underground passages for last, if they are accessible and suitable for your mobility.

activities.text: You will walk alongside the Old Course with a St Andrews Links guide to understand a course that is as much a part of golf history as it is of everyday life in the town. The town acquired it in 1894, and it regularly hosts the Open Championship. A guided walk lets you understand its terrain without playing a round. Book a tour offered on your chosen date and respect the marked boundaries: playing areas are not pedestrian shortcuts.

If you still feel like walking, head to West Sands after your visits in St Andrews. The beach was used to film the opening scene of Chariots of Fire; the dunes bordering the sand also protect the neighboring golf courses. Walk on the beach or designated access paths without cutting through the dunes. Adjust your distance to the wind and tide, then return to the same access point.

days_plan.itin_title: Fife and Dundee in 5 Days: Harbors, Palaces and Castles

visits.text: Marvel at the Eden Project, one of Cornwall's most innovative attractions, where enormous biodome structures house botanical gardens showcasing plant species from around the world. Since opening in 2001, this futuristic complex has captivated visitors with its striking exhibitions, interactive experiences and passionate commitment to environmental education. The massive biomes, built in a reclaimed clay pit, create tropical rainforest and Mediterranean climates under their transparent canopies.

Explore St Austell, an old market town that played a vital role in Cornwall's mining and china clay industries, which brought prosperity to the region. Evidence of the town's historical importance can still be seen in its streets. The St Austell Brewing Company offers tours and tastings of traditional Cornish beers brewed using time-honoured methods.

Wander through the Lost Gardens of Heligan, a hidden gem covering more than 200 acres of restored Victorian gardens and woodlands near Mevagissey. Suspended bridges, moss-covered statues and jungle-like plantings create an atmosphere of rediscovered wonder in these gardens that lay abandoned and overgrown for decades until their restoration began in the 1990s. The story of the gardens' neglect during World War I and subsequent rescue adds poignant historical depth to their natural beauty.

activities.text: Spend a half-day exploring the Eden Project's biomes and outdoor gardens

days_plan.itin_title: Cornwall Coastal Road Trip: Castles, Secret Coves & Celtic Heritage Guide

visits.text: From Scott’s View, three peaks rise above the bends of the River Tweed. The Eildon Hills recall the volcanic past of this landscape, which Walter Scott admired. Wait for a break in the clouds to take photos, and keep a windbreaker handy.

It would be a shame to rush through Dryburgh Abbey: its tree-filled gardens also deserve your attention. Walter Scott is buried in the north transept; the chapter house still preserves traces of medieval plaster and paint. Allow time for these details: from April through September, the last admission is at 4:30 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Borders in 3 Days: Castles and Great Abbeys

visits.text: Marvel at the Green Bridge of Wales, approximately 55 km from St Davids, a 1-hour drive away: a spectacular natural limestone arch jutting dramatically into the sea on the Pembrokeshire coast. Shaped by millennia of wave action, this remarkable geological formation is one of Wales's most photographed natural wonders. The nearby Elegug Stacks, two giant stone pillars rising from the sea, add to this striking coastal landscape and its display of nature's raw power.

Explore St Davids, Britain's smallest city and the most westerly point of Wales, built around its magnificent medieval cathedral. St Davids Cathedral, nestled in a peaceful hollow, is the final resting place of Wales' patron saint and has been a site of pilgrimage for over 1,500 years. The purple-hued stone building with its distinctive square tower represents one of the finest examples of medieval religious architecture in Britain.

Watch a spectacular sunset at Whitesands Beach near St Davids, one of the most stunning coastal experiences in Wales. This beautiful Blue Flag beach offers pristine golden sands backed by dramatic headlands, with views stretching across St Brides Bay. The sunsets here paint the sky in extraordinary colors, creating magical moments that visitors remember long after leaving.

activities.text: Book a boat trip with Thousand Island Expeditions to Skomer Island, home to a colony of puffins

days_plan.itin_title: Wales Road Trip: Conwy Castle, Pembrokeshire Coast & Snowdonia
Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: With neither a dial nor hands, Cotehele’s clock still keeps time by chiming the hours. This curiosity sits alongside tapestries, weapons, and furniture in a house with medieval origins that was extensively remodeled during the Tudor period. Look for the chapel during your visit and check winter restrictions: some rooms close for conservation work.

Cotehele Mill shifts the focus from grand houses to the more hands-on work of a watermill. The workshops and stream reveal the estate’s everyday life at the bottom of a wooded valley. Park at Cotehele Quay: there is no visitor parking at the mill, which you then reach on foot.

activities.text: If you prefer gardens to armor, Cotehele’s terraces offer a break above the Tamar. The Valley Garden preserves an old fishpond and a dovecote, while the orchards recall the importance of fruit in the valley. Choose a short loop near the house to leave enough time for the mill.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast Cornwall in 3 Days: Harbors and Manor Houses

visits.text: Discover St Ives, perhaps the most beloved destination in Cornwall, where expansive golden beaches stretch beneath a picturesque town of cobbled streets and whitewashed cottages. For centuries, this fishing village has attracted visitors drawn by its exceptional light, beautiful beaches and artistic heritage. The combination of seaside charm, cultural attractions and natural beauty makes St Ives irresistible to first-time visitors and returning devotees alike.

Visit Tate St Ives, the modern art gallery that showcases works by artists who have been inspired by Cornwall's extraordinary light and landscape since the 1920s. The gallery's striking architecture, perched above Porthmeor Beach, provides the perfect setting for collections that include works by Barbara Hepworth, Ben Nicholson and other luminaries of the St Ives School. The views from the gallery windows compete with the art on the walls for visitors' attention.

Explore the winding cobbled streets connecting charming corners, seaside pubs and traditional pasty shops that give St Ives its irresistible character. The harbor, still home to a working fishing fleet, provides a picturesque heart to the town, while the beaches on either side offer different characters for swimming, surfing or simply sunbathing. Boat trips depart regularly to spot dolphins or see the iconic Godrevy Lighthouse up close.

Relax on the beautiful beaches of St Ives, which are particularly impressive at low tide when vast expanses of golden sand are revealed. Porthmeor Beach attracts surfers and art lovers drawn to the nearby Tate, while the sheltered Harbour Beach offers calmer waters for families. The town's position on a narrow peninsula means you're never far from the sound of the waves, wherever you wander.

activities.text: Take a boat trip from the harbor to spot dolphins and see Godrevy Lighthouse, inspiration for Virginia Woolf's novel

days_plan.itin_title: Cornwall Coastal Road Trip: Castles, Secret Coves & Celtic Heritage Guide
England Grand Tour: From Cornwall to the Northern Lakes

visits.text: A bistro, a doctor's surgery, a shady pub called “Little Hell”: these are the successive uses of the medieval chapel built into St Ives bridge, one of only four bridges with chapels still standing in England. Dating from the fifteenth century, this small limestone structure is Grade I listed. The key is available from Norris Museum or the town hall.

Houghton Mill, two kilometres upstream, is the last working watermill on the Great Ouse. There has been a mill on this site for over a thousand years. National Trust, open weekends and school holidays—you can buy flour milled on site, which isn't common.

activities.text: The walk from St Ives to Houghton Mill along the Ouse Valley Way is one of Cambridgeshire's best flat walks — water meadows, herons, locks. Allow 45 minutes each way. Oliver Cromwell signed the register of All Saints church in St Ives; the register is on display in the vestibule.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: The background noise here is the Atlantic crashing against cliffs, 500 meters beneath the miners' feet. Botallack's Crowns Engine Houses have clung to the cliff face since 1815: the shafts run 400 meters beneath the sea. A UNESCO site since 2006, the backdrop for Poldark. Descend the paved path to the two steam engines—the view of the waves from down there is worth the walk.

Closed in 1990, Geevor remains frozen in time—the miners' changing room sits untouched since the last shift. Between 1911 and 1990 the mine produced some 50,000 tonnes of black tin. The tunnels run more than 300 meters beneath the sea. The guides are former miners: they know what they're talking about. Book the underground tour in advance during high season.

activities.text: The true end of the earth, without the theme park: Cape Cornwall is a raw, little-visited headland with an old mine chimney on the summit and views over the Brisons. For centuries sailors mistakenly believed this was Britain's westernmost point. A quick stop before Geevor.

days_plan.itin_title: Dark Cornwall: Arthur, Mines and Wreckers 7d

visits.text: St Katharine Docks is the last major historic dock still visible near central London. Opened in 1828 after the demolition of an entire neighbourhood (11,000 people displaced), it was intended for precious goods - ivory, sugar, coffee, wool. Closed in 1968 for failing to adapt to containers, it was converted into a pleasure marina. Today, luxury yachts sit alongside historic barges in a basin metres from the Tower of London. The atmosphere is calm and surprising for anyone arriving from the tourist chaos of Tower Bridge.

activities.text: Stroll along the pontoons and observe the sailboats and barges moored - some are lived in year-round. The restaurant and bar terraces around the dock are pleasant in late afternoon. From St Katharine Docks, you can walk to Wapping High Street in 10 minutes to see the old warehouses converted into flats - one of the most authentic Docklands neighbourhoods.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Walk 800 metres from the Stackpole Quay car park to reach Barafundle Bay. Barafundle was the private beach of the Earls Cawdor, and the wall at the entrance still hints at that history. There are no facilities on the beach: bring water, food and sunscreen. Parking at the Quay is paid (National Trust).

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: Walter Scott said of Stamford that it was “the most beautiful stone town in England” — and while the saying is attributed in various ways, it fits perfectly. Over 600 listed ochre-limestone buildings, spared by the Victorian railway that bypassed the town, form one of the country's most intact historic centres. Come on a Friday, market day, to see the square bustling.

Burghley House stretches over more than a hundred rooms and was built between 1555 and 1587 by William Cecil, Elizabeth I's chief advisor. The state rooms overflow with seventeenth-century paintings, tapestries, and porcelain. The park was designed by Capability Brown and hosts the Burghley Horse Trials every autumn. Open Wednesday to Sunday.

You walk the Welland's meadows from Stamford centre, passing under the George Hotel's hanging sign—a coaching inn founded in the sixteenth century, whose sign has spanned the main street for centuries. It's Stamford's iconic image. The river's meanders offer a peaceful car-free walk.

activities.text: At St Martin's Antiques, drawers overflow with old photographs, mother-of-pearl buttons and pocket watches. This maze of about sixty dealers occupies a former rectory in the pedestrian street — nothing is labelled the same way, everything is negotiable. Arrive in the morning, before coach groups from Peterborough descend.

If you visit on a Friday, Stamford's market has occupied the market square for centuries. Local produce, Lincolnshire cheeses, flowers and crafts. The town also has several independent art galleries in the lanes adjoining Broad Street.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

places.name: Stansted Mountfitchet

visits.text: Deer roam freely, fires crackle in hearths, and armored mannequins stand guard: Mountfitchet Castle is a full-scale reconstruction of a 1066 Norman village on the original site of Robert Gernon's castle. Across 4 hectares, you can touch weapons, try on armor, and be put in the pillory. Open mid-March to mid-November.

The House on the Hill Toy Museum, right next to the castle, is included in the same ticket. Over 80,000 toys from the 1950s to the 1990s fill the rooms—slot machines, life-size Star Wars figures, Victorian teddy bears. An additional admission fee gives access to a haunted manor for enthusiasts.

activities.text: Stansted Mountfitchet's windmill, built in 1787, opens to the public once a month according to the schedule posted at the town hall. If dates align, it's one of the rare chances to see a working windmill in Essex.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

map_keywords: House on the Hill Toy Museum Stansted

visits.text: White quartzite blocks, fractured by freeze-thaw cycles from the last glaciation, standing upright on a bare ridge: the Stiperstones are unmatched in the country. The rock, formed roughly 480 million years ago, was deposited in shallow marine conditions. The ridge path is short but brutal. Manstone Rock, the highest tor, rises to 536 metres.

activities.text: Locals call the summit tor the Devil's Chair, and legend has it that the Devil holds court there on the winter solstice eve. According to local lore, the Luftwaffe bombed the rock during the war, mistaking it for a town. The Bog Visitor Centre (a converted old school) car park is the proper starting point, parking free. Avoid in mist—the rock becomes a trap.

days_plan.itin_title: Welsh Marches, Cotswolds and Bath in 11 days

visits.text: He who holds Stirling holds Scotland: the Great Hall from 1503, Scotland's largest medieval banqueting hall at 42 m long, confirms the Stuarts' ambition. The restored Royal Palace houses the Stirling Unicorns – copies of 16th-century tapestries. Open at 9:30 am before the school groups arrive.

From the ramparts, two battlefields are visible at the same time: Stirling Bridge on the right, where Wallace defeated the English in 1297, and Bannockburn on the left, where Bruce defeated them in 1314.

activities.text: The Wallace Monument is unapologetically kitsch, but the view from the top across the Forth plain is worth the 247 steps. It's a neo-Gothic tower from 1869. Below, Stirling's old quarter—Broad Street, Mar's Wark—deserves an hour's wandering without paying admission.

days_plan.itin_title: Scotland: Highlands & Skye in 12 days
Fife and Dundee in 5 Days: Harbors, Palaces and Castles

visits.text: You first have to descend to reach the fortress: Dunnottar Castle stands on a rocky promontory separated from the coast by a steep-sided hollow. You then explore the open-air ruins with the sea all around you. Check that it is open on the morning of your visit: wind can close access, and the stairs call for shoes with a secure grip.

activities.text: You will stroll along the quays at Stonehaven Harbour for a quieter change of pace after Dunnottar Castle. The harbor also marks the start of the coastal path to the fortress. Keep this visit to a waterfront stroll: completing the full route would add a hike to the itinerary. Keep children away from the edges of the quays.

days_plan.itin_title: Royal Deeside and the Castles of Aberdeenshire in 4 Days

places.name: Stornoway

visits.text: The CalMac ferry from Ullapool drops you off in Stornoway after a 2-hour 45-minute crossing of the Minch – and that crossing is the beginning, not just the journey. The name Stornoway comes from the Old Norse Stjórnavágr, meaning “rudder bay”, which tells you something about how long people have been navigating these waters. The town is the capital and only real urban centre of the Outer Hebrides, with just over 8,000 inhabitants, and it carries that role with quiet confidence. Start with the harbour quay – fishing boats land their catch here every morning, and the smell of peat drifts from the harbour's smokehouses, where seafood is dried before it reaches the island's restaurants.

Lews Castle, the Victorian neo-Gothic pile set in woodland above the harbour, was built in the 1840s for Sir James Matheson, who bought the entire island in 1844 on the back of a fortune made in the opium trade. In 2016, after a £19.5 million restoration, it reopened as Museum nan Eilean - and it's worth every minute inside. Six of the Lewis Chessmen are displayed here: those extraordinary 12th-century carved walrus ivory pieces found in a sandbank at Uig on the west coast of Lewis in 1831, probably made in Norway and lost or hidden here, nobody knows why. The British Museum has 82 of them; this is your chance to see some up close without going to London.

On the way out of Stornoway, the Lewis War Memorial on Cnoc nan Uan hill – a 26-metre Scottish Baronial tower built in 1924 – is visible from half the roads approaching town. It commemorates the island's dead from the First World War, and the number of names on those walls is devastating for a community this size. But the memorial stands near the site of the Iolaire disaster of 1919: a naval yacht carrying 280 Lewis sailors home from the front struck rocks in Stornoway harbour on New Year's Day and sank, drowning 201 men – within sight of their families waiting on the quay. It remains one of the worst peacetime maritime disasters in British waters.

Drive the 28 km to Callanish (Calanais) on the west coast and give yourselves the whole morning. The Callanish Standing Stones were erected around 2750 BCE, several centuries before Stonehenge, and unlike Stonehenge, there are no barriers. You can walk right up to them, run your hand over 3-billion-year-old Lewisian gneiss, the oldest rock in western Europe, and stand in the central circle of 13 stones around the 5-metre monolith at its heart. The site is free to visit all year round. What the builders created here is a cross-shaped arrangement of stone rows radiating from the central circle, positioned on a ridge overlooking Loch Roag and aligned with the extreme rising and setting points of the sun and moon. Every 18.6 years, the full moon appears to skim the southern hills and roll along the horizon, a phenomenon that was almost certainly observed and predicted here.

A few kilometres north of Callanish, Dun Carloway Broch is the best-preserved Iron Age broch in the Western Isles. It still stands 9 metres high, giving you a real sense of what these hollow dry-stone towers looked like when complete. Brochs are found only in Scotland, built around the 1st century CE, probably as high-status residences for tribal chiefs. You can enter, walk between the double walls and climb the internal staircase. The classic Dun Carloway story tells how, in the early 17th century, a raiding clan hid stolen cattle inside the tower until the aggrieved party climbed the outside wall by driving daggers between the stones as handholds, then threw burning heather in from above. Admission is free, with a small visitor centre across the road. Allow for a return drive from Stornoway.

Two kilometres farther on, Gearrannan Blackhouse Village is a group of nine restored stone cottages with thatched roofs perched directly above the Atlantic on Lewis's west coast. The last residents left in 1974, less than 50 years ago, after electricity arrived in 1952 and running water in the 1960s gradually made the traditional communal way of life less essential. The museum house has been restored to its 1950s condition: low ceilings, box beds and a central peat fire without a chimney, the smoke escaping through the thatch. The contrast between life here and what was happening in England at the same time is quietly astonishing. The café and shop reopen in 2026. Allow for a return drive from Stornoway.

activities.text: An Lanntair arts centre, on South Beach, is a modern glass-fronted building overlooking the harbour with a cinema, gallery, café and regular evenings of traditional Gaelic music and ceilidhs. Even if you're only passing through town, check what's on – this is the cultural heartbeat of the islands and an evening here is completely different from anything you'd find on the mainland. The centre is open daily except Sundays.

At Arnol, the preserved Arnol Blackhouse (Historic Environment Scotland) shows an even older version of the traditional dwelling, with the cattle stall at one end still intact and a peat fire still burning inside as it would have for centuries. If you visit only one blackhouse, this is the more atmospheric of the two. Allow for a return drive from Stornoway.

The Butt of Lewis, at the island's northernmost tip, is approximately a 45-minute drive from Stornoway on the A857. The lighthouse, built in 1862, towers over cliffs that take the full force of Atlantic storms with nothing between them and Canada. In bad weather, this is one of Scotland's most dramatic places. When it is calm, look for gannets diving offshore.
