visits.text: The smell of damp earth and rhododendrons greets you at the path entrance, then the lake appears suddenly with the Pantheon and its columns reflected in the water. Henry Hoare II designed this garden between 1743 and 1780, inspired by paintings of Claude Lorrain and Virgil's Aeneid: each temple marks a symbolic stage. The circuit of the lake is 2.5 km. The rhododendrons, added by his grandson after 1791, are the April-May spectacle. Arrive before 10am: the morning light on the lake is optimal and the tour buses haven't yet disgorged their passengers. National Trust, around £20.

Henry Hoare II was in mourning when he began the project: five family members died between 1727 and 1743. The garden was his response. This changes how you read the dark grotto and the stairway up to the Temple of Apollo, god of light. Stourhead House (Palladian, 1721) holds Chippendale the Elder furniture and the Hoare painting collection. Open separately from the garden.

A triangular red-brick tower, built to celebrate... the end of a war in France and the accession of George III. Henry Hoare II commissioned this 49-metre folly from architect Henry Flitcroft, completed in 1772. In 1944, an American aircraft struck it, killing all five crew members and taking off the top 10 metres. The tower was restored in 1986 using a helicopter. From the top: views across Somerset, Wiltshire and Dorset. 205 steps. NT, £5, open weekends April to September.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days

visits.text: Stow-on-the-Wold is the Cotswolds' highest town, perched at 244 metres on the Roman Fosse Way. Its Market Square, which has hosted markets since 1107, once saw up to 20,000 sheep at a single fair—the 'tures', those narrow stone-walled lanes, were used to funnel flocks toward the square. Today, start at the Cotswold Cheese Company on Digbeth Street: over 120 artisan cheeses are stocked, with a strong focus on local producers. Try the Double Gloucester from Smart's Farm, whose tradition goes back to local cheese competitions.

Six kilometres from Stow, Daylesford Organic Farm Shop is a national reference for organic and sustainable farming. You'll find pasture-raised meat, artisan bread, house-made cheeses and an exceptional deli. The farm also has a restaurant, creamery and cookery school. If the budget allows, lunch on site is a fine way to taste what the Cotswolds terroir can deliver.

Don't miss Stow's farmers' market, held on the second Thursday of each month on Market Square from 9am to 1pm. Oils, jams, breads, meats and cheeses direct from local producers—this is where 'zero food miles' makes complete sense in the Cotswolds.

activities.text: An artisan cheese tasting at the Cotswold Cheese Company can be improvised easily with help from the cheesemongers—they'll guide you through the differences between young and aged Double Gloucester, Shropshire Blue and local goat's cheese. Then assemble a platter to take away for a picnic in the Cotswolds countryside.

The gastropub meal is a Cotswolds institution. The Porch House on Digbeth Street claims the title of Britain's oldest inn, with beams carbon-dated to over 1,000 years. Cotswolds lamb regularly features on the menu—raised on local pastures, the meat is finer and more flavourful than average.

days_plan.itin_title: England's Gastronomic Trail: Markets, Pubs & Culinary Heritage
England Grand Tour: From Cornwall to the Northern Lakes
Welsh Marches, Cotswolds and Bath in 11 days

visits.text: Castle Ward changes character as you walk around it. This 18th-century house overlooking Strangford Lough has both a Gothic facade and a classical Palladian facade. Look at both sides before touring the interior; their differences continue inside the house. From Strangford Road, follow the Castle Ward signs to Ballyculter Lodge.

activities.text: Follow the shore of Strangford Lough on Castle Ward's Loughside Walk, starting from the old farmyard. The 4 km loop takes you through woodland and along the waterfront, with views toward the ruins of Audley's Castle. Wear shoes with good traction: the route includes short but steep sections and uneven ground.

days_plan.itin_title: Mourne and Strangford in 3 Days: Gardens, Sea, and Woods

visits.text: Marketed as Game of Thrones magic, it's really an avenue of beech trees planted around 1775 by the Stuart family to impress visitors arriving at Gracehill House. The branches have interlaced into a tunnel above the road. About 90 remain of the original 150, Storm Gertrude in 2016 brought down three. Bregagh Road is now closed to cars to protect the roots. Parking at the Hedges Hotel, five-minute walk.

activities.text: Before 8am or at dusk, raking light does its work and the Belfast coaches are elsewhere. Avoid summer weekends and British school holidays. If the weather is miserable, even better: mist under the beeches delivers exactly the photo everyone's after. Count on thirty minutes on site excluding photo shoots.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Ireland in 7 days: Belfast, Causeway & Derry

visits.text: Begin with Shakespeare's Birthplace on Henley Street: a 15th-century timber-framed house where William was born in 1564. His father John was a wool merchant and glover, and the front half of the house served as his workshop. Shakespeare inherited the property on his father's death in 1601 and rented it out as an inn. The bedroom where he was born is open to visitors, with a copy of the 1623 First Folio—the collection that saved 18 of his plays from oblivion.

Anne Hathaway's Cottage, 1.5km from the centre in Shottery, is the farmhouse where Shakespeare's wife grew up. The beams and period furniture are largely authentic. William married Anne in 1582, aged 18 (she was 26). The garden, recreated from plants mentioned in Shakespeare's plays, is especially pleasant in spring. You can walk there from the centre in 20 minutes.

Nash's House and the site of New Place occupy the location of Stratford's grandest house, purchased by Shakespeare in 1597. The house was demolished in 1759 by an owner exasperated by tourists coming to admire the mulberry tree planted by the playwright—he tore up the tree and razed the house, and the town never forgave him. Archaeological excavations have since uncovered the foundations.

Hall's Croft is currently closed to general visitors during a major conservation project. From outside, view this timber-framed house in Old Town, once the home of Shakespeare's eldest daughter and her physician husband, John Hall, near Holy Trinity Church.

Holy Trinity Church, by the Avon, is the church where Shakespeare was baptised on 26 April 1564 and where he's buried before the chancel. The inscription on his tomb remains famous: 'Good friend for Jesus sake forbear, to dig the dust enclosed here'—a plea that his remains not be moved, as was customary for overcrowded churchyards. Among the chancel windows, some came from Antwerp and date from the 15th century.

In Wilmcote, Mary Arden's Farm is not open to the public and operates as an education centre. You can only view from outside the house where Shakespeare's mother grew up; do not plan on touring the farm or attending craft demonstrations.

activities.text: A boat or canoe trip on the Avon from Stratford is one of the region's most pleasant activities. The river flows between meadows and wooded banks, and you'll glimpse Holy Trinity Church from the water along the way. Rowboat and canoe hire is available on the Avon banks two minutes' walk from the centre.

The Royal Shakespeare Theatre programmes Shakespeare performances year-round. If you've planned your visit ahead, an evening at the RSC is an experience you won't find anywhere else. Tickets sell fast in summer—book several weeks in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: The Midlands and Peak District Essentials

visits.text: Gainsborough's House is one of East Anglia's pleasant surprises: the birthplace of Thomas Gainsborough (1727–1788) was transformed into a museum and gallery after a £10 million renovation completed in 2022. Three floors display his portraits, landscapes, and a Constable collection. The garden houses a mulberry tree planted over 400 years ago.

On Market Hill, the statue of painter Gainsborough stands before the old Georgian town hall, palette in hand. Sudbury was a silk-weaving centre — this textile tradition explains why the gallery's walls are hung with silk produced locally in Sudbury. The Thursday morning market on the square is the one that has changed least over the centuries.

activities.text: “His light was different”: that's what locals repeat when asked why Gainsborough and Constable, born a few miles apart, painted so differently. The Stour valley around Sudbury is ideally explored on foot or by bike along the Stour Valley Path. Bike hire is available in the town centre.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: In 1939, in a Sutton Hoo field, amateur archaeologist Basil Brown uncovered the imprint of a 27-metre ship and a burial chamber filled with seventh-century treasures—garnet-inlaid gold jewellery, helmet, Byzantine tableware. The site, a few kilometres from Woodbridge, rewrote the history of the English Early Middle Ages. The originals are in the British Museum; a replica helmet is displayed on site.

Woodbridge's Ship's Company is currently rebuilding the burial ship at full size in the Longshed on the banks of the Deben - the 27-metre “Ghost Ship” has been taking shape in oak since 2016. You can view the work on a free visit from Woodbridge quay.

activities.text: You explore Sutton Hoo's burial mounds with the audio guide provided at entry, then climb the viewing tower to grasp the site's scale from above. The River View Walk then follows the pine wood to the Deben's shores. National Trust: paid entry, members free, no booking required.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: Journey to Brownsea Island, a National Trust nature reserve in the heart of Poole Harbour that is home to one of Britain's few remaining colonies of red squirrels. This 500-acre island of woodland, heathland and lagoons also holds historical significance as the birthplace of the worldwide Scouting movement, where Baden-Powell held his first camp in 1907. Peacocks roam freely among the paths, and the diverse habitats support an abundance of wildlife including sika deer and numerous bird species.

Explore the island's varied landscapes on self-guided walking trails that reveal different ecosystems from pine woodland to sandy beaches. The outdoor center provides information about the wildlife you might encounter, from kingfishers and ospreys to the island's famous red squirrels. The tranquil atmosphere and lack of vehicles create a peaceful escape just minutes from the bustling mainland.

Discover Swanage, a charming Victorian seaside town that evolved from a smugglers' haven into a beloved family holiday destination during the 19th century. The sandy beach, traditional pier and historic town center retain their old-world charm, while boat trips and coastal walks offer modern adventures. The town's quarrying heritage is visible in the stone buildings and monuments that were shipped from here to build some of London's finest structures.

Hike to Old Harry Rocks, the spectacular chalk sea stacks that stand as sentinels at the eastern gateway to the Jurassic Coast. The challenging climb from Swanage rewards hikers with views of these iconic white pillars rising from aquamarine waters, their brilliant surfaces contrasting with the deep blue sea. This UNESCO World Heritage coastline tells the story of 185 million years of Earth's history in its cliffs, rocks and fossils.

Visit Durlston Country Park, just one kilometer from Swanage, where the historic Great Globe and panoramic coastal views have drawn visitors since Victorian times. This 320-acre park encompasses limestone cliffs, wildflower meadows and wildlife-rich habitats with some of the best views along the Dorset coast. The castle-like Durlston Castle visitor center provides information about the park's geology, wildlife and the fascinating history of the Great Globe monument.

activities.text: Take a self-guided wildlife walk and try to spot the elusive red squirrels that thrive on this protected island
Walk the South West Coast Path from Old Harry Rocks back to Swanage beach for stunning coastal views

days_plan.itin_title: Dorset's Jurassic Coast: Prehistoric Cliffs, Castle Ruins and Dream Beaches
Dorset's Jurassic Coast: Prehistoric Cliffs, Castle Ruins and Dream Beaches

visits.text: The tree was felled on the night of 28 September 2023 by two men sentenced to 4 years and 3 months in prison in July 2025. The Sycamore Gap sycamore, planted about 200 years ago in a photogenic dip in the wall, was the UK's most photographed tree and had appeared in Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves (1991). The stump is visible; a wood sculpture made from the trunk by artist Charlie Whinney is exhibited at the park visitor centre. Shoots are growing from the stump.

activities.text: The dip of Sycamore Gap remains one of Hadrian's Wall's most recognisable shots - with or without the tree. The walk from Steel Rigg car park (NY751677) takes 20 minutes one way. Combine with the climb onto the Whin Sill ridge for a panorama over Crag Lough and Greenlee Lough. 5 km circuit from Steel Rigg.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle

visits.text: From the top of Yat Rock, the Wye unfolds in a meander below, 120 metres down, carving a limestone gorge through the Forest of Dean. The viewing platform is five minutes' walk from the car park. On the ridge, you can still make out the ditches of an Iron Age fort, roughly 2,500 years old. The site is also a known nesting point for peregrine falcons, visible from April to August.

activities.text: Birdwatchers stake out the peregrines here between April and August: a permanently mounted telescope on the platform, RSPB volunteers helping to spot them. Out of season, head instead to the hand-ferry that crosses the Wye below (one cable, two passengers, one pound). Walk to Biblins suspension bridge, a flat 2 km path. Fine morning walk before heading to Tintern.

days_plan.itin_title: Welsh Marches, Cotswolds and Bath in 11 days

places.name: Tarbert

visits.text: The drive south from Stornoway to Tarbert - about 60 km - crosses the invisible boundary between Lewis and Harris somewhere in the mountains of North Harris, where the landscape shifts entirely. Lewis is peat bog and sky; Harris is rock and mountain. The A859 climbs through bare granite scenery that feels Icelandic. Tarbert sits at the narrow isthmus where East and West Loch Tarbert almost meet, bisecting the island - it's where you catch the CalMac ferry to Skye if you need to. The town has a handful of shops, a couple of good cafés and the distillery.

The Isle of Harris Distillery, opened in October 2015, was the first legal distillery ever built on Harris. It was funded partly by a £2.8 million grant and investment from the entire island community – the original team of ten all came from traditional trades: Harris Tweed weavers, farmers, fishermen. Their Harris Gin is made with 9 botanicals including sugar kelp hand-harvested from the local waters and comes in a distinctive blue bottle that won a Gold Award at the World Gin Awards in 2021. Their single malt whisky, The Hearach (Gaelic for “a person from Harris”), is now in production and the first limited releases are available. Tours run Monday to Thursday – book ahead.

Luskentyre (Traigh Losgaintir) is the most photographed beach in the Outer Hebrides, and the photographs do not exaggerate. At low tide, the bay opens into a vast expanse of white sand with water somewhere between aquamarine and turquoise, so startlingly Caribbean in colour that first-time visitors regularly think their eyes are playing tricks on them. Taransay rises low on the horizon a mile offshore. The mountains of North Harris rise directly behind. The beach is reached by a 3-mile single-track road from the A859; come at low tide and in good weather if you can. Toilets at the car park. No other facilities, so bring food and water. Check the tide tables before leaving Tarbert. Allow for a return drive from Tarbert.

Seilebost Beach, immediately south of Luskentyre across the estuary, is smaller, but many photographers prefer it: the view back towards Luskentyre with the Harris hills behind is the classic shot. Farther south, Scarista (Sgarasta Mhor) is a quieter alternative, almost as large as Luskentyre, with a golf course running along the dunes and Cleit Rock standing sentinel above the beach. These three beaches form one of Europe's most extraordinary stretches of Atlantic coastline. Allow for a return drive from Tarbert.

Leverburgh (An t-Ob), at the southern tip of Harris, is a lively little harbour from which the CalMac ferry runs to Berneray and North Uist. The hour-long crossing threads through a maze of skerries and tiny islands, a remarkable demonstration of navigation and a true Hebridean ferry experience. Book your crossing ahead; the Sound of Harris ferry is popular and can fill up. Leverburgh also has a good community grocery shop and a couple of places to eat, making it worth stopping for lunch before or after the beach loop. Allow for a return drive from Tarbert.

activities.text: An Cliseam (Clisham), at 799 metres, is the highest peak in the Outer Hebrides. The ascent from the A859 near Ardvourlie takes about 3 to 4 hours return and offers panoramic views over Harris, Lewis and - on a clear day - as far as St Kilda 60 km offshore. The path is rough and boggy in places; proper hill walking gear is essential.

For a shorter afternoon outing, the Golden Road, winding along South Harris's rocky east coast, is one of the most dramatic roads in the Outer Hebrides. Its nickname comes from the cost of building it across such difficult terrain rather than from its scenery. Every bend reveals a different arrangement of small lochs, rocky outcrops and sea views. Stop wherever you like: there are no crowds. Allow for a return drive from Tarbert.

The walk to Huisinis Beach, at the very end of the B887 on Harris's northwestern peninsula, is one of the island's best-kept secrets. The beach is small and sheltered. Wildlife at Huisinis includes grey seals on the rocks below and eagles above the ridge. Allow for a return drive from Tarbert.

days_plan.itin_title: Outer Hebrides Road Trip: Lewis, Harris and the Island Chain
Outer Hebrides Road Trip: Lewis, Harris and the Island Chain

map_keywords: An Cliseam Clisham Harris highest point

activities.text: Tarn Hows offers a lakeside walk without a climb to a summit. The National Trust’s marked loop is 3.2 km long and circles the lake on a maintained path, with views toward the hills of the Lake District. Start from the main parking lot and stick to this loop to leave time for Grasmere.

days_plan.itin_title: Lake District in 3 Days: Lakes and Writers’ Homes

visits.text: Tarr Steps looks like a crossing built for giants across the Barle. Its 17 spans support large stone slabs, though their exact age remains uncertain. View this low structure from the riverbank; if the water rises or covers the stones, do not cross, and respect any barriers.

activities.text: Follow the Barle from Tarr Steps for a short walk beneath the trees. The riverside woods extend the bridge’s setting into a landscape of water, stone, and moss. Stay on the same bank and retrace your steps: this walk does not use the Hinds Pitt footbridge or require completing a full loop.

days_plan.itin_title: North Devon and Exmoor: 3 Days of Headlands and Villages

visits.text: Tate Britain, opened in 1897 on the banks of the Thames at Millbank, houses the world's largest collection of works by J.M.W. Turner (1775-1851). Turner bequeathed to the nation nearly 300 oil paintings and some 30,000 watercolours and works on paper - the Clore Gallery, accessible from the main entrance, displays about a hundred works permanently, free of charge. If you only know Turner for his misty seascapes, you'll be surprised: he also painted the 1834 fire of Parliament from the Thames bank, and his painting documenting the scene is one of the museum's most striking. Admission to the permanent collections is free.

Beyond Turner, Tate Britain covers British art from the 16th century to today - Hogarth, Constable, Bacon, Hockney. If you're there in summer, the central Duveen Hall is a monumental neoclassical nave entrusted each year to an artist for a temporary and free installation.

activities.text: Take the Tate Boat from Millbank Pier - it links Tate Britain to Tate Modern along the Thames, stopping at the London Eye. It's an original way to connect the two museums in 20 minutes, with views of both banks. The boat ticket includes a discount at the other Tate.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries
What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Tate Modern has occupied the former Bankside Power Station since 2000, built between 1947 and 1963 by architect Giles Gilbert Scott - the same man who designed the red London telephone box. The power station closed in 1981 after oil price increases. Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron won the conversion competition in 1995 from 148 candidates: their masterstroke was preserving the turbine hall intact, an industrial nave 155 metres long and 35 metres high, now dedicated to gigantic installations. Admission to the permanent collections is free.

The Blavatnik Building extension, opened in 2016, increased exhibition space by 60%. Go up to level 10 for the free panoramic terrace - you have St Paul's facing you, Tower Bridge to the right, the City to the left. It's one of the best free viewpoints in London.

activities.text: Cross the Millennium Bridge on foot - this pedestrian bridge, inaugurated in 2000 and closed two days later due to excessive vibrations (reopened in 2002 after correction), directly links Tate Modern to St Paul's Cathedral on the north bank. The view from the middle of the bridge, with St Paul's on one side and Tate on the other, is one of London's finest.

Shakespeare's Globe Theatre is a 5-minute walk east of Tate Modern. This reconstruction of the 1599 Elizabethan theatre opened in 1997 and presents open-air performances from April to October. You can stand in the 'groundling pit' for cheaper access. Even off-season, the guided tour of the theatre is enlightening.

places.name: Tenby

visits.text: Rhossili Bay is a 5 km Atlantic sand beach, closed to the north by the Llangennith dunes and to the south by the Worm's Head promontory. From the cliffs of Rhossili village, the view across the entire bay is one of the most photographed in Wales. The National Trust car park at the top of the cliff is often full at weekends in summer—arrive before 10am or after 5pm.

Worm's Head is a marshy island shaped like a dragon—worm comes from the Old Norse ormr, serpent or dragon—connected to the mainland by a rocky causeway accessible only 2h30 either side of low tide. Several people have been trapped by the tide trying to return on foot, including the poet Dylan Thomas himself, stranded there for a whole night. The National Coastwatch Institute office, at the start of the causeway, displays tide times: check them without fail before crossing. Grey seals regularly haul out on the rocks.

The Helvetia wreck is one of Gower's most famous. This Norwegian three-master was carrying 500 tonnes of timber from Canada to Swansea when a storm forced it to take refuge in Rhossili Bay on 1 November 1887. The anchors didn't hold, the wind shifted, the ship ran aground on the sand—the entire crew survived. The wooden ribs of the hull, buried in the sand for over 130 years, appear and disappear depending on storms and tides. Visible at low tide, about 30 minutes' walk from the cliff path.

Tenby is a medieval town whose walls are among the best preserved in Britain—Grade I listed, they form an almost complete triangle around the old quarter. The first stones date back to the 13th century, under the Earls of Pembroke. In 1260, the Welsh prince Llewelyn ap Gruffydd sacked the town: the new walls, higher and better reinforced, date from this reconstruction. Jasper Tudor—uncle of the future Henry VII—had them repaired and raised in 1457. Enter through the Five Arches, the D-shaped barbican gate still standing on the east side, and lose yourself in the cobbled lanes sloping down to the harbour.

St Mary's Church in Tenby is one of the largest medieval churches in Wales. Inside, look for the memorial to Robert Recorde—a Tenby native, this 16th-century mathematician invented the '=' sign. Another memorial is dedicated to Mayor Thomas White, who, according to local tradition, helped Jasper Tudor and the young Henry Tudor flee the town through underground tunnels in 1471 to reach the harbour and sail to Brittany—a journey that preceded Henry's conquest of the English throne in 1485.

The Tudor Merchant's House, at the bottom of Quay Hill, is a 15th-century house run by the National Trust. A wealthy Tenby merchant's Tudor-era dwelling is carefully recreated—period furniture, tapestries and fragments of original frescoes. Allow 30 minutes.

Castle Hill, at the tip of the promontory, offers the classic Tenby panorama: the pastel houses of the harbour to the left, North Beach to the right, and offshore the silhouette of St Catherine's Island with its Victorian fort. This island played the role of a high-security prison in Sherlock series 4. The Tenby Museum (Wales' oldest independent museum, opened in 1878) is housed in the ruins of the medieval castle at the summit.

Bosherston Lily Ponds are a network of three artificial lake arms created in the 18th century by the Cawdor family by damming an estuary—an idea born after a visitor noticed how a high tide transformed the valley into a romantic lake. Now a National Nature Reserve managed by the National Trust, the ponds are covered with white water lilies in June and July. Over 20 species of dragonfly have been recorded here, otters live here, and herons constantly perch on the jetties. The circular walk around the ponds (3 km) is flat and accessible to all.

Broad Haven South, at the end of the ponds, is an immense beach—golden sand, dunes, and in the centre a limestone monolith isolated from the sea called Church Rock, rising like a cathedral. It's a serious bodyboarding beach in swell conditions; in calm weather, the water is transparent and shallow.

Barafundle Bay is regularly ranked among Europe's most beautiful beaches. Nestled between cliffs and accessible only on foot (15 minutes from Stackpole Quay), it never suffers from the overcrowding of beaches with adjacent parking. Golden sand, turquoise water in fine weather, no facilities on the beach itself—bring your picnic. The stone arch with the National Trust sign above the beach is one of Pembrokeshire's most recognisable images.

At the end of the day, push on to St Govan's Chapel: a tiny 13th-century chapel (possibly older) wedged in a vertical fissure in the coastal cliffs at the bottom of a 52-step staircase. A hermit is said to have lived there, according to legend surrounded by rocks that closed in to protect him from his enemies. Check before leaving if the area is open—it's sometimes closed for military exercises (Castlemartin firing range).

activities.text: The walk to the end of Worm's Head (about 1.5 km from the causeway) gives access to a natural arch, a blowhole and seabird colonies. Allow a minimum of 2h30 on the island to have time to return before the tide cuts off the passage. Don't attempt the crossing if the sea is rough.

Sunset at Rhossili is renowned throughout the Gower Peninsula. From the clifftop above the beach, you watch the sun descend directly into the sea with Worm's Head in the foreground. Bring a picnic and wait—it's worth the patience.

The boat crossing to Caldey Island takes 20 minutes from Tenby harbour. This private island has been inhabited by Cistercian monks since 1929, who produce their own chocolate and perfumes made from herbs. Access is seasonal (generally April to October). Outside ferry hours, tour Tenby's three main beaches (North, South and Castle Beach) by following the clifftop path.

The Bosherston-Broad Haven South-Barafundle Bay coastal loop is the best circuit for this day: 10 km from the Stackpole Quay or Bosherston car park, alternating between paths around the ponds and clifftop coastal path. The section between Broad Haven South and Barafundle passes Stackpole Head, a limestone promontory with rock stacks in the sea. Allow 3 hours. In June-July, the lily pads on the ponds are in flower—don't miss this moment.

visits.text: A port without the sea since the fifteenth century, Tenterden still appears in the roster of the Cinque Ports. In 1449 the town was attached as a limb of Rye. Coastal change then cut off all access to the Channel: the town now sits sixteen kilometres inland. The High Street and its Georgian façades bear witness to wealth built on wool and ships.

Attached to the Cinque Ports in 1449 as a limb of Rye, Tenterden enjoyed tax exemption and representation at royal coronations—a privilege still exercised at the coronation of Charles III. The pinnacled tower of St Mildred's Church once served as a beacon against the Spanish Armada. Nelson's daughter, Horatia, was the vicar's wife.

activities.text: Board the Kent & East Sussex Railway from Tenterden Town station: steam locomotives, period rolling stock, Weald scenery. The line connects Tenterden to Bodiam—a stop to combine with tomorrow's castle visit. Check timetables at kesr.org.uk; some services are seasonal.

days_plan.itin_title: Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports

visits.text: Thaxted is not short on ambition: the town's medieval hall—the Guildhall—was built around 1450 as a three-story timber building, with an open ground floor that formerly served as a cloth market. Gustav Holst lived here from 1914 and worked on “The Planets” in this setting—it was Jupiter's central theme that he later adapted as a hymn tune named “Thaxted.” John Betjeman wrote that no town in Essex could compare with Thaxted for beauty.

St John the Baptist Church dominates Thaxted from its hill—one of Essex's largest and finest parish churches, with pointed arches and stained glass. The organ, regularly played in concert during Thaxted's annual festival, is renowned for its quality.

activities.text: In Thaxted, view John Webb's Windmill from the outside: its red-brick tower, built in 1804, stands near the town. The windmill is currently closed to interior visits for restoration, so you cannot climb upstairs or visit its small rural museum.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Three chalk stacks lined up at sea, crowned by a red-and-white lighthouse: the Needles tick every British iconography box. The name comes from a fourth, sharper needle that collapsed during a storm in 1764. The current lighthouse dates to 1859.

Around twenty distinct shades of sand compose Alum Bay's cliffs—quartz, feldspar, mica—a rare geological curiosity in Europe. Small bottles sold on-site let you layer your own gradient souvenir. Marconi installed the world's first permanent radio station here in 1897, commemorative monument at the summit.

A few minutes' walk above the Needles brings you to Needles Old Battery, run by the National Trust. Victorian fortifications, tunnel to the viewpoint in the rocks, and Cold War secret: British rocket tests. The tea room has a lovely terrace.

activities.text: Reckon about £3 single for the chairlift descending from Alum Bay's summit to the beach. Gentle thrills and unbeatable views of the stacks. Family tariffs via Supersaver tickets (£9 for 12 tickets). At the bottom, tourist boat trips approach the lighthouse, £9 adult.

days_plan.itin_title: England's South Coast 6d: Bristol to Brighton

visits.text: The Shard is designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, who conceived it as a 95-storey 'vertical city'. The building stands 309.6 metres tall and has dominated London's skyline since its inauguration on 5 July 2012. The viewing platform 'The View from The Shard' occupies levels 68 to 72 - at 244 metres, you have a 360° view extending up to 64 kilometres on a clear day. During 2011 construction, a fox moved into level 72 by entering through the stairs. It survived several weeks feeding on workers' leftovers - it's now called Romeo and is the building's official mascot. Book online, and prefer late afternoon slots for the light on Tower Bridge.

activities.text: A 5-minute walk from the Shard, Borough Market is one of London's oldest food markets - present on this site since at least the 13th century. You'll find British and European producers, cheeses, charcuterie, fresh oysters and quality street food. Open Wednesday to Saturday. Avoid Friday lunchtime - it's peak rush.

Southwark Cathedral, steps from the market, is London's oldest Gothic church - its nave dates from the 13th century. Shakespeare baptized his brother Edmund there in 1607. Admission is free and the serenity of the place contrasts radically with the market bustle just outside.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

places.name: Thornton Le Dale

visits.text: Plan a day trip from Thornton-le-Dale to visit Knaresborough. Knaresborough sets the tone on arrival: limestone houses cling to a cliff above the River Nidd, and the Victorian viaduct cuts across the horizon like a film backdrop. Walk down to the water for the classic view of the boats and colorful façades—this is where the town really makes sense, rather than from above.

Plan a day trip from Thornton-le-Dale to visit Knaresborough Castle. Knaresborough Castle has overlooked the Nidd since the 14th century. It was built by the Normans and dismantled after the English Civil War on Cromwell's orders in 1648; only the square keep remains—but the view from the gardens overlooking the cliff is remarkable. Allow around 45 minutes for the on-site museum, which traces the town's history.

Plan a day trip from Thornton-le-Dale to visit Mother Shipton's Cave. Do not miss Mother Shipton's Cave, officially England's oldest visitor attraction with an admission charge, open to the public since 1630. The site consists of two wonders side by side on the banks of the Nidd: the cave where the prophetess Ursula Southeil is said to have been born in 1488 (she supposedly predicted the Spanish Armada and the Great Fire of London), and the Petrifying Well, whose mineral-rich water gradually encrusts objects hung beneath it—a teddy bear takes three to five months to “petrify”. Allow at least an hour and buy your ticket online, especially in high season.

Plan a day trip from Thornton-le-Dale to the White Horse of Kilburn and Sutton Bank. On your way north, stop at the White Horse of Kilburn for one of Yorkshire's most unobstructed views. This horse figure, 96 meters long and 70 meters high, was cut into the chalk on the hillside in 1857—it is visible from over 30 kilometers away in clear weather. The nearby Sutton Bank viewpoint offers a panorama over the whole plain of York that is worth the detour on its own.

Thornton-le-Dale rounds off the day in fitting style. The village has been regularly voted Yorkshire's most beautiful—since at least 1907, when a newspaper poll bestowed that title. Walk around the village green with its 13th-century medieval cross and stocks (last documented use: 1874), then follow the stream to Beck Isle Cottage, a Grade II listed 17th-century timber-framed thatched cottage that appears on thousands of calendars and chocolate boxes. The house is private—it can be admired from outside, from the small stone bridge.

Before leaving the village, walk to All Saints Church in the eastern part of the village. The building dates to the 14th century, but evidence of religious use of the site goes back to the 7th century. Inside, look for musket ball marks on the nave pillars—they date from the English Civil War, when a group of Parliamentarian soldiers sought refuge here from Royalists.

activities.text: An evening walk along Thornton Beck, the stream running through the village. The 2-mile route to the hamlet of Ellerburn and its St Hilda's Church (dating back to at least 1050) is peaceful and easy—allow about an hour. It is best to set off just before the light begins to fade.

The village has several independent cafés and pubs around the green, ideal for a late-day stop. If you pass through in August, the Thornton-le-Dale Scarecrow Festival transforms the village into a life-size scarecrow gallery—a strangely endearing event.

visits.text: Hard to reach, Three Cliffs Bay has the Pennard Pill winding between its dunes before it meets the sea. The three limestone cliffs that give the beach its name overlook the sand, and the ruins of 12th-century Norman Pennard Castle crown the ridge. Park at Southgate and walk 30 minutes along the coast path. Watch the tide when crossing the sand. Strong currents: avoid swimming.

days_plan.itin_title: Complete Wales: 12 Days North to South

visits.text: Stand among the legendary ruins of Tintagel Castle, perched dramatically on a rugged headland with cliffs plunging to the Atlantic on three sides. While not much remains of the medieval castle itself, the association with King Arthur and the dramatic new footbridge spanning a deep chasm between two impossibly steep cliffs make this one of Cornwall's most unforgettable attractions. The legends claim this as Arthur's birthplace, and the atmosphere of myth and mystery pervades every stone.

Cross the spectacular footbridge that links the mainland to the island portion of Tintagel Castle, a modern engineering marvel that recreates an ancient connection severed by centuries of erosion. The vertiginous walkway offers heart-stopping views down to the waves crashing on rocks far below. Archaeological excavations have revealed that this site was an important settlement during the Dark Ages, lending some historical basis to the Arthurian legends.

Explore Merlin's Cave beneath the castle headland, accessible at low tide via a dramatic sea cave that cuts completely through the promontory. Legend holds that the wizard Merlin lived in this cave and that it was here he first met the infant Arthur. The combination of dramatic natural features and powerful mythology makes Tintagel one of the most evocative historic sites in Britain, drawing visitors who seek both history and legend.

activities.text: Book castle tickets in advance, especially during holidays and weekends, as this is one of Cornwall's most popular attractions

visits.text: Tintern was founded in 1131 by Cistercians, on the Welsh bank of the Wye. The current church, roofless since the dissolution of the monasteries in 1536, dates mainly from the 13th-14th centuries. The eroded Gothic arches and open-air nave inspired Wordsworth (1798) and fascinated Turner, who painted them repeatedly. This is the birth of British picturesque tourism, literally.

activities.text: If you have a morning to spare, cross into the Forest of Dean ten minutes' drive away: a former royal hunting forest, still populated by free-roaming deer, wild boar and sheep. The Sculpture Trail (1986, one of Europe's first) runs roughly 6 km through the woods. Free map at Beechenhurst centre. Good plan: combine with Puzzlewood, the Forbidden Forest set from the last Star Wars films.

days_plan.itin_title: Welsh Marches, Cotswolds and Bath in 11 days

visits.text: Robin Hood filmed here, Cromwell half-demolished it, and today fawns graze along the artificial lake. Old Wardour Castle is England's only hexagonal castle, built around the 1390s for Lord Lovell. Besieged twice during the English Civil War, it has remained a romantic ruin since 1644. English Heritage manages the site: £9, free audio guide on-site. A grotto from 1792 incorporates three prehistoric standing stones moved from a local circle.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days

places.name: Tobermory

visits.text: Tobermory, capital of the Isle of Mull, takes its name from the Gaelic Tobar Mhoire—"Mary's well"—referring to a sacred spring dedicated to the Virgin. The town was founded in 1788 by the British Fisheries Society as a planned herring port. The row of houses painted pink, yellow, blue, and red lining the quayside dates from the 19th century: the first building to be painted was the Mishnish Hotel in 1961, the others followed. At the harbor's edge, Tobermory Distillery has operated since 1798—don't miss the guided tour of one of Scotland's oldest commercial distilleries. For a cultural aside: the BBC series Balamory (254 episodes, 2002-2005) was filmed here. Beneath the harbor waters supposedly lies the wreck of a Spanish Armada galleon sunk in 1588—the treasure has never been found.

A few minutes' walk from the harbor, Aros Park is a natural space managed by the Forestry Commission, crossed by trails that follow streams and lead to small waterfalls within dense forest cover. Access is free. Also don't miss An Tobar Arts Centre, housed in a former school, which hosts exhibitions, live traditional music, and a café with harbor views.

Allow for approximately 31 km from Tobermory, a 47-minute drive. Do not miss Duart Castle, a medieval fortress on a promontory overlooking the Sound of Mull near Craignure: built in the 13th century, it passed to the MacLeans in the 14th century, stood abandoned and ruined for two centuries, and was purchased and restored from 1911 by the 26th chief of Clan MacLean. It is one of the few castles occupied by the same clan for 700 years. Views extend over the Firth of Lorn and the surrounding islands. Admission is charged. Book your ticket in advance during high season.

Allow for approximately 14 km from Tobermory, a 21-minute drive. At the northern end of Mull, Calgary Bay is the island's largest white-sand beach, framed by cliffs and woodland. Its name inspired the Canadian city: families of Scottish settlers expelled during the Highland Clearances took the name with them when they settled in Alberta. The bay is almost deserted outside high season: arrive in the morning to have the sand to yourself.

activities.text: Offshore from Mull, the waters of the Sound of Mull rank among the best marine wildlife viewing areas in the UK. Boat trips depart from Tobermory to observe dolphins, gray seals, minke whales, and white-tailed sea eagles that nest on the island following their reintroduction. Local operators generally depart in the morning for best conditions. Book ahead in season.

Allow for approximately 20 km from Tobermory, a 30-minute drive. Ben More (966 m) is the only Munro in the Inner Hebrides outside Skye. The ascent from the shore of Loch na Keal takes between 5 and 7 hours round trip. If you are not equipped for the summit, hiking in the surrounding glens is still spectacular. In clear weather, Ireland can be seen from the summit.

Allow for approximately 17 km from Tobermory, a 26-minute drive. The island of Ulva, reached by a short ferry crossing from the Ulva Ferry jetty on Mull's west coast, makes an off-the-beaten-track excursion. The island has fewer than 20 residents. You can see the ruins of homes that belonged to the 700 people who lived there before the Clearances. The ferry operates on demand: move the sign on the shore and someone will come to collect you.
