visits.text: Tomintoul invites you to slow down around its square and along its long Main Street. The village brings together shops, cafés, and information points about the landscapes of Glenlivet. The Discovery Centre is on the square, while the estate visitor center is at the end of Main Street. Use the center’s large parking lot to explore the streets on foot; this short stop does not include a museum visit.

activities.text: If you are looking for a short walk in the uplands, start at the Glenlivet Estate Visitor Centre in Tomintoul. The estate offers an easy woodland trail near ponds and wildlife observation points. The center also has restrooms and a parking lot. Schedule this stop on a weekday to benefit from the welcome and advice of the staff, who are there Monday through Friday.

days_plan.itin_title: Speyside and the Moray Coast: Whisky and Villages in 3 Days

visits.text: Built after 1066 to control the Medway crossing on the route from Hastings to London, Tonbridge Castle is the work of Richard FitzGilbert, cousin of William the Conqueror. The 13th-century golden sandstone gatehouse is one of the finest examples of its kind in England. The included audio guide covers nine hundred years of history from the first timber motte-and-bailey.

If the monthly market is on that day - usually the second Sunday of the month - settle on the banks of the Medway with Kent cheeses and artisan bread. The redeveloped riverfront facing the castle has tables with a view of the medieval gatehouse. On weekdays, the artisan bakers on the High Street do just as well.

activities.text: Embark with Tonbridge River Trips aboard the Enid May, an electric cruiser with the skipper's commentary on the town's medieval history. Kingfishers, cormorants, and dragonflies animate the banks between Georgian houses and the first reaches of the nature park. Available in summer; durations from 45 minutes to 2 hours depending on the chosen excursion.

days_plan.itin_title: Surrey to Kent: Castles and Gardens in 10 Days

places.name: Tongue

visits.text: Cape Wrath is the northwesternmost point of the British mainland—and reaching it involves a small ferry across the Kyle of Durness, followed by an 11-mile minibus ride over a military training area. The route is run by a single operator and operates from May to September, weather permitting. At the cape, the 1828 Stevenson lighthouse stands above 280-metre cliffs of Torridonian sandstone, the same ancient rock as the mountains of Torridon. On clear days, Orkney is visible 45 miles to the northeast. The minibus driver's commentary is part of the experience—book ahead. From Tongue, plan a return trip to the ferry departure point on the Kyle of Durness, followed by the crossing and minibus journey.

Smoo Cave, 2 km east of Durness on the A838, has Britain's largest sea-cave entrance—40 metres wide and 15 metres high. Its unusual feature in the UK is that the first chamber was formed by the sea, while the inner chambers are freshwater passages carved by the Allt Smoo stream dissolving dolomitic limestone. These are entirely separate geological processes that happened to meet. A 20-metre waterfall drops through a hole in the ceiling of the inner chamber. You can walk into the first chamber and to the waterfall platform free at any time; guided boat tours of the inner chamber run from April to October. The name comes from Old Norse—“smjúga” or “smuga”, meaning a narrow hole or hiding place. Plan a return trip from Tongue to Durness, then walk down to the cave.

Balnakeil Beach, 2 km west of Durness, is a broad arc of white sand on a sheltered bay that looks surprisingly tropical when the sun shines on the water. A ruined 17th-century church stands behind the beach; the grave of Donald McMurchow, a murderer who paid for the church's construction in exchange for burial within its walls rather than in unconsecrated ground, is still visible. Balnakeil Craft Village—a collection of former Cold War early-warning-station buildings converted into artists' studios and workshops—is worth a walk. Plan a return trip from Tongue for the beach and craft village.

activities.text: The Kyle of Tongue causeway, carrying the A838 across the tidal Kyle, is one of the most photographed spots on the north coast. Pull over at the parking area at the southern end and look north: the ruins of Castle Varrich on its hill, the causeway cutting across the blue water, the cone of Ben Loyal (764 m) - sometimes called the Queen of Scottish Mountains - in the background. Spend 20 minutes here.

days_plan.itin_title: North Coast 500 with Orkney: Scotland's Ultimate Coastal Circuit

map_keywords: Kyle of Tongue causeway Ben Loyal

visits.text: A former trading port, Topsham still has merchants’ houses facing the estuary along The Strand. Their Dutch-inspired facades recall maritime trade, making this more than just an English village setting. View them from the street, and don’t count on visiting the interior of Topsham Museum: its website announces a closure for renovation work.

activities.text: When the tide exposes the mudflats, the Exe Estuary Trail takes on a completely different character around Topsham. The walk follows a landscape of channels and shores where birds draw the eye as much as boats do. Bring binoculars if you have them, check the tides, and stay on designated paths.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: A flower garden can also tell a story about poison. At Torre Abbey, the Agatha Christie Potent Plants Garden connects plants with the author’s novels and her knowledge of pharmacy, with toxic species among the plantings. Read the labels before looking for connections to the plots, and do not touch or taste any plants.

activities.text: You’ll walk along Princess Gardens to return to Torquay’s waterfront after visiting the gardens at Torre Abbey. The harbor and Torbay’s promenades reveal the town’s seaside character, very different from the moorland planned for later in the trip. Choose a short walking loop and keep a windbreaker handy, even when the sun comes out.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: The NC500 officially starts and ends in Inverness, but the circuit makes more sense clockwise—west first, east last, saving the spectacular Caithness coast and Highland passage for the final days. Head southwest along the A82 and A87 towards Kyle of Lochalsh. You will pass the area of Eilean Donan Castle—Scotland's most photographed castle, perched on a tiny island where three lochs meet, built in the 13th century to defend against Viking raids, bombarded in 1719 when Spanish troops supporting the Jacobites stored 343 barrels of gunpowder there, then rebuilt stone by stone from 1919 to 1932. Stop for the view from the road bridge; the castle itself merits 45 minutes if you have time. If visiting from your overnight base in Torridon, allow for a return drive.

From Kyle of Lochalsh, take the A896 north into Glen Torridon. This valley is one of the most geologically extraordinary places in Scotland: the mountains on either side are Torridonian sandstone, around 750 million years old, sitting directly on Lewisian gneiss that is 3 billion years old. Almost nowhere else in the world does rock of such different ages sit in direct contact. Beinn Eighe (1,010 m) and Liathach (1,055 m) loom over the road. The National Trust for Scotland manages a deer museum at Torridon village - worth a 20-minute stop to understand the landscape before exploring it.

activities.text: The Torridon hills offer some of the finest - and most serious - ridge walking in Scotland. The approach to Liathach from the road up the glen is for experienced hillwalkers only; the summit ridge involves Grade 2 scrambling in places and the exposure is significant. For a more accessible but still dramatic walk, the path to Coire Mhic Fhearchair on Beinn Eighe reaches the dramatic corrie of the Triple Buttress at 750 m - one of the grandest mountain corries in Scotland. Allow 4 to 5 hours for the round trip and wear proper walking boots.

days_plan.itin_title: North Coast 500 with Orkney: Scotland's Ultimate Coastal Circuit

visits.text: For an overview of Totnes, Totnes Castle is worth the climb. The castle combines a Norman motte with a stone enclosure crowning its summit, with the town and the Dart below. The climb is short but steep: keep your walking shoes on and check opening days before your visit.

activities.text: Rebuilt after a fire, Eastgate still spans the main street in Totnes. As you head uphill toward High Street, also look for Butterwalk, whose covered walkway once sheltered dairy products from the sun and rain. Take this walk from a parking lot on the outskirts: the details are easier to appreciate beneath the arcades than behind the wheel.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: Tower Bridge was inaugurated on 30 June 1894 by the future Edward VII. Built over 8 years by 432 workers, it cost £1.18 million. Its Gothic stone appearance is an illusion: the structure is entirely steel, clad in Cornish granite and Portland stone to harmonize with the nearby Tower of London. Each bascule weighs 1,200 tonnes, with a 410-tonne counterweight allowing them to lift in 5 minutes. In 1894, the bascules lifted 6,194 times - 17 times per day. Today: about 800 times a year. Check lift times on the bridge website before your visit.

The glass walkways at 43 metres height offer a plunging view over the Thames - the glass floor installed in 2014 lets you look directly beneath your feet at the cars and river. In the Engine Rooms, the original steam engines are still in place: until 1976, 30 people worked here continuously, with over 20 tonnes of coal consumed per week.

activities.text: For the best photographs of Tower Bridge, position yourself on the south bank, east side of the bridge - you have the Tower of London in the background and morning light on the north facade. In the evening, from London Bridge (800 metres to the west), the view of illuminated Tower Bridge with the City is unbeatable.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: The Tower of London, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988, is one of the most remarkable Norman fortresses in Europe. The White Tower - its 27-metre-high central keep with walls 4.5 metres thick - was built from 1078 on the orders of William the Conqueror using Caen stone imported from Normandy. It has served in turn as a royal palace, an armoury, a prison for high-ranking prisoners and a royal zoo. Anne Boleyn was executed here, the two sons of King Edward IV mysteriously disappeared here, and Guy Fawkes was tortured here after the Gunpowder Plot of 1605. Today the Tower houses the Crown Jewels in the Jewel House: more than 23,000 gems, including the 530-carat Cullinan I diamond set in the Sovereign's Sceptre, and the 105-carat Koh-i-Noor diamond in the Queen Mother's crown. The Crown Jewels have been on public display since 1661 - one of the most visited attractions in Britain. Book your tickets online in advance.

activities.text: Don't miss the guided tour by the Yeoman Warders (the Beefeaters): these guards in Tudor uniforms bring history to life with quintessentially British verve. Tours depart every 30 minutes from the main entrance—they're included in admission.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries
What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Nelson's Column measures 51.5 metres - exactly the distance from HMS Victory's mainmast to the main deck. This is no coincidence. The statue of Nelson at the top (5.5m in Scottish sandstone) looks towards the Admiralty, and towards Cape Trafalgar in Spain where he died in 1805. The bronze lions at the column's base weren't added until 1867 - Landseer, an animal painter (not sculptor), worked from a real lion's corpse, but decomposition had already begun; as a result, the paws resemble a cat's. Also look for the northwest fourth plinth: since 1999 it's hosted rotating contemporary artworks, often surprising.

The National Gallery has bordered the square's north side since 1838. Admission is free - which is an anomaly for a museum of this calibre. You'll find around 2,300 works: Van Eyck, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, Rembrandt, Turner, Monet, Van Gogh. If you only have an hour, focus on the Sainsbury Wing rooms for Flemish and Italian primitives. Allow at least 2 hours if you want to cover the essentials.

Facing the National Gallery, spot the statue of George Washington - standing on American soil imported specially, as Washington had sworn never to set foot on British ground. It's a gift from the State of Virginia presented in 1921.

activities.text: In late afternoon, the square comes alive with street performers and musicians - the atmosphere is very different from the touristy morning. Sit on the fountain steps and watch: Trafalgar Square is one of the few places in London where all layers of the city genuinely intersect.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Hard to imagine anything more eccentric: the Natural History Museum at Tring—formerly the Walter Rothschild Zoological Museum—was opened in 1892 as a private museum by a 21-year-old Baron Rothschild who traveled by zebra-drawn carriage. Inside you'll find specimens of extinct animals like the thylacine and great auk, thousands of taxidermy specimens from around a hundred countries, and even Mexican fleas dressed in traditional costumes to examine with a magnifying glass. Free entry, managed by London's Natural History Museum.

Tring Park spreads across 300 acres of woods and meadows just outside town—remarkably quiet in the early morning. The monument to Nell Gwyn (Charles II's mistress), overlooking the main clearing, is a local curiosity. Open access, with the main trail starting from the town center.

activities.text: Take the Ridgeway from Tring for a ridge walk with views over the Chilterns. The most accessible starting point is the Wigginton Road parking lot. On clear days, you can glimpse the Hertfordshire plain in the distance. Waterproof footwear recommended out of season.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Explore Truro, Cornwall's only city, where the magnificent Victorian cathedral with its unusual three spires towers above the historic streets. While urban amenities and cultural offerings exceed those found elsewhere in the region, Truro maintains a distinctly laid-back Cornish character with its independent shops, cafes and the vibrant Lemon Street Market. The city serves as an excellent base for exploring the surrounding area while offering more significant cultural attractions.

Visit the Royal Cornwall Museum to discover the fascinating history of this unique region, from prehistoric times through the tin mining era to the present day. The museum's collections illuminate the distinctive Cornish culture and the Celtic language that sets this peninsula apart from the rest of England. Exhibitions explore the mining heritage that brought prosperity and shaped the landscape, now recognized with UNESCO World Heritage status.

Admire the Cathedral of the Blessed Virgin Mary, a Victorian Gothic masterpiece completed in 1910 that ranks among the finest 19th-century churches in England. The three soaring spires create an unmistakable silhouette above the city, while the interior features beautiful stained glass and impressive stone vaulting. The cathedral's relatively recent construction makes it unusual among England's great churches, most of which date from medieval times.

activities.text: Browse the Hall for Cornwall's performance schedule for evening entertainment options

days_plan.itin_title: Cornwall Coastal Road Trip: Castles, Secret Coves & Celtic Heritage Guide

activities.text: If visibility is good, walk to Wistman’s Wood from Two Bridges along the West Dart trail. The oaks, mosses, and lichens form a fragile habitat that the park asks visitors to observe without entering the wood. The round trip is about four kilometers: stay outside the wood, expect wet ground, and do not block any access when parking.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: Journey aboard the Talyllyn Railway, the world's first preserved railway, known affectionately as 'The Railway with a Heart of Gold.' This historic steam train, operating since 1865, carries passengers on a scenic 55-minute journey from the coastal town of Tywyn seven miles into the heart of Snowdonia National Park. The gentle pace allows time to absorb the stunning Welsh landscapes, from pastoral valleys to dramatic mountain scenery.

Travel to Nant Gwernol, the railway's terminus deep in a wooded ravine surrounded by ancient oak forests and cascading waterfalls. The narrow-gauge locomotives puff and whistle through countryside that has changed little since Victorian times, creating an authentically nostalgic experience. Walking trails from the station lead to spectacular viewpoints and the atmospheric ruins of old slate quarries.

Explore Tywyn, a traditional Welsh seaside town that serves as the gateway to the Talyllyn Railway and the southern reaches of Snowdonia. The town's long sandy beach stretches for miles, backed by dunes and offering views across Cardigan Bay to the Llŷn Peninsula. St Cadfan's Church houses the Cadfan Stone, bearing the earliest known written Welsh, connecting visitors to 1,400 years of Welsh linguistic heritage.

activities.text: Hike from Nant Gwernol station through the forest to discover hidden waterfalls and old quarry workings

days_plan.itin_title: Wales Road Trip: Conwy Castle, Pembrokeshire Coast & Snowdonia

visits.text: Expressionist, almost hip: this 111-metre horse cut into the chalk looks like a Picasso drawing rather than a real animal. Dated by Oxford Archaeology to between 1380 and 550 BC—the Late Bronze Age—it's the oldest chalk horse in Europe. It exists only because generations of local people have continually re-chalked it. NT parking £5, free access.

Dragon Hill, the flat-topped hill below, is where Saint George supposedly killed the dragon. The circle of bare chalk at its summit? 'Dragon's blood,' according to local legend. Geologically, it's a natural chalk outcrop kept clear. Arrive early for an unobstructed view over the Vale from the ridge.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop

visits.text: Allow for approximately 19 km from Ullapool, a 29-minute drive. On the A832 towards Ullapool, stop at Gruinard Bay, which has a broad beach of reddish-pink sand and turquoise water. Opposite lies Gruinard Island, "Anthrax Island." In 1942, the British government tested biological bombs containing the Vollum 14578 strain of anthrax on sheep there as part of Operation Vegetarian. The island remained under quarantine for 48 years. In 1986, 280 tonnes of diluted formaldehyde were poured over each acre of the island. It was declared safe in 1990 and bought back for £500, the price agreed in 1942, by the original owner's heirs.

Explore Ullapool, founded in 1788 as a herring port according to Thomas Telford's plans—the largest settlement for dozens of kilometers around, with 1,300 inhabitants. Its name likely comes from the Old Norse Ulla-Bolstadr ('Ulla's domain'). The waterfront, its white houses, and the late-day light over Loch Broom merit a long stroll.

Ullapool Museum, housed in a former Telford church from 1829, traces the village's history from Viking origins through herring fishing and the clearances. The Ceilidh Place is one of the northwest's liveliest cultural centers: café, bookshop, live music venue, and art gallery. Check the program before arriving.

The walk along the waterfront to Rhue lighthouse, 3 km northwest of Ullapool, offers views over the Summer Isles and Stac Pollaidh (613 m)—one of the northwest's most photographed mountains. The sunset from Rhue over the Summer Isles is among the Highlands' finest. Bring binoculars: otters and sea eagles are often visible from the coast.

activities.text: 20 km south of Ullapool on the A835, Corrieshalloch Gorge National Nature Reserve is the smallest of Scotland's 43 national nature reserves. The gorge is 1.5 km long, 60 meters deep, and only 10 meters wide. Its Gaelic name, Coire Shalach, means "ugly corrie." It formed 10,000 to 13,000 years ago during the melting of Quaternary glaciers. The Falls of Measach (46 meters) are crossed by a Victorian suspension bridge designed by Sir John Fowler—one of the engineers of the Forth Bridge. Cross the bridge for the best views of the falls, then access the viewpoint overlooking the chasm from the opposite bank. Most spectacular after rain.

Boat trips from Ullapool harbor allow you to reach the Summer Isles. Tanera Mòr, the largest, was the seat of an 18th-century herring fishery and now hosts a private post office issuing its own stamps. You can observe seals, dolphins, puffins, and gannets. Trips generally last 2 to 3 hours. Book your trip directly on the pontoon—places fill quickly in July-August.

days_plan.itin_title: Scottish Highlands: 15 Days of Castles, Lochs and Wild Landscapes
North Coast 500 with Orkney: Scotland's Ultimate Coastal Circuit
Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye
Scotland Road Trip: Edinburgh, Highlands & Isle of Skye

visits.text: Uppingham School, founded in 1584 by Robert Johnson - who also founded Oakham School that same year - occupies a large part of the town centre. Its limestone buildings surround courtyards and gardens. In 2022, The Times named Uppingham the best town to live in in the Midlands.

Uppingham's Goldmark gallery exhibits internationally renowned contemporary artists in an intimate town-centre space. Recognised among the Midlands' most active private galleries, it regularly presents sculpture, ceramics, and painting exhibitions. Free entry.

activities.text: Mature cheeses and artisan bread from Uppingham's Friday market can be enjoyed on the square's benches — unapologetic Anglo-Saxon simplicity. The town is dotted with antique dealers and second-hand bookshops that make wandering its streets highly engaging. Lunch at the Falcon Hotel, a sixteenth-century coaching inn.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: Ventnor cultivates its climate anomaly. The Botanic Garden, perched on the Undercliff, benefits from a microclimate roughly 5 degrees warmer than the British average. Result: palms, eucalyptus, Iberian wall lizards roaming free. The garden occupies the former site of the Royal National Hospital for Diseases of the Chest, sanatorium closed in 1964.

Below, the town retains its Victorian charm as a former spa resort. Small bay, waterfalls tumbling from the cliff, bandstand with signposts pointing distances to Tokyo or Sydney. Cool in winter, pleasant in shoulder season.

activities.text: At Ventnor Botanic Garden, explore the Victorian tunnel on a guided tour: its exit in the cliff is inaccessible. Mushrooms grow in the dark in the mushroom chamber. Hops grown on site go into the garden's beer. For lunch in the garden, head to the Plantation Room Café.

days_plan.itin_title: England's South Coast 6d: Bristol to Brighton
Isle of Wight in 4 days: From Osborne to the Chalk Cliffs

visits.text: The Victoria & Albert Museum, founded in 1852 from the profits of the 1851 Great Exhibition, is the world's largest museum of decorative arts and design. Its 145 galleries across 12.5 acres house 2.3 million objects covering 5,000 years of human creativity. Its first director Henry Cole declared he wanted to make the museum 'a schoolroom for everyone'—thus inventing the concept of the museum café to encourage visits. Queen Victoria laid the foundation stone of the current building in 1899 during her last public appearance. Don't miss the Cast Courts on the ground floor: two immense halls filled with life-size plaster casts of the world's greatest artworks, including Michelangelo's David—Queen Victoria, shocked by David's anatomy, demanded that a modesty fig leaf be placed on the statue during official visits. Also seek out the Great Bed of Ware, a 16th-century bed three metres wide mentioned by Shakespeare, and the 1937 evening coat designed by Elsa Schiaparelli with a collar in the form of a bouquet created by Jean Cocteau. Allow at least 2.5 hours.

activities.text: On Friday evenings, the V&A stays open until 10pm with special events—a pleasant way to visit the galleries without daytime crowds.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

visits.text: Follow the streets of Vindolanda before heading to its museum: the buildings take on a different sense of scale. A succession of forts stood here, and the visible masonry overlies earlier wooden structures. Look for the baths and the remains of the civilian settlement; after rain, choose shoes that can handle mud.

Mud ruins shoes, but at Vindolanda Museum it helped preserve organic objects. Waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils protected traces of Roman life that walls alone cannot reveal. Allow 1 hour for the museum after the fort, and do not confuse this visit with the Roman Army Museum, which is at a different site.

days_plan.itin_title: Hadrian’s Wall and Northumberland: 7 Days Between the Sea and the Forts

places.name: Virginia Water

visits.text: Genuine Roman columns in an English park: that's the paradox of Virginia Water. The fragments were a gift to George IV in 1816 from the ruler of Tripoli – they came from the Roman city of Leptis Magna, in present-day Libya. After eight years at the British Museum because there were no plans for them, royal architect Jeffry Wyatville arranged them into picturesque ruins in 1826. An 8.5-kilometre circuit of the lake (2 hours), a nine-metre waterfall, a Canadian totem pole. Parking £5, park free.

days_plan.itin_title: London to Bath: Surrey, Hampshire & Wiltshire in 10 Days

map_keywords: Virginia Water Lake Windsor Great Park

visits.text: The Wallace Collection is one of London's best-kept secrets: a collection of 5,500 artworks housed in Hertford House, a Georgian townhouse on Manchester Square, five minutes from Oxford Street. Admission is free. The collection, assembled by four generations of Marquesses of Hertford and by Richard Wallace in the 19th century, was bequeathed to the nation by Lady Wallace in 1897 with one condition: nothing can be added or removed. The centrepiece is Fragonard's The Swing (c.1768), considered the absolute masterpiece of Rococo. A courtier had commissioned the painting from a religious painter, who refused the overly licentious subject and suggested Fragonard—the scene shows a woman on a swing kicking off her shoe, allowing her lover to admire beneath her skirts while her husband remains in shadow. This painting relaunched Fragonard's career. Right next to it, Frans Hals' The Laughing Cavalier (1624): this portrait of an unknown 26-year-old man painted with brushstrokes of stunning modernity was purchased in 1865 by the 4th Marquess of Hertford outbidding a Rothschild. The gallery also includes works by Rembrandt, Velázquez, Rubens, Poussin and a remarkable armoury.

activities.text: Free guided tours of the Great Gallery are offered at 3pm Friday through Sunday. It's the most efficient way to understand the major works in 30 minutes.

days_plan.itin_title: London's Major Museums and Galleries

visits.text: Locals still call it “the burg”—Alfred the Great ringed it with earth ramparts in the 9th century to stop the Vikings, and the grid plan is still there. The grass banks of the Kinecroft rise 10 metres high. An entire town built in haste as a fortress, and it's survived 1,200 years of history. Free access.

The grass ramparts are worth the detour—but the ruins of the Norman castle (built around 1067 on William the Conqueror's orders, never taken by siege) are the other face of the same place. The castle was the last to fall to the Parliamentarians in 1646, after Oxford. The gardens are freely accessible. The motte still measures 13 metres high.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop

visits.text: The Naze Tower, built in 1720 by Trinity House to guide ships along this flat coast, stands 26 meters tall. A spiral staircase of 111 steps takes you through eight floors to a panoramic terrace with views of the North Sea and, on clear days, Harwich's cranes. An art gallery, museum, and café occupy the floors.

Fossil cliffs within reach—yet hardly anyone knows that The Naze's cliffs are two Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) for their marine fossils and Hamford Water's salt marshes. A marked trail runs along the cliff edge with sea views.

activities.text: Descend The Naze cliffs at Walton-on-the-Naze to search for fossils in the exposed clay layers. Visitors regularly pick up shark teeth and fossilized shells. Low tide essential—check before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Wantage is the birthplace of Alfred the Great, born in 849 according to his biographer Asser. The marble statue unveiled in 1877 by the Prince of Wales shows him standing, battle-axe and manuscript in hand—the warrior king and the learned king in one block. The market square hasn't moved since the 12th century. Free.

days_plan.itin_title: Thames & Vale of White Horse: a 6-day loop

visits.text: Scott's Grotto in Ware was dug into a chalk hillside in the 1760s by Quaker poet John Scott. Six interconnected chambers lined with shells, flints, and pieces of colored glass extend for 20 meters. Samuel Johnson described it in 1773 as a “fairy hall.” Open Saturdays and public holidays from April to September. Bring a flashlight—the site has no lighting.

Wedged between modern 1960s houses, this network of galleries is the most extensive shell grotto in the UK according to Historic England. A fragment of the Berlin Wall was embedded in the entrance hall during the 1990–91 restoration as a time marker. The site's survival came down to luck: 1960s developers planned to demolish it, but the town council blocked the scheme.

activities.text: Stroll along the River Lea in Ware to the Gazebos, a row of small Georgian pavilions lining the quay—remnants of 18th-century summerhouses, listed as Grade II*. The pedestrian quay is freely accessible.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

activities.text: Warminster is an unremarkable garrison town except for one thing: since Christmas 1964, thousands of witnesses have reported unexplained sounds and unidentified luminous objects, dubbed 'The Warminster Thing'. Journalist Arthur Shuttlewood of the Warminster Journal documented the phenomenon for years. Sceptics point to the military bases on Salisbury Plain and their nocturnal exercises. Enthusiasts still climb Cley Hill to scan the skies. No official explanation has ever been given.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days

visits.text: Warwick Castle is one of England's best-preserved medieval castles. Æthelflæd, daughter of King Alfred the Great, founded a fort here in 914 to repel the Danes. William the Conqueror converted it to a stone castle in 1068. Caesar's Tower rises to 45 metres, Guy's Tower to 39 metres. The 'Kingmaker' Richard Neville, the Earl of Warwick who played English kings according to his interests in the 15th century, held court here. Canaletto painted the castle five times—making it the English building most depicted by the Venetian painter. Allow a full half-day.

Warwick's historic centre is compact and pleasant to explore on foot from the castle. The Lord Leycester Hospital, founded in 1571 as a retirement home for wounded soldiers, is a splendid ensemble of timber-framed buildings that frames a medieval gate. The great church of St Mary contains the Beauchamp Chapel—one of England's richest perpendicular Gothic chapels.

Ten kilometres from Warwick, Kenilworth Castle clearly merits the detour—it's England's largest castle ruin and one of the most romantic. Its great Norman keep dates from the 12th century; the artificial lake that once surrounded it, now drained, was medieval England's largest artificial lake. Picture the scene: Elizabeth I stayed here for 19 days in 1575, welcomed by her favourite Robert Dudley in festivities that cost the equivalent of several million modern pounds—fireworks, banquets, jousts. Walter Scott was so taken with it that he drew his novel 'Kenilworth' (1821) from the story. Allow 1.5 hours to tour it.

Royal Leamington Spa, 5km from Warwick, is the Midlands' most elegant spa town. The 19th-century Pump Rooms are now an art gallery and cultural centre. Jephson Gardens, designed by Victorian gardener Edward Milner, are among the Midlands' best-maintained urban gardens. Regent Street and The Parade are lined with Regency facades.

activities.text: The River Avon runs alongside Warwick Castle for several kilometres—local operators offer canoe or rowboat trips from the banks of the castle park. It's the ideal angle to see Caesar's and Guy's towers reflected in the water, from the same perspective as Canaletto's 18th-century paintings. Allow 1.5 hours for a leisurely outing.

The River Leam path between Leamington Spa and Warwick (5km) follows the wooded banks between the two towns—a fine walk or cycle linking the two historic centres. Start from Jephson Gardens and follow the river up to the castle walls.

days_plan.itin_title: The Midlands and Peak District Essentials

visits.text: 79 metres deep: the bottom of Wast Water lies below sea level. It's England's deepest lake, ringed by the Screes - 550 m of scree cliffs plunging straight into black water. Scafell Pike, England's highest peak (978 m), towers at the eastern end. In 2007, Wast Water was voted 'Britain's favourite view' by ITV viewers.

activities.text: The narrow road follows the lake for 5 km to Wasdale Head. The Screes path, on the southern shore, crosses unstable ground: hiking boots are essential.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern England: 12 Days from Manchester to Newcastle

places.name: Watford

visits.text: There are no rides here: Warner Bros. Studio Tour London showcases the sets and filmmaking techniques used in the Harry Potter movies. In Leavesden, near Watford, props and animated creatures offer a behind-the-scenes look at filming. The operator gives an average visit time of 3 hours 30 minutes; advance booking is essential, and you should keep your confirmation handy on arrival.

days_plan.itin_title: Around London in 5 Days: Royal Palaces and Gardens

map_keywords: Warner Bros. Studio Tour London Leavesden

visits.text: Stone forms giant scissors inside Wells Cathedral: your eyes keep returning to the arches spanning the nave. Their shape was a response to a problem with the tower’s stability, not a decorative whim. Construction of the current cathedral began around 1175. Plan to visit in the morning and check restrictions related to services before booking; tourist access is more limited on Sundays.

An episcopal palace with swans that ring a bell: The Bishop’s Palace offers more than its medieval walls. The birds in the moat learned this trick to ask for food. The residence dates to the early 13th century, and you can visit both the palace and its gardens. Look for the bell near the gatehouse, without expecting a guaranteed demonstration, then compare the combined palace and cathedral ticket with the other options before buying admission.

Continue on foot to Vicars’ Close, where the rows of houses look like a carefully aligned stage set. Yet this medieval street is still part of cathedral life. An elevated passage allowed the vicars to reach the cathedral without getting their feet wet. Look at the chimneys and the connection to Vicars’ Hall from the public areas; not all the houses are open to visitors.

If you enjoy legends, Wookey Hole Caves offers an encounter with a witch turned to stone. This is a rock formation associated with local folklore, set among the underground chambers. Admission also includes family attractions, but this stop focuses on the caves. Book your admission and bring a warm layer; as a guide, allow for approximately 8 km and 20 minutes of round-trip driving from Wells, included in the time allocated for this visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Bristol and Somerset in 5 days, from Docks to Caves
Somerset in 4 days: Wells, Glastonbury and Cheddar

places.name: Wells Next The Sea

visits.text: Holkham Hall is one of England's great Palladian country houses, and it deserves a morning. Thomas Coke, 1st Earl of Leicester, began it in 1734—his inspiration went back to a six-year Grand Tour of Italy (1712–1718) during which he met Lord Burlington and architect William Kent, but he waited sixteen years before launching the project. Construction took 25 years and required demolishing the old village of Holkham to clear the space. Enter the Marble Hall: its ionic columns in alabaster and its 12-metre coffered ceiling are among the most imposing neoclassical interiors in the country. After the visit, walk to Holkham beach behind the estate—three kilometres of pristine sand bordered by pines, almost always deserted outside summer weekends. This is where the final scene of Shakespeare in Love (1998) was filmed.

Burnham Thorpe, six kilometres from Holkham, is a village of 144 inhabitants that has the immense merit of being the birthplace of Horatio Nelson, born in 1758 at the parsonage—the house was demolished in 1803, but a plaque marks the spot. Nelson's father, the Reverend Edmund Nelson, was rector of All Saints church for 48 years. Inside the church, the lectern, altar and rood screen were carved from timber from the frigate HMS Victory. Nelson lived here from 1786 to 1793 while waiting to be assigned to a new ship, and organised a final farewell dinner for the villagers before embarking on HMS Agamemnon.

Wells-next-the-Sea is a lively port on the north Norfolk coast, with fishing boats and colourful beach huts lined up along the sea wall. Walk along the quay in the morning as the boats return, then follow the path beside the channel for about one mile to reach the beach, which opens onto broad expanses of sand edged with pine trees. The town has fine Georgian architecture and several characterful pubs along the Quay.

Cromer, about 35 kilometres east of Wells-next-the-Sea, a 35-minute drive away, is Norfolk's iconic Victorian seaside resort, with its 1901 pier and still-active theatre at the end of the jetty - one of the few surviving “end-of-the-pier shows” in England. St Peter and St Paul's Church has the tallest church tower in Norfolk (49 metres). Cromer is also famous for its crabs, renowned throughout the country: stop at the market or a fishmonger's shop to buy some.

activities.text: Seal watching at Blakeney Point: Blakeney Point is home to England's largest grey seal colony, as well as common seals. Excursion boats departing from Morston Quay, about 10 kilometres from Wells-next-the-Sea, a 10-minute drive away, allow you to get within a few metres of them. The colony numbers up to 3,000 individuals depending on the season.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia Road Trip: Norfolk, Suffolk and Cambridge
From Cambridge to London: Eastern England in 6 days

map_keywords: Burnham Thorpe All Saints Church Nelson birthplace

visits.text: Marvel at Durdle Door, the iconic natural limestone arch that has become the symbol of the Jurassic Coast and one of England's most photographed landmarks. This spectacular geological formation, created over millions of years as the sea eroded the Portland limestone, frames turquoise waters that rival any Mediterranean cove. The dramatic cliffside setting and crystal-clear waters draw visitors year-round, though the beach is most magical outside peak summer season.

Explore Lulworth Cove, an almost perfectly circular bay that is considered one of the finest examples of coastal erosion in the world and a premier destination for geology enthusiasts. The unique formation occurred as the sea breached the harder Portland limestone and then eroded the softer rocks behind, creating this remarkable natural amphitheater. The Fossil Forest on the cliff path reveals petrified tree stumps from ancient forests that grew here 150 million years ago.

Walk the spectacular coastal path connecting Lulworth Cove to Durdle Door, one of the most scenic short hikes in all of England. The route crosses dramatic chalk cliffs with ever-changing views of the turquoise waters and rocky coastline below. This stretch of the Jurassic Coast reveals layers of geological history spanning 185 million years, visible in the multi-colored cliff faces and embedded fossils.

activities.text: Try coasteering, rock-pooling or swimming in the crystal-clear waters of this UNESCO World Heritage coastline

days_plan.itin_title: Dorset's Jurassic Coast: Prehistoric Cliffs, Castle Ruins and Dream Beaches

visits.text: From the plain, the white horse suddenly emerges from the chalk slope: 55 metres high, visible from afar. A horse probably existed here as early as the seventeenth century to commemorate Alfred the Great's victory at Edington in 878, but the current outline dates from 1778 when Lord Abingdon's steward remodelled the original. It was cemented in the 1950s and tarnishes between cleanings. Climb up to Bratton Camp above: 9.3-hectare Iron Age fort with two ditches and ramparts. View across to the Mendips on clear days. Free, parking on B3098.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days

visits.text: Westminster Abbey was built from 1245 on the orders of Henry III, who wanted to rival the great Gothic cathedrals of France. Since William the Conqueror on 25 December 1066, 40 monarchs have been crowned here - the only exceptions are Edward V, likely murdered in the Tower of London before his ceremony, and Edward VIII, who abdicated before the scheduled date. More than 3,300 people are buried here, including 30 sovereigns. Plan at least 90 minutes to see it properly, and take the audio guide - without it, you'll miss a lot.

Don't miss Poets' Corner in the south transept: Chaucer, Shakespeare (memorial), Dickens, Tennyson, Kipling are commemorated here. Dickens ended up there against his wishes - he'd requested a quiet burial in Kent. The Dean of Westminster orchestrated the move to add prestige to the place. Lord Byron was refused for his 'scandalous life' - his memorial stone wasn't laid until 1969, 145 years after his death.

The Chapter House, accessible from the cloisters, houses Britain's oldest door - dated to the 1050s through dendrochronology. The cloisters themselves are the only free access to the Abbey: if budget is tight, at least enter through there to soak up the atmosphere.

activities.text: Attend Evensong if your timing allows - the evening choral service is free and open to all. It's an experience with nothing touristy about it: you're in a working abbey, with a professional choir, in one of England's most beautiful Gothic naves. Check timings on the Abbey website before you go.

days_plan.itin_title: What to See in London: Westminster, Museums & Tower Bridge

visits.text: Fall in love with Weymouth, a traditional seaside town whose Georgian esplanade and golden sands have made it one of Britain's most popular holiday destinations for over two centuries. The colorful houses lining the harbor, their doors decorated with nautical knockers, create a quintessentially English coastal scene. The shallow, gently shelving beach and calm waters make this an ideal destination for families and swimmers of all abilities.

Stroll along Weymouth's historic harbor, where boats and yachts bob at their moorings and fresh seafood restaurants serve the day's catch. The old town's narrow streets reveal Georgian architecture and maritime heritage at every turn, from the harbor-side fish market to the Tudor-era waterfront buildings. The working harbor atmosphere, with fishermen mending nets and boats preparing to sail, connects visitors to Weymouth's enduring maritime traditions.

Walk along Chesil Beach, the remarkable 18-mile shingle bank connecting Portland to the Dorset mainland that is one of Britain's most distinctive coastal features. This vast barrier beach, accumulated over thousands of years, grades from small pebbles in the west to large cobbles in the east, a natural phenomenon that allowed local fishermen to determine their position in fog simply by the size of the stones. The Fleet lagoon behind the beach supports rare wildlife and offers peaceful walking away from the crowds.

activities.text: Sample fresh Dorset seafood, including the local specialty mackerel, at one of the harbor-side establishments

days_plan.itin_title: Dorset's Jurassic Coast: Prehistoric Cliffs, Castle Ruins and Dream Beaches

visits.text: Robin Hood's Bay, 8 kilometres south of Whitby, is one of England's most beautiful coastal villages—and the most notorious. In the 18th century, it was the Yorkshire coast's most active smuggling hub: gin, brandy, tobacco and silk arrived from the Netherlands and France, and legend has it that a bale of silk could cross the village from harbour to clifftop without ever leaving the houses, thanks to underground tunnels linking the cottages. Customs officers attempting searches sometimes had buckets of boiling water thrown at them from first-floor windows. Locals call the village 'Bay Town'. Leave your car at the top—only residents can drive down to the harbour—and plunge into the lanes on foot.

Robin Hood's Bay Museum, in an old house near the harbour, displays fossils found on local beaches, fishing gear and documents on smuggling and shipwrecks. Small and free, it gives context to a walk through the village. Half an hour suffices.

Whitby Abbey, perched on the east cliff 70 metres above the harbour, is the most photogenic Gothic ruin on England's north coast. The site has been inhabited for over 3,000 years: in 657, Hilda — an abbess of royal blood, great-niece of Northumbria's first Christian king — founded the first monastery here, which hosted the famous Synod of Whitby in 664 — the meeting that decided the English Church would follow the Roman Easter calendar rather than the Celtic one. The current Benedictine abbey dates from the 12th century, its limestone Gothic arches from the 13th. In 1890, Bram Stoker holidayed in Whitby and found in the town library the name of a 15th-century Wallachian prince nicknamed “Dracula”. The rest is literary history: published in 1897, Dracula remains the defining Gothic novel and has never been out of print. Managed by English Heritage. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

St Mary's Church, Whitby, right next to the abbey, is one of England's most unusual churches: founded in the 12th century, it was expanded over the centuries by local seafaring families who made the interior their own with private canopied pews, creating an absolutely unique, crowded wooden interior. It was in the surrounding graveyard that Stoker noted names on the tombstones — including “Swales”, the first name of Dracula's first victim in the novel.

The 199 steps leading from the old town at the foot of the cliff up to the abbey were carved into sandstone in the 17th century. In Stoker's novel, Dracula bounds up these steps in the form of a large black dog to reach the graveyard after his ship is wrecked in the harbour. The climb takes 10 minutes, with a beautiful view over Whitby's red rooftops and the Esk estuary gradually unfolding as you ascend.

The Captain Cook Memorial Museum, in Grape Lane, occupies the house of merchant John Walker where the young James Cook lived and studied navigation from 1746 to 1749, before joining the Royal Navy. It was here, late at night by candlelight, that he learned algebra, trigonometry and astronomy. The house has remained almost as it was in the 18th century — the rooms, the attic where Cook slept, original engravings from his voyages. Allow an hour.

The Dracula Experience, on Marine Parade, takes you on a staged tour of Stoker's novel through soundscapes and special effects in the cellars of an old building. The building itself supposedly has a history: one of the earliest known deeds to the property reportedly bears Isaac Newton's signature — a local anecdote that Whitby guides repeat, though it can't quite be verified. Allow 45 minutes for the tour.

The waterfalls at Hayburn Wyke, south of Whitby, fall directly onto a pebble beach surrounded by ancient woodland - one of England's very rare coastal waterfalls. Allow for a return trip during the day from Whitby to the Hayburn Wyke Inn car park by car. The access path starts at the Hayburn Wyke Inn car park and descends through the woods in 25 minutes. The pebbles on the beach sometimes contain ammonite fossils.

activities.text: The lower part of Robin Hood's Bay is worth walking all the way down to: lanes so narrow your shoulders brush the walls, cottages built one on top of another into the cliff, the tiny harbour with its cobles (traditional fishing boats). If the tide's out, the exposed rocks on the beach reveal ammonites and belemnites — with good shoes, it's free fossil hunting.

Allow for a return trip during the day by car from Whitby to the Hayburn Wyke Inn car park, followed by a hike along the coastal woodland path to the waterfalls and the beach. A 5-kilometre return walk through ancient woods, rewarded with a pebble beach that is almost always deserted. Bring waterproof shoes.

Whitby harbour at the end of the day, when the fishing boats return and gulls wheel above the quays, is a scene to rival any photo from the trip. Look for pubs and fish & chip shops on both banks of the Esk — queues outside the good places will guide you better than guidebooks.

visits.text: Whitstable is one of the most charming addresses on the Kent coast. The town owes its worldwide reputation to its native oysters, cultivated here since Roman times—in 80 AD, the Romans were already shipping them to Rome. In 1793, the Whitstable Oyster Fishery Company was established by Act of Parliament to regulate fishing, and at its peak, 60 million oysters per year made their way to London. Start at the still-active harbour, with its brightly coloured fishing boats. If you're there on a Sunday, the Harbour Market offers local crafts, ceramics, and fresh seafood. Arrive early for the best oysters.

Walking up to Tankerton brings you to Whitstable Castle, a neo-Gothic house built in 1790 for the Pearson family—despite its name, it's not a medieval castle but an elegant private residence converted into a cultural space. The gardens are free to access and worth exploring; the orangery tearoom is perfect for a break. Next door, Tankerton Slopes offer lovely views of the pebble beach and its brightly painted fishermen's huts.

Pop into the Whitstable Museum and Gallery: it houses the Invicta locomotive, one of the world's oldest, a survivor from the Crab and Winkle line—England's first passenger railway, inaugurated in 1830 between Whitstable and Canterbury. The museum also traces the history of oyster fishing and dedicates a section to Peter Cushing, the legendary horror actor who lived in Whitstable for nearly forty years.

activities.text: An oyster lunch at the harbour is the essential ritual. Whitstable produces both native oysters (available only in months with an R, from September to April) and rock oysters available year-round. Several spots line the East Quay: choose a waterfront table and order a dozen with buttered bread.

Walk along the Saxon Shore Way to Tankerton Beach: a peaceful stroll over pebbles with, at low tide, the Street—a ridge of pebbles extending several hundred metres into the sea. On certain days, you can walk knee-deep in water. Sunsets from here are among the most beautiful on Kent's north coast.

days_plan.itin_title: Southeast England & Kent Circuit: White Cliffs and Secret Gardens

visits.text: Ferry back from Stromness to Scrabster, then south along the A99 toward Wick. John O'Groats is worth stopping at for the sign and the view across to the Orkney islands you've just come from - though be clear that it is not the most northerly point of mainland Scotland (that is Dunnet Head, 20 km to the west). The most interesting stop near here is the ruin of Castle Sinclair Girnigoe, on a cliff promontory 5 km north of Wick: a 15th-century fortress that partly collapsed into the sea, its walls split by geological fault lines. Walk from the car park and allow 45 minutes.

The Whaligoe Steps, south of Wick on the A99, consist of 365 hand-cut sandstone steps descending a sheer cliff to a tiny natural harbour barely large enough for three boats. It was built in the 18th century for the herring fishery - fisherwomen carried baskets full of fish up these steps to the road above. The views from the top and bottom are extraordinary. The steps are steep and uneven; allow 30 minutes.

Wick was the herring capital of the world in the 19th century, processing millions of barrels a year for export to the Baltic states and the West Indies. The Wick Heritage Museum has one of the best collections of Victorian industrial photography in Scotland - nearly 70,000 glass plates taken by Johnston & Sons between 1863 and 1977 documenting the town, the fleet and the fishery. Entry is free and the museum is run entirely by volunteers. Allow 1 hour.

activities.text: The Flow Country, west of Wick and accessible via the A882 through Halkirk, is Europe's largest blanket bog—4,000 square kilometres of rolling peaty tundra storing more carbon per square metre than tropical rainforest. In 2023 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site—the first peatland in the world to receive this designation, recognised not just as a landscape but as a critical carbon store whose protection matters to the entire planet. The RSPB's Forsinard Flows visitor centre has a boardwalk across the bog, an observation tower and guided visits in season. A surreal, silent landscape unlike anywhere else in Great Britain. Plan a day trip from Wick to the Forsinard Flows visitor centre and back.

days_plan.itin_title: North Coast 500 with Orkney: Scotland's Ultimate Coastal Circuit

visits.text: The “Cathedral of the Moors” is St Pancras Church in Widecombe-in-the-Moor. The nickname comes from the scale of the church and its tower, striking in such a compact village. Look for carved details if the interior is open; otherwise, walking around the building and the square already gives you a sense of its proportions.

People and livestock shared the longhouses at Hound Tor Deserted Medieval Village, each occupying one end. The remains of the 13th-century houses make this shared living arrangement tangible beneath the tor’s granite outcrops. The approach crosses the moorland and includes a climb: wear sturdy shoes and abandon the walk if fog obscures landmarks.

activities.text: Climb toward Haytor along trails across the moorland before continuing toward Hound Tor and Widecombe. The granite outcrops dominate the eastern part of the park and offer views toward the Devon coast in clear weather. There is no need to climb the rocks to enjoy the scenery; stay below them if the wind picks up.

days_plan.itin_title: South Devon and Dartmoor in 5 Days, from Exeter to Plymouth

visits.text: Sober facade, explosive interior: the Double Cube Room measures 18 metres long, 9 metres wide, 9 metres high, with painted ceiling, gilding, and Van Dyck family portraits hung on the walls since 1653. The D-Day landings were planned from these State Rooms in 1944. Inigo Jones and John Webb's Palladianism perhaps reaches its English zenith here. The house still belongs to the Earls of Pembroke, the family installed by Henry VIII after the dissolution of Wilton Abbey. Open Easter to October, £20.

days_plan.itin_title: Deep Wiltshire: from Salisbury to Newbury in 7 days

visits.text: A planned town by Edward I in 1281, razed and rebuilt on a hill after a devastating 1287 storm engulfed the old town—now beneath the waves. Winchelsea is one of the best-preserved examples of medieval town planning in England: grid streets, more than 140 listed buildings. Today perhaps England's smallest town, with only a few hundred inhabitants.

St Thomas the Martyr Church, truncated by fourteenth-century French raids, was never fully rebuilt—the nave is still missing. What remains is sublime: six medieval canopied tombs including that of Admiral Gervase Alard (1312), the oldest admiral effigy in England. Spike Milligan is buried in the churchyard.

activities.text: Descend into Winchelsea's medieval cellars—an underground network of stone vaults testifying to the town's role in the wine trade in the fourteenth century, when it was one of the kingdom's principal ports. The Court Hall Museum organises guided tours by appointment in high season.

days_plan.itin_title: Kent and Sussex in 12 Days: The Weald, Coast and Cinque Ports

places.name: Winchester

visits.text: Hampton Court Palace, 20 km south-west of London on the banks of the Thames, is one of England's best-preserved palaces. Allow a day for the return trip from Winchester. Henry VIII stayed here from 1525 and housed some of his wives here. The Tudor kitchens, capable of feeding 600 people a day, have been recreated as they were in the 16th century. The French formal gardens, designed for William III in the late 17th century, contain England's best-known hedge maze. Allow at least 2½ hours.

Winchester Cathedral is the world's longest medieval cathedral: 170 metres long, built between 1079 and 1532. Inside, the Perpendicular Gothic nave impresses with its height. Jane Austen is buried in the main nave. The bones of Saxon kings of Wessex, including Cnut the Viking, rest in gilded mortuary chests on the choir gallery. Don't miss diver William Walker: between 1906 and 1911, this man worked alone underwater to shore up the foundations with 83,000 bags of concrete and 115,000 blocks – the cathedral was sinking.

In Winchester Castle's Great Hall hangs the famous Round Table. This oak disc measuring 5.5 metres in diameter and weighing 1.2 tonnes was crafted around 1290 for King Edward I, probably for a tournament celebrating his daughter's betrothal. Henry VIII had it painted in 1522 depicting King Arthur with his own features. It's not Arthur's real table – but the object itself is 700 years old.

activities.text: Walk along the River Itchen from the centre of Winchester. This crystal-clear waterway, one of England's most renowned trout rivers, flows between medieval mills. Winchester City Mill was rebuilt in 1744 on a mill site dating back to the Domesday Book (1086).

places.name: Windermere

visits.text: Welcome to the Lake District - UNESCO-listed since 2017, but this landscape has been changing people for far longer. This is where the English Romantics invented, in the 18th century, the very idea of going to the mountains for pleasure. Stop first at Ambleside to get your bearings and kit up if needed: it's the gateway to the park and outdoor shops are plentiful. Spot the Bridge House as you pass - a tiny 17th-century house perched on a bridge over Stock Ghyll, so narrow you wonder how a family could have lived there.

Dove Cottage in Grasmere is where it all began for English Romantic poetry. Wordsworth and his sister Dorothy lived here from 1799 to 1808 - eight years during which he wrote I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud, inspired by an entry in his sister's journal describing daffodils seen near Ullswater. The building had previously been an inn, the Dove and Olive, open as early as 1617 - which explains the low ceilings and thick walls. Wordsworth paid 8 pounds in annual rent and welcomed Coleridge, Walter Scott and Thomas de Quincey. Visits are guided and take place in small groups: book online in advance, as summer slots fill quickly. Plan a return drive from Windermere.

Take an hour to stroll through Grasmere: St Oswald's Church, where Wordsworth attended services every Sunday and where he is buried in the churchyard, creates a distinctive atmosphere. Nearby Grasmere lake, with its hire boats at the northern end, is a good place to unwind after visiting Dove Cottage. Plan a return drive from Windermere.

Hill Top in Near Sawrey goes far beyond memories of Peter Rabbit. Beatrix Potter bought this small farmhouse in 1905 with the proceeds from her books, then became a determined Herdwick sheep breeder and campaigner for the conservation of the Lake District. On her death in 1943, she left the National Trust 4,000 acres and 15 farms on condition that they continued to be worked using traditional methods - it is largely thanks to her that the park still looks as it does. The house has remained almost unchanged since 1943. Book your slot online in advance - it is compulsory in high season and places fill quickly. Plan a return drive from Windermere to Near Sawrey.

Hawkshead is the best-preserved medieval village in the Lake District - its cobbled lanes and whitewashed 16th-century houses have not been disfigured by modern rebuilding. The young Wordsworth studied here at the Grammar School between 1779 and 1787; his desk, carved with his name, can still be seen. Hawkshead is quieter than Windermere and deserves time to explore. Plan a return drive from Windermere.

activities.text: The walk around Loughrigg Fell from Grasmere is one of the park's most accessible: 8 km, 200 metres of elevation gain, with views of Grasmere lake and Rydal Water. Allow 2 hours 30 minutes at an easy pace. The path is waymarked and passable all year, but waterproof boots remain essential. Plan a return drive from Windermere to the starting point in Grasmere.

Grasmere Gingerbread is a unique speciality: halfway between a biscuit and a cake, spiced, and sold since 1854 in the same shop beside the church. The original recipe is kept in a safe at the local bank. Join the queue - it is worth the detour. Plan a return drive from Windermere.

The ascent of Catbells from Keswick Landing Stage or Hawse End is one of the Lake District's most popular walks: 451 metres of elevation gain, a narrow ridge with 360° views of Derwentwater, Borrowdale and the surrounding fells. Alfred Wainwright described it as “a hill for everyone”. Allow 3 hours including photo stops. You can descend on the Newlands Valley side to vary the route. Plan a return drive from Windermere to the starting point, separate from the walk.

A cruise on Lake Windermere - England's largest natural lake at 17km long - is the most contemplative way to end the day. Boats run back and forth between Ambleside, Bowness and Lakeside. Take the last departure in the evening for the light.

visits.text: It is better to set aside a full morning for Windsor Castle than to rush through its rooms. Founded in the 11th century, this royal residence combines castle defenses with state apartments that still play a role in the life of the monarchy. The contrast becomes apparent as you move from the courtyards to the interiors. The castle is closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, royal activities may affect access, and the uphill walk from town calls for good shoes.

St George’s Chapel brings a change of scale after the state apartments at Windsor Castle. This church remains an active place of worship, and services determine access, so a castle ticket does not guarantee entry at any time. Look up at the vaulting before taking in the details. The chapel normally closes to visitors at 4 p.m. and is not open for sightseeing on Sundays; check the day’s restrictions as well.

activities.text: Walk across the Thames on Windsor Bridge to reach Eton, then follow High Street toward Eton College. Simply crossing the river changes the scenery: the castle gives way to a shopping street and school buildings. The outdoor walk is worthwhile even without entering the college. To visit inside, check the available heritage tours and book separately; do not assume a working school is a monument you can enter freely.

visits.text: Wivenhoe's quayside smells of tar and fresh seaweed: crooked medieval houses lean over the Colne estuary, where sailboats and fishermen have coexisted for centuries. The village combines a former shipbuilding industry with a community of artists linked to the nearby University of Essex.

From the outside, the Nottage Maritime Museum in Wivenhoe could easily be mistaken for a shed. Inside is an eclectic collection of nautical objects linked to Captain Nottage, a Victorian officer and yachtsman. Open on weekends in summer, with free admission.

activities.text: Walk the Wivenhoe Trail for 6 km along the River Colne to Colchester's Hythe. The trail follows the riverbank with views of boats and marshes. You can return from Colchester by train to Wivenhoe station.

days_plan.itin_title: Hertfordshire and Essex in 12 Days: Castles and Coast

visits.text: Woburn Abbey was founded by Cistercian monks in 1145, dissolved by Henry VIII in 1538 and given to the Russell family, the future Dukes of Bedford, who still live there. The 1,200-hectare estate is home to nine species of deer in its deer park - the largest private enclosure in the United Kingdom. The abbey and its gardens are currently closed for renovation: check that they have reopened before setting off.

Woburn Safari Park isn't just a family attraction—it's one of England's largest drive-through wildlife parks, with lions, tigers, and rhinos observable from your car. The park, opened in 1970, also includes a walk-through area with lemurs and sea lions. If children aren't in the group, the deer park will suffice.

activities.text: You walk through Woburn village's Georgian centre, whose reconstruction after the 1724 fire created a remarkably homogeneous architectural ensemble. Independent shops and antique dealers line the cobbled streets. The Heritage Centre, housed in the former St Mary's church, is free and gives a good overview of local history.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: Woodbridge's Tide Mill still creaks beside the Deben — one of the few tide mills still in working order in England. Built in the eighteenth century on a much older mill site, it produced flour until 1957. Now restored by volunteers, it turns at high tide at weekends from May to September.

activities.text: You follow the cycle path along the Deben from Woodbridge towards Melton, with views of moored sailing boats and reed beds. Coastal Suffolk, flat and traffic-free, is best appreciated by bike. Bikes are available for hire in Woodbridge; allow two hours for a leisurely round trip.

days_plan.itin_title: East Anglia, Cambridge & Rutland: 13-Day Road Trip

visits.text: Inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1987, Blenheim Palace also impresses through its close connection to Churchill, who was born here. The state rooms convey the scale of this home of the Dukes of Marlborough. Buy a ticket that includes the palace interior and bring a payment card, as the estate is cashless.

After the palace, a simple family grave: at St Martin’s Church in Bladon, the remembrance of Winston Churchill changes scale. His grave is in the parish churchyard, outside the Blenheim estate. Make a quiet stop on your way back to Oxford; the parish asks visitors not to leave flowers or mementos on this private grave.

activities.text: If you have had your fill of indoor rooms, walk through the gardens of Blenheim Palace to the Water Terraces. Their formal layout contrasts with Capability Brown’s landscaped park: a landscape that looks natural but is the result of deliberate design. Choose a short loop on the estate map and wear shoes suitable for wet paths.

You will continue your outing in Woodstock with the Town Walk, which starts on Park Street. This town walking route covers about 1.7 km and offers a different perspective on the town beyond the entrance to Blenheim. Download the leaflet before setting out; the embroidered hangings that tell the town’s history can be viewed at the town hall by appointment only.

Oxford and Blenheim in 4 days: Colleges and Churchill

places.name: Wroxham

visits.text: Before you take out a boat, pause to understand what you're about to cross—the Norfolk Broads are nothing natural. What you see is the result of thousands of peat pits dug by hand in the Middle Ages to supply Norwich with fuel, flooded in the fourteenth century when sea levels rose. Nobody understood this until 1952, when botanist Joyce Lambert established the man-made origin of the site after systematic surveys of the banks. The result of this historical accident: 200 kilometres of navigable waterways, 63 lakes and seven rivers linked together, and a national park that shelters a quarter of the UK's rarest species—including the only British habitat of the swallowtail butterfly (Papilio machaon brittanicus).

St Helen's Church in Ranworth is nicknamed the “cathedral of the Broads”: perched on a slight rise at the edge of Ranworth Broad, its fifteenth-century tower is visible from the water several kilometres away. Climb to the top of the tower (89 steps) for the most complete view of the Broads. Inside, the church preserves one of England's finest medieval rood screens, dating from 1450, with its polychrome paintings remarkably well preserved. Ranworth Broad Nature Reserve next door has a floating centre on stilts with bird observation facilities.

The ruins of St Benet's Abbey, accessible only by boat or on foot from the bank, constitute the only Broads site visited each year by the Bishop of Norwich during a ceremony on a boat in August. Founded in 1020 by King Cnut (the same who founded Bury St Edmunds Abbey), it is the only English abbey that was never formally dissolved by Henry VIII—the Bishop of Norwich remains theoretically its abbot. An eighteenth-century windmill was added within the ruins themselves, creating a singular silhouette in the Broads landscape.

Wroxham is your base for taking to the water—it's the “capital of the Broads” and the first pleasure boat hire company opened here in the 1870s. Today, hundreds of boats are available by the day or by the week, with no locks on the route. If you have children, or even if you don't, pop into Roys of Wroxham: nicknamed “the world's largest village store”, this institution since 1895 occupies several buildings in the centre and sells pretty much everything.

activities.text: Hire a motor boat for a half-day on the Broads from Wroxham: no licence is required and a few minutes' instruction is enough. Follow the River Bure towards Horning or head upstream to Barton Broad, the second-largest lake in the Broads. The calm of the waterways—6 km/h speed limit on most stretches—is striking. In summer, book ahead.

activities.text: Yarmouth Pier extends from town over the Solent, with sailboats and ferries in view. Opened in 1876, this wooden pier offers one last stroll before the crossing to Lymington. Check its access conditions and plan your return to the terminal around the arrival time required for your ferry.

days_plan.itin_title: Isle of Wight in 4 days: From Osborne to the Chalk Cliffs

visits.text: York Minster stops you dead as you enter the city - it dominates everything. It's northern Europe's largest medieval cathedral, and its construction lasted 252 years (1220–1472). The first church on this site was built in wood in 627 for the baptism of King Edwin of Northumbria. Inside, look up: 128 medieval stained-glass windows, the UK's largest collection - including the Great East Window, with the same surface area as a tennis court. In 1984, lightning cracked the Rose Window into 40,000 pieces; signs of restoration are visible if you look closely. Climb the 275 steps of the central tower - the view over York from up there is the city's best. Allow at least 2 hours.

The Shambles is mentioned in the Domesday Book of 1086 - back then, butchers hung meat from hooks still visible on some facades. The overhanging upper storeys lean so close from one side to the other you could almost shake hands from window to window. The street is often cited as the inspiration for Diagon Alley in Harry Potter, which J.K. Rowling has never confirmed or denied. Avoid it between 11am and 4pm in summer - the flow is relentless; early morning or evening, it's a different atmosphere.

The National Railway Museum is the world's largest railway museum - and it's free. Look first for Mallard: this locomotive set the world speed record for steam in 1938, 202.8 km/h, a record that still stands. Move on to Queen Victoria's and Edward VII's royal silk-and-wood carriages - the gap between royal comfort and third-class carriages in the same era is striking. A 1960s Japanese Shinkansen sits alongside a Eurostar in the same shed: 150 years of engineering in a single glance.

York Castle Museum occupies the city's former prisons, including the one where Dick Turpin, the famous highwayman, awaited his execution in 1739. Inside, you'll find a fully reconstructed Victorian street - Kirkgate - with its shops, blacksmith and horse-drawn omnibus. This isn't a dusty museum: the reconstruction is detailed enough to make you linger. The 20th-century toy room is northern England's most nostalgic collection - allow an hour and a half.

York's Chocolate Story answers a question everyone should ask: how did a provincial Yorkshire town become the world capital of British chocolate? Terry's opened here in 1767 - the first shop was near Bootham Bar - and Rowntree's followed in 1862, inventing the KitKat, Smarties and Aero. The guided tour takes you from the ritual origins of cocoa in Central America to Yorkshire production lines, with tasting included. Book online - tickets are cheaper there and there may be a wait in high season.

activities.text: The Jorvik Viking Centre stands on the exact site of a Viking quarter excavated in the 1970s - 1,000 years of organic waste perfectly preserved in clay, including shoes, combs, food and even intestinal parasites. You board a cart that takes you down to the archaeological level, with recreated sounds and smells - yes, smells are included. Book online: without a booking, the queue can exceed an hour, for a visit lasting about 45 minutes.

York's walls are England's best-preserved: a continuous 3.4km stretch accessible free of charge, built in the 13th–14th centuries on Roman and Viking foundations. The stretch between Bootham Bar and Monk Bar is best - direct views of York Minster, gardens below, medieval lanes visible from the battlements. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the full circuit, less if you only do the northern section.

Walking ghost tours take place every evening in the lanes of the historic centre. The best-known stop is Treasurer's House, where a plumber claimed in 1953 to have seen a legion of Roman soldiers walking beneath the basement - their legs hidden halfway up, as though following a Roman road buried long ago. An archaeological investigation did indeed find Roman paving at that depth. Departures are generally at 8pm; allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

To wind down at the end of the evening, head down to the Ouse from Lendal Bridge and walk to Skeldergate Bridge - a 2km round trip along the riverbanks. The riverside pub terraces are good places for a last pint before heading back.
